summary: We study an extremal problem involving three disks inside the unit disk. Two disks are initially placed so that they are tangent to each other and internally tangent to the unit circle. A third disk of maximum possible radius is then inserted, subject to tangency with both original disks. We prove that the minimum possible sum of the areas of the three disks is 11π/18, attained when their radii are 1/2, 1/2, and 1/3. Surprisingly, the minimizing configuration does not consist of three equal disks, despite the symmetry of the problem. Three different proofs are presented, based on Descartes' circle theorem, geometric inversion, and a parametrization using tangency points.
tags: Circle packing; Descartes' circle theorem; inversion; extremal geometry; geometric optimization
title: Three Circles in a Unit Disk: Three Solutions to an Extremal Problem

summary: This dataset supports the manuscript “Assessing the Interpretability of QM/MM Interaction Energies: A Representation-Aware Diagnostic Framework,” submitted to the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling (ci-2026-038804). The numerical data describe three retrospective peptide–enzyme case studies: prolyl endopeptidase (PEP; primary nine-peptide electronic-energy analysis, 82 retained configurations), historical beta-secretase 1 (BACE1; 63 audited snapshots, 52 retained after cleaning), and reconstructed angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE; 131 valid QM/MM decompositions, with a distinct 73-configuration GIF/IP/LP core comparison). These data support question-specific representation diagnostics and descriptive configurational-contrast analysis; they do not establish universal applicability or external affinity-prediction performance. Version v4 adds recovered simulation input files, topology and parameter files, preparation and analysis scripts, and file-level provenance manifests. The input supplement contains 8,597 recovered source files, together with the unchanged earlier numerical archive and verification records (8,740 regular files in total). It includes GROMACS run inputs for PEP and BACE1, ACE OpenMM production configurations and Amber input files, Zn-model parameterisation/validation inputs, ORCA component inputs with their coordinate and point-charge dependencies, and separately identified sensitivity, matched-perturbation, and unsuccessful diagnostic branches. The earlier numerical archive is also retained as a separate top-level download for continuity. No scientific numerical results were changed. The computational representations differ among the case studies. Primary PEP uses mixed AMBER03/CHARMM27 production protocols and inherited embedding charges. Historical BACE1 uses dynamically selected gas-phase receptor clusters and is retained for representation auditing. Corrected ACE uses snapshot-specific electrostatic embedding with a documented receptor-QM definition. The three enzymes do not share a single fixed-fragment computational representation. The original structural-analysis program that produced the historical 4 Å contact subsets C–E was not recovered. Curated subset memberships and scripts reproducing the statistics from those memberships are provided. Additional historical provenance limitations, evidence levels, and relocated source paths are documented in the supplement README and manifests. MD trajectories and bulk simulation outputs are not included. File recovery and integrity checks do not imply that the full historical simulation workflow has been rerun in a fresh environment. Third-party force-field distribution files retain their original attribution and licensing terms.
title: Data for: Assessing the Interpretability of QM/MM Interaction Energies: A Representation-Aware Diagnostic Framework

summary: Flagship 55/60 Can randomized or justified quasi-experimental intervention isolate the manufacturing effect from cell-lot, material and culture confounding? CAUSAL VERIFICATION AND COUNTERFACTUAL CONTROL IN NANOROBOT-ASSISTED REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT This 777-page Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Nano Regenerative Biomanufacturing series investigates intervention-defined causal treatment contrast rather than observational association. Its scientific coupling is causal inference x microscale interventions x biological functional validation. The evidence perimeter is prospective and nonclinical, using closed in-vitro systems, organ-on-chip platforms or authorized ex-vivo material; neither clinical efficacy nor autonomous human intervention is claimed. The falsifiable question is: Can randomized or justified quasi-experimental intervention isolate the manufacturing effect from cell-lot, material and culture confounding? The proposed minimum demonstration is: Randomize tool action within balanced chip batches, retain sham and medium-only controls, and repeat on a second platform. Strong comparators include correlational predictor, nonrandomized matched cohort and randomized sham manipulation. The central competing explanation is shared medium, selection, interference or time-dependent confounding. The noncompensatory stop rule is: negative controls exhibit the claimed effect or modest unmeasured confounding reverses it. Every eligible, stopped, refused and unsuccessful experiment belongs to the full denominator. Thirty conditional mathematical plates specify different analytic roles, measurements, units and blind failure tests. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 individual research investigations. Two hundred Research Gates organize twenty causal challenge families across ten primary physical observables, each with an independently read companion, concealed intervention, matched comparator, explicit rival and refusal gate. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future experimental and evidence instruments. All are experimental plans rather than executed observations. The source Atlas and methodology ancestors provide reference architecture but do not establish the new integrated candidate. Source-supplied ancestry includes 10.5281/zenodo.23046134 and 10.5281/zenodo.23486020; source-associated external DOI candidates must be bibliographically checked before citation. summary: This repository provides the data, Python scripts, numerical outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting a methodological investigation of negative multifractal spectrum estimates in stochastic cascades and digital images. The study distinguishes formally negative annealed multifractal spectra, which can arise in stochastic cascade models, from negative finite-resolution estimates that may depend on measurement and preprocessing procedures. The repository includes: 1. Synthetic image datasets generated using hierarchical random maps (HRM), Fourier-based synthesis (FFT), midpoint displacement (MPD), and binary geometric constructions. 2. Numerical experiments investigating uniform background floors, noise, quantization, clipping, scale-window dependence, and grid-phase sensitivity. 3. Analyses of Dirichlet multiplicative cascades, including Genuine, Shuffled, and Decoy controls. 4. Multifractal estimates based on multiplier moments and Chhabra–Jensen procedures, together with whole-image bootstrap uncertainty estimates. 5. Auxiliary experiments concerning finite-ensemble histogram spectra and supersampling. 6. Scripts, CSV result tables, execution logs, and figure-reproduction materials. 7. A manuscript-to-data mapping file (MANUSCRIPT_MAP.csv), documentation, and SHA-256 checksums supporting traceability and integrity verification. The repository documents reproducibility checks, including the comparison of 180 baseline cases and the reproduction of two computational figures. These checks should not be interpreted as independent validation of every numerical experiment or as proof of universal estimator reliability. The results emphasize that formally negative multifractal spectra and negative estimates obtained from finite digital observations have distinct mathematical interpretations. In particular, negative estimated values do not imply negative Hausdorff dimensions. The dataset is independent of any specific journal submission and is intended to support transparent examination, replication, and further methodological research. summary: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis of Global Armed Violence (1989–2025): C Software, 1,000 Permutation Tests and Cartographic Projection Audit This software and reproducibility package accompanies a computational-geometric investigation of geopolitical centrality based on the Uppsala Conflict Data Program Georeferenced Event Dataset (UCDP GED), version 26.1, covering the period 1989–2025. The study introduces a dynamic application of convex hull peeling (Convex Onion) to the spatial and temporal analysis of global armed violence. The method is grounded in the affine invariance of convex-layer membership and provides a hierarchical representation of spatial depth through successive convex hulls. Unlike conventional measures of centrality based on averages, distances, or event density, this approach examines the innermost geometric structure of the global distribution of recorded conflict locations. The dataset contains 358,130 events with day-level date precision , corresponding to 54,381 distinct geographical locations . The cumulative analysis identifies 1,134 convex layers in the final configuration. Software Components The archive includes four C-based computational components: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis: Chronological construction and updating of nested convex hulls, enabling the identification and tracking of the innermost geometric core from 1989 to 2025. Monte Carlo Permutation Analysis: A reproducible experiment involving 1,000 random permutations of complete geographical coordinate pairs across fixed chronological event positions, assessing the relationship between historical event ordering and geometric-core trajectories. Interactive Geometric Visualization: Offline visualization of the evolution of the innermost core, including annual configurations and changes in its geographical position. Cartographic Projection Comparison: Comparative analysis of convex-layer structures using planar longitude–latitude coordinates and the nonlinear Mollweide equal-area projection. Principal Findings The 2025 analysis identifies an innermost geometric location in Ethiopia under the original coordinate representation, whereas the Mollweide projection produces a two-location innermost layer in Sudan. The permutation experiment demonstrates that chronological event ordering influences the historical trajectory of the geometric core, although all permutations preserve the same final spatial configuration when the complete set of locations remains unchanged. These findings illustrate the distinction between affine-invariant geometric structure and centrality that depends on nonlinear cartographic representation. Reproducibility and Scientific Scope The package contains the original C source code, Windows executables, execution scripts, input datasets, computational outputs, visualization files, and technical documentation. The archive supports independent inspection, methodological evaluation, replication, and further development of computational-geometric approaches to spatial conflict analysis. The identified geometric core should not be interpreted as the location of maximum conflict intensity, the greatest number of fatalities, or a causal centre of global geopolitical instability. It represents a mathematically defined form of spatial depth whose interpretation depends on the adopted geometrical representation. Associated Research The Cartographic Construction of Geopolitical Centrality: Affine-Invariant Convex Layers and Global Armed Violence, 1989–2025. Data Source Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP), Georeferenced Event Dataset (GED), version 26.1. The UCDP data are attributed to their original providers. Dataset licensing and software provenance are documented separately in the archive.

summary: The digitalization of banking services in Nigeria has exponentially increased the incidences of electronic fraud (e-fraud) and the regulatory responses thereto, including the freezing of customers' accounts. While banks have a statutory and contractual duty to protect the financial system from fraud under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Regulatory Framework for Bank Verification Number (BVN), and various anti-money laundering directives, this duty often collides with the customer's constitutional right to property and the contractual duty of a banker to honour its customer's mandate. This article examines the legal basis and extent of a bank's liability for wrongful freezing of a customer's account and for losses arising from e-fraud. It interrogates the tension between a bank's duty of care, duty to obey regulatory directives, and its fiduciary obligations. Using doctrinal and analytical methodologies, the paper reviews some Nigerian case laws as well as CBN's Regulation on Instant Electronic Payments, the Cybercrimes Act 2015 (as amended), and the NDIC framework. The study finds that while banks enjoy qualified immunity when acting pursuant to a valid court order or clear CBN directive, indiscriminate freezing of accounts based on mere suspicion, internal PND (Post No Debit) without due process, or failure to deploy adequate cyber security measures amount to breach of contract and negligence, attracting damages. The paper advocates for a stricter liability regime, statutory timelines for account unfreezing, and mandatory compensation for wrongful freezing.
tags: Bank Liability, Wrongful Account Freezing, E-Fraud, Post No Debit (PND), Banker-Customer Relationship, Due Process, Digital Banking.

summary: The digitalization of banking services in Nigeria has exponentially increased the incidences of electronic fraud (e-fraud) and the regulatory responses thereto, including the freezing of customers' accounts. While banks have a statutory and contractual duty to protect the financial system from fraud under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Regulatory Framework for Bank Verification Number (BVN), and various anti-money laundering directives, this duty often collides with the customer's constitutional right to property and the contractual duty of a banker to honour its customer's mandate. This article examines the legal basis and extent of a bank's liability for wrongful freezing of a customer's account and for losses arising from e-fraud. It interrogates the tension between a bank's duty of care, duty to obey regulatory directives, and its fiduciary obligations. Using doctrinal and analytical methodologies, the paper reviews some Nigerian case laws as well as CBN's Regulation on Instant Electronic Payments, the Cybercrimes Act 2015 (as amended), and the NDIC framework. The study finds that while banks enjoy qualified immunity when acting pursuant to a valid court order or clear CBN directive, indiscriminate freezing of accounts based on mere suspicion, internal PND (Post No Debit) without due process, or failure to deploy adequate cyber security measures amount to breach of contract and negligence, attracting damages. The paper advocates for a stricter liability regime, statutory timelines for account unfreezing, and mandatory compensation for wrongful freezing.

summary: This dataset accompanies Rabia Bousbia Laiche’s article Green Hydrogen as a Strategic Lever for Energy Transition in Algeria: An Energy Mix Optimization Approach Based on Linear Programming (2026). summary: The rational management of water resources and the control of hydroagricultural techniques in the Oued Souf area are complex and crucial to a harmonious and sustainable development. The Oued Souf area is presently facing the problem of upwelling from groundwater, which is harmful to cultures and homes. In order to minimize this problem, several aerated lagoon treatment plants were set up; this technique allows an efficient control of pollution due especially to the upwelling phenomenon. The aim of this study is to provide information about the efficiency and the management of an aerated lagoon treatment system at two plants of the Oued Souf area, the Hassani Abdelkrim and the Reguiba plants. The obtained results show that the removal efficiency of organic load is significant (greater than 50%), thus indicating that aerated lagoon system is well suited to arid areas. published by the   Journal of Biodiversity and Environmental Sciences | JBES
title: Treatment of domestic and agricultural water by natural lagoon system in arid areas, case of Oued Souf, Algeria

summary: Abstract This document gives a technical and functional description of Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints (ALF): a way to verify that an AI model or algorithm in production still makes the decisions that were reviewed and approved, and to stop its output from taking effect if it does not. The problem. Current AI trust mechanisms prove identity and origin, not behaviour: Model signing (OpenSSF Model Signing, led by Google, NVIDIA and HiddenLayer; NVIDIA NGC signed models) proves which file a model is. Attestation and transparency logs (for example Apple Private Cloud Compute) prove which software a server runs. Neither shows what the model actually decides. A model can be fine-tuned, quantised, wrapped in a prompt or proxy layer, or replaced behind the same name or signature, and an AI agent can act on its output before anyone notices. How it works. Fingerprint generation. A compact cryptographic fingerprint of decision behaviour is created without access to source code, model weights or training data. For machine-learning models it is built by sampling decision boundaries. For rule-based or traditional code it is built from normalised control-flow and decision structure. Sealed-probe verification. In the highest-assurance mode, the model is tested with a sealed set of inputs that the computing system cannot see in advance. Four views must match together: decision boundaries, monotonicity and consistency, constraint activation, and constraint topology. A different model wrapped to imitate the approved one cannot pass all four. Approved-fingerprint registry. Each approved model or algorithm version has a reference fingerprint that can be checked at any time. Run-time check at the point of effect. Inside a trusted execution environment (for example a confidential VM or a confidential GPU), the live fingerprint is compared with the approved one after computation finishes and before the output is used. Fail-closed enforcement. If the fingerprint does not match, approval is automatically invalidated and the output is withheld. The capability needed to act (send, pay, move, transmit) is not released. Validation receipts. Each decision produces a tamper-evident receipt anchored in a ledger, for audit and incident analysis. Where it applies. The same mechanism applies to AI agents and model-serving platforms, payment and digital-currency systems (including offline wallets), vehicles and robots, and satellites. It complements existing technology rather than replacing it: model signing and model registries (NVIDIA NGC, Google Kaggle); verifiable and confidential AI clouds (Apple Private Cloud Compute, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS, and NVIDIA, Intel and AMD confidential hardware); agent platforms (Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services); payment flows (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Ant Group); vehicle software governance under UN Regulation 156; Chinese AI platforms (Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, Tencent, Huawei, Zhipu AI). It also gives a technical signal for the EU AI Act's substantial-modification rule and for China's generative AI filing regime, both of which depend on knowing whether the deployed system is the one that was assessed. summary: This article examines a method for developing students' chemical language through digital storytelling. The proposed methodological solution involves a sequence of activities in which students not only create a digital story but also translate the content of a chemical phenomenon from its observed form into a verbal explanation, a microcosm model, and a symbolic notation. The method includes setting up a chemical situation, identifying the linguistic core of the topic, a sequential description of the process, peer review of the scenario, creation of a digital story, and reverse transformation of the information. To evaluate the results, criteria for terminological and symbolic accuracy, understanding of the meaning of chemical notation, logical explanation, and coherence of chemical language are identified. The proposed approach can be used in studying exchange reactions, electrolytic dissociation, oxidation-reduction, and organic reactions.

summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript "Right Ventricular Function and the Mechanical Power–Mortality Gradient During Invasive Ventilation: A Candidate Echo-Informed Ventilator Tolerance Phenotype." Contents: SQL extraction queries (Charlson comorbidity index; plateau-pressure–based "strict" mechanical power), Python analysis code (primary logistic models with stratum-specific estimates and multiplicative interaction; adjustment ladder; RERI; RV-stratified restricted cubic splines; simulation-based power analysis; main-effects-versus-interaction decomposition), and aggregate-level derived results. No patient-level data are included; source data (MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-ECHO, and the hour-resolution respiratory-support dataset) are available to credentialed users via PhysioNet. Version v2026-11 (Revision 1): this version accompanies the first revision of the manuscript submitted to BMC Pulmonary Medicine. It retains the original v2026-08 code and aggregate outputs unchanged (code/, data_aggregate/, README_v2026-08.md) and adds revision_2026-11/, containing hourly respiratory-support and treatment extraction scripts; the frozen primary model (pre-echo SOFA and vasopressor use in the 24 h before echocardiography, with the original model retained as a sensitivity analysis); prespecified sensitivity analyses; RV-dysfunction text-to-category mapping (aggregate counts only); risk-scale RERI with bootstrap CIs; simulation-based power; figure and table code; aggregate outputs; and FROZEN_SPEC_and_AUDIT.md documenting frozen variable definitions and timing audits. No patient-level data are included. Final version (2026-11-07): updates the earlier v2026-11 upload. An independent implementation rebuilt all 1,903 analytic stays from source data and reproduced the exposure within the specified tolerance, RV grades and mortality outcomes under the calendar-day rule (code and aggregate results in revision_2026-11/independent_validation/). Revised analyses now use age at hospital admission rather than MIMIC-IV anchor age (417 ages changed; 00_age_at_admission.py); exposure-hour counts and recomputation checks use invasive-ventilation hours only; and 28-day mortality is explicitly defined in calendar days. All revised outputs were regenerated. No patient-level data are included. Clean-copy verification on macOS (2026-11-07): the age-corrected package was extracted into an empty local directory, supplied only with the two authorised local cohort inputs, and rerun through scripts 00, 01, 02, 04, 07, 08, 09, 10 (500 simulations for each of 1.20, 1.25 and 1.30), 11 and 12. All hourly and treatment intermediates were re-extracted from source. The comparator reported "11/11 files match." with Python 3.9.6, NumPy 2.0.2, pandas 2.3.3 and matplotlib 3.9.4. The primary interaction was OR 1.14 (95% CI 0.93–1.40), P=0.221. README run commands and REPRODUCTION_LOG.md document the procedure and scope; this analysis rerun is distinct from source reconstruction and does not constitute independent confirmation by the cohort-building author. The deposit remains a draft pending final author approval.

summary: Analysis package for a study of copy-specific assignment at the two 23S rRNA copies of Helicobacter pylori . The package contains the seventeen supplementary tables, the analysis and figure code, the recorded software versions, the reconstruction log for the long-read alignments, and a per-read phase-evidence table. What is reproducible. The six-criterion classification of 103 matched isolates is re-runnable and every verdict was re-derived from the counts with zero mismatches. The reference metadata for all cited works is captured from Europe PMC and every DOI was verified against its record. The figures are generated by script and each passes a programmatic overlap, clipping and text-on-line audit before export. The short-read counts at the two A2143 coordinates are reproduced from the archived alignment, whose header records the exact command and tool versions. What is not. The original NCBI query string and its date were not retained, so the cohort cannot be rebuilt verbatim; per-accession inclusion flags are given instead. The barrnap installation originally used on the analysis machine is missing a Perl module and does not run; the rRNA copy numbers were therefore archived values in earlier versions and are re-derived with barrnap 1.10.5 in this version. The original parameter sets for two of the three long-read procedures were not retained; those procedures were re-run and both original and re-run values are reported side by side and never pooled. One cell of the long-read table reproduces exactly; the others do not, and this is stated in the manuscript. Changes in version 4. The package matches the manuscript. All thirteen supplementary tables are present, including Supplementary Tables S12 and S13, which were absent from the previous version, and Supplementary Table S1 now carries the genome length and assembly level of all 1,483 retained genomes rather than leaving those columns empty. A new Supplementary Table S1b lists the seven excluded genomes that could be recovered from local storage, with their lengths; the genome-length window is 1.5 to 1.7 Mb and this version states the evidence that fixes its bounds. Three new scripts are included: the marker-control experiment (scripts 26 and 27), in which the single copy-differentiating base of the isolate was set to A in both copies, to C in both, to T in both, and exchanged between them, with the reads realigned to each control; and the structural diagnostic of the two 26695 23S copies (script 28), which reports that copy 1 contains no ambiguous base while copy 2 contains one N at genome position 1,475,696. The four control reference sequences are deposited under results/marker_control/. Changes in version 6. This version restores the complete file set. The previous version was published from an incomplete upload, so most of the figures, several of the supplementary tables and part of the analysis code were missing from that record. Zenodo caps a record at 100 files and this package has 134, so the package is now deposited as a single archive, hp23s_copy_assignment_package.zip , which holds every file at the path it occupies in the source repository; this README, the SHA-256 manifest and the archive of rRNA calls and copy sequences are additionally placed loose in the record. From version 10 the manuscript itself is not deposited, in the archive or loose. Every member of the archive is listed in SHA256SUMS.txt with its SHA-256, and that manifest is regenerated here, which corrects the entry for this README (the previous manifest had been computed before the last edit of the file). DOI.txt now lists the version DOIs, and the data-availability sentence in the manuscript names the concept DOI rather than one version, so that it cannot point at a superseded record. Changes in version 7. This version is a manuscript round: the text is rebuilt from the same locked data by the same script, and no reported value changes. Three defects in the supplementary apparatus are correcte

summary: This repository provides the data, Python scripts, numerical outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting a methodological investigation of negative multifractal spectrum estimates in stochastic cascades and digital images. The study distinguishes formally negative annealed multifractal spectra, which can arise in stochastic cascade models, from negative finite-resolution estimates that may depend on measurement and preprocessing procedures. The repository includes: 1. Synthetic image datasets generated using hierarchical random maps (HRM), Fourier-based synthesis (FFT), midpoint displacement (MPD), and binary geometric constructions. 2. Numerical experiments investigating uniform background floors, noise, quantization, clipping, scale-window dependence, and grid-phase sensitivity. 3. Analyses of Dirichlet multiplicative cascades, including Genuine, Shuffled, and Decoy controls. 4. Multifractal estimates based on multiplier moments and Chhabra–Jensen procedures, together with whole-image bootstrap uncertainty estimates. 5. Auxiliary experiments concerning finite-ensemble histogram spectra and supersampling. 6. Scripts, CSV result tables, execution logs, and figure-reproduction materials. 7. A manuscript-to-data mapping file (MANUSCRIPT_MAP.csv), documentation, and SHA-256 checksums supporting traceability and integrity verification. The repository documents reproducibility checks, including the comparison of 180 baseline cases and the reproduction of two computational figures. These checks should not be interpreted as independent validation of every numerical experiment or as proof of universal estimator reliability. The results emphasize that formally negative multifractal spectra and negative estimates obtained from finite digital observations have distinct mathematical interpretations. In particular, negative estimated values do not imply negative Hausdorff dimensions. The dataset is independent of any specific journal submission and is intended to support transparent examination, replication, and further methodological research. summary: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis of Global Armed Violence (1989–2025): C Software, 1,000 Permutation Tests and Cartographic Projection Audit This software and reproducibility package accompanies a computational-geometric investigation of geopolitical centrality based on the Uppsala Conflict Data Program Georeferenced Event Dataset (UCDP GED), version 26.1, covering the period 1989–2025. The study introduces a dynamic application of convex hull peeling (Convex Onion) to the spatial and temporal analysis of global armed violence. The method is grounded in the affine invariance of convex-layer membership and provides a hierarchical representation of spatial depth through successive convex hulls. Unlike conventional measures of centrality based on averages, distances, or event density, this approach examines the innermost geometric structure of the global distribution of recorded conflict locations. The dataset contains 358,130 events with day-level date precision , corresponding to 54,381 distinct geographical locations . The cumulative analysis identifies 1,134 convex layers in the final configuration. Software Components The archive includes four C-based computational components: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis: Chronological construction and updating of nested convex hulls, enabling the identification and tracking of the innermost geometric core from 1989 to 2025. Monte Carlo Permutation Analysis: A reproducible experiment involving 1,000 random permutations of complete geographical coordinate pairs across fixed chronological event positions, assessing the relationship between historical event ordering and geometric-core trajectories. Interactive Geometric Visualization: Offline visualization of the evolution of the innermost core, including annual configurations and changes in its geographical position. Cartographic Projection Comparison: Comparative analysis of convex-layer structures using planar longitude–latitude coordinates and the nonlinear Mollweide equal-area projection. Principal Findings The 2025 analysis identifies an innermost geometric location in Ethiopia under the original coordinate representation, whereas the Mollweide projection produces a two-location innermost layer in Sudan. The permutation experiment demonstrates that chronological event ordering influences the historical trajectory of the geometric core, although all permutations preserve the same final spatial configuration when the complete set of locations remains unchanged. These findings illustrate the distinction between affine-invariant geometric structure and centrality that depends on nonlinear cartographic representation. Reproducibility and Scientific Scope The package contains the original C source code, Windows executables, execution scripts, input datasets, computational outputs, visualization files, and technical documentation. The archive supports independent inspection, methodological evaluation, replication, and further development of computational-geometric approaches to spatial conflict analysis. The identified geometric core should not be interpreted as the location of maximum conflict intensity, the greatest number of fatalities, or a causal centre of global geopolitical instability. It represents a mathematically defined form of spatial depth whose interpretation depends on the adopted geometrical representation. Associated Research The Cartographic Construction of Geopolitical Centrality: Affine-Invariant Convex Layers and Global Armed Violence, 1989–2025. Data Source Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP), Georeferenced Event Dataset (GED), version 26.1. The UCDP data are attributed to their original providers. Dataset licensing and software provenance are documented separately in the archive.

summary: The digitalization of banking services in Nigeria has exponentially increased the incidences of electronic fraud (e-fraud) and the regulatory responses thereto, including the freezing of customers' accounts. While banks have a statutory and contractual duty to protect the financial system from fraud under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Regulatory Framework for Bank Verification Number (BVN), and various anti-money laundering directives, this duty often collides with the customer's constitutional right to property and the contractual duty of a banker to honour its customer's mandate. This article examines the legal basis and extent of a bank's liability for wrongful freezing of a customer's account and for losses arising from e-fraud. It interrogates the tension between a bank's duty of care, duty to obey regulatory directives, and its fiduciary obligations. Using doctrinal and analytical methodologies, the paper reviews some Nigerian case laws as well as CBN's Regulation on Instant Electronic Payments, the Cybercrimes Act 2015 (as amended), and the NDIC framework. The study finds that while banks enjoy qualified immunity when acting pursuant to a valid court order or clear CBN directive, indiscriminate freezing of accounts based on mere suspicion, internal PND (Post No Debit) without due process, or failure to deploy adequate cyber security measures amount to breach of contract and negligence, attracting damages. The paper advocates for a stricter liability regime, statutory timelines for account unfreezing, and mandatory compensation for wrongful freezing.

summary: Abstract This document gives a technical and functional description of Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints (ALF): a way to verify that an AI model or algorithm in production still makes the decisions that were reviewed and approved, and to stop its output from taking effect if it does not. The problem. Current AI trust mechanisms prove identity and origin, not behaviour: Model signing (OpenSSF Model Signing, led by Google, NVIDIA and HiddenLayer; NVIDIA NGC signed models) proves which file a model is. Attestation and transparency logs (for example Apple Private Cloud Compute) prove which software a server runs. Neither shows what the model actually decides. A model can be fine-tuned, quantised, wrapped in a prompt or proxy layer, or replaced behind the same name or signature, and an AI agent can act on its output before anyone notices. How it works. Fingerprint generation. A compact cryptographic fingerprint of decision behaviour is created without access to source code, model weights or training data. For machine-learning models it is built by sampling decision boundaries. For rule-based or traditional code it is built from normalised control-flow and decision structure. Sealed-probe verification. In the highest-assurance mode, the model is tested with a sealed set of inputs that the computing system cannot see in advance. Four views must match together: decision boundaries, monotonicity and consistency, constraint activation, and constraint topology. A different model wrapped to imitate the approved one cannot pass all four. Approved-fingerprint registry. Each approved model or algorithm version has a reference fingerprint that can be checked at any time. Run-time check at the point of effect. Inside a trusted execution environment (for example a confidential VM or a confidential GPU), the live fingerprint is compared with the approved one after computation finishes and before the output is used. Fail-closed enforcement. If the fingerprint does not match, approval is automatically invalidated and the output is withheld. The capability needed to act (send, pay, move, transmit) is not released. Validation receipts. Each decision produces a tamper-evident receipt anchored in a ledger, for audit and incident analysis. Where it applies. The same mechanism applies to AI agents and model-serving platforms, payment and digital-currency systems (including offline wallets), vehicles and robots, and satellites. It complements existing technology rather than replacing it: model signing and model registries (NVIDIA NGC, Google Kaggle); verifiable and confidential AI clouds (Apple Private Cloud Compute, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS, and NVIDIA, Intel and AMD confidential hardware); agent platforms (Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services); payment flows (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Ant Group); vehicle software governance under UN Regulation 156; Chinese AI platforms (Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, Tencent, Huawei, Zhipu AI). It also gives a technical signal for the EU AI Act's substantial-modification rule and for China's generative AI filing regime, both of which depend on knowing whether the deployed system is the one that was assessed. The related application PCT/IB2026/055615 (filed 4 June 2026, publicly disclosed 16 July 2026) claims priority from it. Author: Sangam Das. summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript "Right Ventricular Function and the Mechanical Power–Mortality Gradient During Invasive Ventilation: A Candidate Echo-Informed Ventilator Tolerance Phenotype." Contents: SQL extraction queries (Charlson comorbidity index; plateau-pressure–based "strict" mechanical power), Python analysis code (primary logistic models with stratum-specific estimates and multiplicative interaction; adjustment ladder; RERI; RV-stratified restricted cubic splines; simulation-based power analysis; main-effects-versus-interaction decomposition), and aggregate-level derived results. No patient-level data are included; source data (MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-ECHO, and the hour-resolution respiratory-support dataset) are available to credentialed users via PhysioNet. Version v2026-11 (Revision 1): this version accompanies the first revision of the manuscript submitted to BMC Pulmonary Medicine. It retains the original v2026-08 code and aggregate outputs unchanged (code/, data_aggregate/, README_v2026-08.md) and adds revision_2026-11/, containing hourly respiratory-support and treatment extraction scripts; the frozen primary model (pre-echo SOFA and vasopressor use in the 24 h before echocardiography, with the original model retained as a sensitivity analysis); prespecified sensitivity analyses; RV-dysfunction text-to-category mapping (aggregate counts only); risk-scale RERI with bootstrap CIs; simulation-based power; figure and table code; aggregate outputs; and FROZEN_SPEC_and_AUDIT.md documenting frozen variable definitions and timing audits. No patient-level data are included. Final version (2026-11-07): updates the earlier v2026-11 upload. An independent implementation rebuilt all 1,903 analytic stays from source data and reproduced the exposure within the specified tolerance, RV grades and mortality outcomes under the calendar-day rule (code and aggregate results in revision_2026-11/independent_validation/). Revised analyses now use age at hospital admission rather than MIMIC-IV anchor age (417 ages changed; 00_age_at_admission.py); exposure-hour counts and recomputation checks use invasive-ventilation hours only; and 28-day mortality is explicitly defined in calendar days. All revised outputs were regenerated. No patient-level data are included. Clean-copy verification on macOS (2026-11-07): the age-corrected package was extracted into an empty local directory, supplied only with the two authorised local cohort inputs, and rerun through scripts 00, 01, 02, 04, 07, 08, 09, 10 (500 simulations for each of 1.20, 1.25 and 1.30), 11 and 12. All hourly and treatment intermediates were re-extracted from source. The comparator reported "11/11 files match." with Python 3.9.6, NumPy 2.0.2, pandas 2.3.3 and matplotlib 3.9.4. The primary interaction was OR 1.14 (95% CI 0.93–1.40), P=0.221. README run commands and REPRODUCTION_LOG.md document the procedure and scope; this analysis rerun is distinct from source reconstruction and does not constitute independent confirmation by the cohort-building author. The deposit remains a draft pending final author approval.

summary: Vacuum is an absolutely static reference system. When light propagates in a vacuum, it moves in an absolutely static reference system. The propagation speed of light in a medium is a constant, which has nothing to do with the motion state of the light source, the observer or the receiver. When light propagates in a medium, it is dragged by the inertia of the medium. While light propagates in a vacuum, the vacuum is absolutely static, which cannot drag the light to move, and the speed, position, and direction of light in a vacuum are fixed. Based on this theory, a light interference experiment can be performed as proof, using a Michelson interferometer. The principle of the experiment is to split the laser into two beams of light at a half-reflecting mirror,one of which passes through a vacuum quartz tube and reaches the Mirror M1,The light reflects back from M1,Passing through a vacuum quartz tube,Project onto the screen through a half mirror; The other beam of light does not pass through the vacuum quartz tube,reaches the Mirror M2,The light reflects back from M2,Project onto the screen through a half mirror.however, both of the beams converge on the screen, forming interference fringes.Because the speed, position, and direction of light in a vacuum are fixed and the absolute motion of the earth will drive the vacuum quartz tube to move,when the absolute direction of the earth's motion and the direction of light propagation are parallel to each other,light will have an extra optical path in the tube; when they are perpendicular to each other, light will not have the extra optical path in the tube, so after the instrument has turned 90 degrees, the interference fringes will move. The key to this experiment is to create a vacuum. The structure of the experiment is simple that I hope someone could make an experimental verification. According to this theory, it can be concluded that the essence of Fizeau experiment , sagnac effect and Hoek experiment is the same. The reverse process of Fizeau experiment is sagnac effect, vice versa. According to this theory, the Fizeau experiment has a calculated result of movement at 0.236 fringes and a measured value at 0.23 fringes; in the case of Ruyong Wang's experiment "Generalized Sagnac Effect", the moving phase difference has a calculated result at 0.000251 and measured value at 0.000246 in the experiment. Obviously, this theory is more consistent with the experimental measurement results and the theoretical explanation is more real and natural. The sagnac effect, Mach-Zehnder interferometer and Michelson interferometer can all be used to conduct experiments based on this principle to verify whether there is an absolutely stationary reference system. Among them, the sagnac effect has the highest accuracy, the Mach-Zehnder interferometer the second and the Michelson interferometer the lowest. If Michelson and Morley had used a 11m-long vacuum quartz tube for the experiment, they might have observed a movement of 0.373 interference fringesand there might have no so-called "dark clouds". This experiment is actually to measure the sagnac effect of the Earth's rotation by using a Michelson interferometer.

title: A HypotheticalExperimental Approach to Prove the Existence of an AbsolutelyStationary Reference Frame by Using the Michelson Interferometer

summary: Objective. To assess cardiovascular functional reserve in men and identify the major phenotypes of exercise intolerance based on a comprehensive evaluation of clinical and instrumental parameters. Materials and Methods. At the first stage, 400 men without a previously established diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) were examined. One hundred participants with relevant symptoms, cardiovascular risk factors, and/or potential indicators of reduced functional reserve were selected for an in-depth assessment. The protocol included clinical evaluation, the six-minute walk test, exercise stress echocardiography, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing when corresponding data were available. Parameters of left ventricular diastolic function and global longitudinal strain, right ventricular function, chronotropic response, and gas exchange were analyzed. Functional stratification was performed according to predefined pathophysiological criteria. Results. Five functional phenotypes were identified: preserved functional reserve (21%), diastolic (17%), impaired right ventricular–pulmonary arterial coupling (15%), chronotropic (14%), and peripheral (33%). The phenotypes differed in exercise tolerance, changes in E/e′, TAPSE/SPAP ratios, heart rate response, and peak oxygen uptake. The lowest Peak VO₂ values were observed in the peripheral phenotype, whereas the most pronounced increase in E/e′ during exercise was observed in the diastolic phenotype. Conclusion. Comprehensive exercise-based assessment makes it possible to characterize the heterogeneity of functional limitations in the examined men and distinguish phenotypes associated with different presumed pathophysiological mechanisms. Further studies are required to establish the diagnostic and prognostic value of the proposed stratification approach.

summary: Biometric authentication has become a primary mechanism for accessing critical systems, from corporate facilities and banking applications to healthcare records and smart home devices. The term bio-key encompas ses both the use of physiological and behavioural traits as authentication keys and the hardware security tokens (FIDO2 keys) that integrate biometric sensors. Despite widespread adoption, there is no formal ontology that in tegrates the full bio-key authentication chain, namely enrollment, biometric capture, template storage, matching, decision, and access grant, with security assurance levels, privacy requirements, and governance mechanisms. This gap produces semantic interoperability failures, inconsistent security assessments, and weak auditability, especially when biometric templates are compromised or when authentication decisions are contested. The critical asymmetry is that biometric traits are irrevocable: unlike passwords, a com promised fingerprint or iris pattern cannot be reissued. Existing ontologies focus on biometric modalities in isolation or on hardware tokens, but none formally models the complete chain as a data governance and privacy problem. This doctoral project proposes two complementary contributions: (i) a formal ontology, built with the OntoView method, that describes bio-key authentication chains, their security levels, privacy constraints, and governance gates, serving as an instrument for interoperability, risk assessment, and regulatory compliance; and (ii) a verification method, based on the on tology, that specifies and evaluates biometric gates and audit requirements, with direct impact on privacy protection and social well-being. For high value targets, the ontology distinguishes single-party authentication from quorum-based authentication (M-of-N), in which M co-present custodians must each authenticate with their own bio-key and the access secret is split among N parties. The ontology and method will be validated by encoding reported cases, by expert evaluation, and by an empirical study on a si mulated multi-modal biometric testbed with scripted spoofing, replay, and collusion scenarios.

summary: Vacuum is an absolutely static reference system. When light propagates in a vacuum, it moves in an absolutely static reference system. The propagation speed of light in a medium is a constant, which has nothing to do with the motion state of the light source, the observer or the receiver. When light propagates in a medium, it is dragged by the inertia of the medium. While light propagates in a vacuum, the vacuum is absolutely static, which cannot drag the light to move, and the speed, position, and direction of light in a vacuum are fixed. Based on this theory, a light interference experiment can be performed as proof, using a sagnac effect. The principle of the experiment is to split the laser into two beams of light at a half-reflecting mirror, one of which passes through a vacuum quartz tube and reaches the screen, the other passes through a vacuum quartz tube from the other directionand and reaches the screen; however, both of the beams converge on the screen, forming interference fringes. Because the speed, position, and direction of light in a vacuum are fixed and the absolute motion of the earth will drive the vacuum quartz tube to move,when the absolute direction of the earth's motion and the direction of light propagation are parallel to each other,light will have an extra optical path in the tube; when they are perpendicular to each other, light will not have the extra optical path in the tube, so after the instrument has turned 90 degrees, the interference fringes will move. The key to this experiment is to create a vacuum. The structure of the experiment is simple that I hope someone could make an experimental verification. According to this theory, it can be concluded that the essence of Fizeau experiment , sagnac effect and Hoek experiment is the same. The reverse process of Fizeau experiment is sagnac effect, vice versa. According to this theory, the Fizeau experiment has a calculated result of movement at 0.236 fringes and a measured value at 0.23 fringes; in the case of Ruyong Wang's experiment "Generalized Sagnac Effect", the moving phase difference has a calculated result at 0.000251 and measured value at 0.000246 in the experiment. Obviously, this theory is more consistent with the experimental measurement results and the theoretical explanation is more real and natural. The sagnac effect, Mach-Zehnder interferometer and Michelson interferometer can all be used to conduct experiments based on this principle to verify whether there is an absolutely stationary reference system. Among them, the sagnac effect has the highest accuracy, the Mach-Zehnder interferometer the second and the Michelson interferometer the lowest. If Michelson and Morley had used a 11m-long vacuum quartz tube for the experiment, they might have observed a movement of 0.373 interference fringes and there might have no so-called "dark clouds". This experiment is actually using the Sagnac effect to measure the Earth's rotation.

summary: Executable analysis pipeline (Jupyter notebook for Kaggle) and complete results for a study on spectroscopic screening of food adulteration with a stated risk of false accusation. Seven chemometric and deep-learning classifiers (PLS-DA, SVM, random forest, ROCKET, 1D-CNN and a multitask 1D-CNN with and without Beer-Lambert mixup) are compared under grouped, repeated cross-validation. Their out-of-fold scores feed three conformal layers: (i) class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal triage into PASS, FLAG and REFER decisions, with an ablation against marginal calibration and an analysis of calibration size and deployment batch shift; (ii) cross-conformal detection of adulterants absent from training (DD-SIMCA, leave-one-adulterant-out, network embeddings) with Benjamini-Hochberg batch screening; and (iii) a leave-level-out audit for level-batch confounding whose threshold is calibrated by a semi-synthetic Beer-Lambert simulation built from real ATR-FTIR spectra. Four public datasets are analysed (NIR hyperspectral imaging of extra-virgin olive oil; ATR-FTIR of turmeric with wheat flour; MIR of strawberry purée; ATR-FTIR of edible oils); they are not redistributed here (see README for sources and licences). The archive contains the notebook with the outputs of the run reported in the article, all result tables (CSV), figures (PNG), a results summary, run logs and environment information.

summary: The FBT spectral-capacity action is the heat trace of one specified geometric Dirac operator at fixed spectral resolution. This paper states its domain and trace hypotheses, exact first and second variations, stationarity tests, coupled relative-torus 4 + 2 expression, and complete finite-computation requirements. The current application uses the embeddingto-operator map already supplied by DCQ6 and FBT10D on the closed coherent product. No second source map is required. The degree-24 regular magnetic realization, its singular-end analysis and the separate torus numerical benchmark are removed from the main development. Their removal leaves the functional and the relative-torus geometry intact. The global line-extension obstruction is retained to explain this separation. The inherited twist, its closed domain and all metric, spin and connection variations are used together. Exact fibre integration preserves the full heat trace; the four-dimensional quadratic action and normal stability certificates are cited from FBT10D with their original scope. General spectral error bounds retain feedback through omitted modes and distinguish affine connection tests from nonlinear geometric families. A final ledger separates established results from resolution selection, balance-layer selection, full nonlinear control and real-time interpretation. This revision introduces no new numerical sign certificate or physical mass prediction.
title: FBT10A: The Spectral–Capacity Action of the Fracture–Berry–Tension Framework

summary: Description This dataset provides harmonised administrative and surveillance health data describing the epidemiology and health system burden of varicella (ICD-10: B01) and herpes zoster (ICD-10: B02) in Bulgaria during the period 2023–2025 . The analysed time window corresponds to the post-COVID-19 period and precedes the introduction of mandatory varicella vaccination (2026) , providing an important baseline for evaluating vaccination policies and monitoring changes in disease epidemiology. The dataset integrates aggregated information from several national administrative and surveillance systems: 1. National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) – hospital reimbursement through clinical pathways. 2. National Health Information System (NHIS) – national digital health infrastructure containing information on hospitalisations, outpatient medical examinations, and vaccination administration. 3. National Social Security Institute (NSSI) – sick leave records, sick leave duration, and compensation payments. 4. National Statistical Institute (NSI) – population denominators used for epidemiological rate calculations. National infectious disease surveillance system – mandatory reporting of infectious diseases according to Bulgarian public health legislation. All datasets are aggregated administrative records and contain no personally identifiable information . Data are aggregated at the regional (oblast) level and reported at monthly resolution , except for population denominators, which are annual. Regional names have been standardised to English transliterations , while the original Bulgarian names are preserved. All financial variables in this dataset are reported in Bulgarian lev (BGN) , which was the official currency of Bulgaria during the study period 2023–2025 . Bulgaria adopted the euro (EUR) in 2026 . However, the Bulgarian lev had long operated under a currency board arrangement with a fixed exchange rate to the euro . The official fixed exchange rate was: 1 EUR = 1.95583 BGN This exchange rate remained unchanged throughout the study period and can be used to convert financial variables in this dataset to euros for international comparison. Case Definition and Surveillance Classification Case definitions follow Ordinance No. 21 of 18 July 2005 on the registration, notification and reporting of infectious diseases , issued by the Bulgarian Ministry of Health. Clinical criteria A person presenting with: acute onset fever moderately impaired general condition polymorphic pruritic rash consisting of macules, papules, vesicles and crusts Laboratory criteria Laboratory confirmation may include: detection of varicella-zoster virus antigen detection of virus-specific antibodies viral isolation detection of viral nucleic acid Epidemiological criteria person-to-person transmission exposure to a common source of infection Case classification Classification Definition Possible case Meets clinical criteria Probable case Meets clinical criteria and has an epidemiological link Confirmed case Meets clinical and laboratory criteria During outbreaks, a case meeting clinical criteria and having an epidemiological link may also be classified as confirmed. Diagnoses included in the dataset The dataset contains healthcare utilisation and surveillance data related to the following ICD-10 diagnoses : Varicella (B01) ICD-10 code Description B01.0 Varicella meningitis B01.2 Varicella pneumonia B01.8 Varicella with other complications B01.9 Varicella without complications Herpes zoster (B02) ICD-10 code Description B02.0 Zoster encephalitis B02.1 Zoster meningitis B02.2 Zoster with nervous system complications B02.7 Disseminated herpes zoster B02.8 Zoster with other complications B02.9 Herpes zoster without complications Clinical Pathways (NHIF) Hospital care in Bulgaria is reimbursed through clinical pathways  defined by the National Health Insurance Fund. The dataset includes the following pathways: 1. KP104 -

Known regressions and limits (from RESULTS_v105final.md ). Paired Monte Carlo with bootstrap coefficients gives planted high over medium BYI 0.889 (WEAK). The dHT of suppressed trees still rises with stand density at fixed share in 22,951 of 25,200 evaluations. HiGy.R (the FVS-HI R mirror at the top level) was not updated and still mirrors the v104 engine; the Python engine is the engine of record. The frames AK_SURV.csv and AK_PLT_GEO.csv now carry the C2-P0 BYI read by the engine (only the BYI column changed; deposit identifiers kept); AK_HCB.csv , the column dictionary and BYI_all.tif still describe the earlier

summary: The study aimed to optimize preoperative modeling and the individualized selection of surgical treatment for genital prolapse in women of childbearing age. Materials and methods: A retrospective-prospective descriptive comparative analysis of clinical and functional data from 85 fertile women (Group 1: n=45 with connective tissue dysplasia markers; Group 2: n=40 without manifest CTD) was conducted. Anatomical defects were quantified using the international POP-Q system, levator muscle tone was evaluated via perineometry and 3D/4D pelvic floor ultrasound, and systemic connective tissue dysplasia was assessed using clinical risk scores. Results: Standardized objective quantification using POP-Q, integration of obstetric history, levator defect scoring, and metabolic/CTD markers allowed for the development of a predictive mathematical risk matrix. Custom laparoscopic reconstructive techniques (pectopexy and laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy with autologous/mesh organ-preserving repair) yielded 95.6% 2-year anatomical success compared to 77.5% in standard vaginal repair. Conclusion: Personalized surgical strategies and preoperative modeling based on multiple functional, anatomic, and connective tissue parameters significantly improve long-term outcomes, preserve reproductive capacity, and minimize recurrence in fertile women with pelvic floor dysplasia
tags: pelvic organ prolapse, childbearing age, surgical reconstruction, outcome prediction, pelvic floor, personalized medicine, connective tissue dysplasia, recurrence, operative gynecology
title: OPTIMIZATION OF THE PREOPERATIVE MODELING STRATEGY AND PERSONALIZED SELECTION OF SURGICAL TREATMENT FOR PELVIC FLOOR DYSPLASIA IN FERTILE PATIENTS

summary: A sixth-generation (6G) mobile network must share the radio resources of each base station among services with different requirements for delay, throughput, and energy use. Radio access network (RAN) slicing addresses this problem by allocating radio resources among logically separated services, and increasingly autonomous controllers are proposed to manage these allocations. Two proposed enhancements are a learned meta-agent that adjusts the controller’s configuration and a quantum optimizer for difficult discrete allocation decisions. Here we examine when these enhancements add value beyond strong classical controls using SHARP, a safety-preserving multi-cell RAN slicing controller whose per-slot capacity constraint is enforced independently of the added optimization layers. The meta-agent is evaluated against the best static parameter setting and the controller’s built-in adaptation. Its learned policy selects the same value in every observed state, so in deployment it coincides with a fixed setting (V = 3) and does not outperform the best static setting; its role is to locate that setting without a manual sweep. Relative to the default setting inherited from the host study, the located setting improves slot-level power-budget compliance by five to ten percentage points during constrained regimes at a one to two percent goodput cost, while the controller’s Lyapunov virtual queue already provides long-run adaptation of the power constraint. For the discrete allocation problem, plain QAOA does not outperform the classical baselines. Warm-started QAOA with a rotated mixer shows improvement only in the rugged regime evaluated here: it incurs no observed losses to the greedy seed in 48 comparisons and strictly improves six of 16 instances under the IBM-Heron-calibrated noise model, increasing normalized frame utility from 0.927 to 0.941. This gain is measured in frame utility rather than delivered goodput, and its attribution to quantum sampling remains unresolved because a matched classical seeded-perturbation control is not included. The greedy solution remains the fallback when the quantum device does not return within the planning deadline. We therefore formulate a controllerspecific break-even condition relating the expected utility gain, device availability, and quantum-dispatch cost, and derive the corresponding hardware requirements. All results are simulation outputs; no quantum hardware is executed and no quantum advantage is claimed.
title: Bounding the benefit of agentic meta-adaptation and quantum-assisted optimization for safe multi-cell 6G radio access network slicing

summary: Higgs-pair production through gluon fusion is sensitive both to the Higgs self-coupling and to additional scalars exchanged in the s channel. We compute gg → hh at leading order in QCD in the CP-conserving two-Higgs-doublet model with Yukawa alignment (A2HDM), keeping the full top-quark mass dependence and every interference term among the box, the light-Higgs triangle and the heavy-scalar triangle. Previous A2HDM studies of heavy scalars decaying to Higgs pairs used the narrow-width approximation. We contrast two benchmark points. When the heavy scalar H decouples from the top-quark loop, the modified couplings of h weaken the destructive box–triangle interference, and the 13 TeV cross section rises to 1.27 times the Standard Model value without any resonance. For m_H = 300 GeV, below the ttbar threshold, the cross section reaches 3.69 times the Standard Model value; interference with the continuum changes the integrated resonant contribution by only about 4%, but turns the parton-level m_hh distribution into a peak–dip structure. The two mechanisms are therefore separated by the shapes of the m_hh and p_T spectra rather than by the rate. Both benchmarks are illustrative and satisfy a simplified set of theoretical and experimental constraints. Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24029211

summary: The analytical dataset, extraction provenance and analysis code for a study of how the cross-validation splitting rule affects machine-learning performance reported on literature-compiled membrane data. 452 canonical CO2/N2 measurements from 75 open-access studies published 2020-2026. Every value carries the page it was read from, a content hash and the DOI of its source. A panel of models was evaluated under cross-validation grouped by source study, and one random forest was also evaluated under a random row split. Version 1.0.2 replaces the dataset of version 1.0.1 with the one the manuscript analyses: rows found ineligible in review were removed, four studies outside the stated membrane scope were excluded, and measurements printed twice under different sample names were merged (sample_aliases.json). It adds the fold assignments and out-of-fold predictions for both splitting rules, the review decisions and analyses, and the analysis code with its notebook. Contents: adjudication.json : contradictions and how each was resolved analysis_code.zip : analysis code, the notebook, and the exact library versions audit_draw.json : the random audit: the sample, recorded before any row was seen audit_log.jsonl : the random audit: one verdict per row, with the time it was given audit_result.json : the random audit: agreement and the error-rate bound citation_table.csv : every value attributed to its source DOI dataset.csv : the analytical dataset exclusion_decisions.json : the post-review decision on each flagged row, who made it, and the page quotation it rests on expansion_protocol.json : the preregistered expansion protocol extraction_model.json : the extraction model's architecture, read from its files fulltext_decisions.csv : the screening ledger human_decisions.csv : the researcher's corrections leakage_diagnostic.json : the grouped-versus-random comparison over five seeds model_summary.csv : every model's grouped cross-validation result, all cohorts observations.csv : pre-canonicalisation observations oof_predictions_primary.csv : outer-fold assignments and every model's out-of-fold prediction reconciliation.json : counts and losses at every stage from search hit to analytical row reviewer_checks.json : sensitivity analyses added in review rights_decisions.csv : the release decision recorded for each source study rights_ledger.csv : the rights ledger rights_manifest.json : what was released and withheld, with the dataset checksum sample_aliases.json : measurements a study printed twice under different sample names, merged into one row, with the source quotation for each secondary_permeability.json : CO2 permeability as a secondary target, added in review source_repairs.json : the sentence justifying each repair split_comparison_predictions.csv : fold assignments and predictions under the grouped and the random split study_reconciliation.csv : the outcome of every study screened at full text validation_report.json : the extraction quality-control report, page by page No source PDF, rendered page image or figure reproduced from a source is included. Each study is identified by DOI so that it can be retrieved from its publisher under that publisher's terms. 14 studies released their extracted values but not the short sentences quoted as evidence, because their licence could not be established or is not a Creative Commons licence; those sentences are marked as withheld in the files and listed in rights_manifest.json. Every analysed row is present, so the deposit reproduces the analysis reported in the manuscript.
title: Machine learning for CO2/N2 separation performance across membrane material families: a grouped cross-validation study - analytical dataset and provenance

summary: Flagship 55/60 Can randomized or justified quasi-experimental intervention isolate the manufacturing effect from cell-lot, material and culture confounding? CAUSAL VERIFICATION AND COUNTERFACTUAL CONTROL IN NANOROBOT-ASSISTED REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT This 777-page Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Nano Regenerative Biomanufacturing series investigates intervention-defined causal treatment contrast rather than observational association. Its scientific coupling is causal inference x microscale interventions x biological functional validation. The evidence perimeter is prospective and nonclinical, using closed in-vitro systems, organ-on-chip platforms or authorized ex-vivo material; neither clinical efficacy nor autonomous human intervention is claimed. The falsifiable question is: Can randomized or justified quasi-experimental intervention isolate the manufacturing effect from cell-lot, material and culture confounding? The proposed minimum demonstration is: Randomize tool action within balanced chip batches, retain sham and medium-only controls, and repeat on a second platform. Strong comparators include correlational predictor, nonrandomized matched cohort and randomized sham manipulation. The central competing explanation is shared medium, selection, interference or time-dependent confounding. The noncompensatory stop rule is: negative controls exhibit the claimed effect or modest unmeasured confounding reverses it. Every eligible, stopped, refused and unsuccessful experiment belongs to the full denominator. Thirty conditional mathematical plates specify different analytic roles, measurements, units and blind failure tests. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 individual research investigations. Two hundred Research Gates organize twenty causal challenge families across ten primary physical observables, each with an independently read companion, concealed intervention, matched comparator, explicit rival and refusal gate. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future experimental and evidence instruments. All are experimental plans rather than executed observations. The source Atlas and methodology ancestors provide reference architecture but do not establish the new integrated candidate. Source-supplied ancestry includes 10.5281/zenodo.23046134 and 10.5281/zenodo.23486020; source-associated external DOI candidates must be bibliographically checked before citation. Research Gate lexical differentiation is not proof of scientific originality. The PDF is English-only and a separate QA record states outstanding independent physics, biology and DOI verification. summary: This repository provides the data, Python scripts, numerical outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting a methodological investigation of negative multifractal spectrum estimates in stochastic cascades and digital images. The study distinguishes formally negative annealed multifractal spectra, which can arise in stochastic cascade models, from negative finite-resolution estimates that may depend on measurement and preprocessing procedures. The repository includes: 1. Synthetic image datasets generated using hierarchical random maps (HRM), Fourier-based synthesis (FFT), midpoint displacement (MPD), and binary geometric constructions. 2. Numerical experiments investigating uniform background floors, noise, quantization, clipping, scale-window dependence, and grid-phase sensitivity. 3. Analyses of Dirichlet multiplicative cascades, including Genuine, Shuffled, and Decoy controls. 4. Multifractal estimates based on multiplier moments and Chhabra–Jensen procedures, together with whole-image bootstrap uncertainty estimates. 5. Auxiliary experiments concerning finite-ensemble histogram spectra and supersampling. 6. Scripts, CSV result tables, execution logs, and figure-reproduction materials. 7. A manuscript-to-data mapping file (MANUSCRIPT_MAP.csv), documentation, and SHA-256 checksums supporting traceability and integrity verification. The repository documents reproducibility checks, including the comparison of 180 baseline cases and the reproduction of two computational figures. These checks should not be interpreted as independent validation of every numerical experiment or as proof of universal estimator reliability. The results emphasize that formally negative multifractal spectra and negative estimates obtained from finite digital observations have distinct mathematical interpretations. In particular, negative estimated values do not imply negative Hausdorff dimensions. The dataset is independent of any specific journal submission and is intended to support transparent examination, replication, and further methodological research. Licensing: Original Python code is distributed under the MIT License. Original datasets, figures, tables, and documentation are distributed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Any third-party components remain subject to their respective licenses.
title: Negative Multifractal Spectra in Stochastic Cascades and Digital Observations: Reproducibility Data and Code

summary: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis of Global Armed Violence (1989–2025): C Software, 1,000 Permutation Tests and Cartographic Projection Audit This software and reproducibility package accompanies a computational-geometric investigation of geopolitical centrality based on the Uppsala Conflict Data Program Georeferenced Event Dataset (UCDP GED), version 26.1, covering the period 1989–2025. The study introduces a dynamic application of convex hull peeling (Convex Onion) to the spatial and temporal analysis of global armed violence. The method is grounded in the affine invariance of convex-layer membership and provides a hierarchical representation of spatial depth through successive convex hulls. Unlike conventional measures of centrality based on averages, distances, or event density, this approach examines the innermost geometric structure of the global distribution of recorded conflict locations. The dataset contains 358,130 events with day-level date precision , corresponding to 54,381 distinct geographical locations . The cumulative analysis identifies 1,134 convex layers in the final configuration. Software Components The archive includes four C-based computational components: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis: Chronological construction and updating of nested convex hulls, enabling the identification and tracking of the innermost geometric core from 1989 to 2025. Monte Carlo Permutation Analysis: A reproducible experiment involving 1,000 random permutations of complete geographical coordinate pairs across fixed chronological event positions, assessing the relationship between historical event ordering and geometric-core trajectories. Interactive Geometric Visualization: Offline visualization of the evolution of the innermost core, including annual configurations and changes in its geographical position. Cartographic Projection Comparison: Comparative analysis of convex-layer structures using planar longitude–latitude coordinates and the nonlinear Mollweide equal-area projection. Principal Findings The 2025 analysis identifies an innermost geometric location in Ethiopia under the original coordinate representation, whereas the Mollweide projection produces a two-location innermost layer in Sudan. The permutation experiment demonstrates that chronological event ordering influences the historical trajectory of the geometric core, although all permutations preserve the same final spatial configuration when the complete set of locations remains unchanged. These findings illustrate the distinction between affine-invariant geometric structure and centrality that depends on nonlinear cartographic representation. Reproducibility and Scientific Scope The package contains the original C source code, Windows executables, execution scripts, input datasets, computational outputs, visualization files, and technical documentation. The archive supports independent inspection, methodological evaluation, replication, and further development of computational-geometric approaches to spatial conflict analysis. The identified geometric core should not be interpreted as the location of maximum conflict intensity, the greatest number of fatalities, or a causal centre of global geopolitical instability. It represents a mathematically defined form of spatial depth whose interpretation depends on the adopted geometrical representation. Associated Research The Cartographic Construction of Geopolitical Centrality: Affine-Invariant Convex Layers and Global Armed Violence, 1989–2025. Data Source Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP), Georeferenced Event Dataset (GED), version 26.1. The UCDP data are attributed to their original providers. Dataset licensing and software provenance are documented separately in the archive.
title: Convex Onion Geopolitical Centrality
