summary: This analysis examines how computational configuration choices shape resource efficiency in confidential genomic collaboration across institutions. A descriptive secondary analysis uses 14 PRINCESS benchmark configurations published in 2017, comprising seven batch sizes evaluated with compression enabled and disabled across three sites. Matched runtime differences, ratios and joint memory comparisons identify configuration tradeoffs. With compression enabled, increasing batch size from 100 to 10,000 variants reduces runtime by 75.49 percent, while expansion to one million variants provides only 0.38 percent further improvement despite requiring 32.69 times as much memory. Without compression, runtime reaches its observed minimum at 8,000 variants and subsequently increases. Compression enabled records longer enclave runtime in every matched pair. These patterns reveal diminishing processing gains and configuration dependent resource tradeoffs, without isolating their underlying mechanisms. The contribution is a comparative interpretation distinguishing faster execution from economical resource use. The findings refine a resource constraint perspective and support joint evaluation of execution time and memory when configuring protected genomic workflows, with numerical recommendations bounded by the observed benchmark environment.
title: BENCHMARKING CONFIDENTIAL GENOMIC COMPUTING EFFICIENCY THROUGH BATCH SIZE, COMPRESSION, AND MEMORY USE ACROSS COLLABORATIVE SITES

summary: Replication materials for “AI and Intergenerational Spirals in Repair Knowledge” by Laurentiu Guinea. The paper develops a three-period overlapping-generations model in which young people choose independent practice or AI delegation, middle-aged people correct mistaken learning beliefs and rebuild skills, and older people repair goods and transmit instructions. The package reproduces the intergenerational spiral, partial-diffusion and stochastic extensions, and the two-product analysis. It contains MATLAB and R scripts, independent Python verification, numerical outputs, manuscript sources and figures, and a descriptive analysis of Open Repair Alliance data. Model parameters are illustrative; the repair records do not estimate or causally test the behavioural mechanism. Instructions and software requirements are included in the README files. Original code is licensed under MIT. Original documentation is licensed under CC BY 4.0. Open Repair Alliance data and derived ORA tables and figures retain CC BY-SA 4.0. These licences apply to their respective materials, not as alternative licences for the entire archive. See LICENSE.txt for attribution and scope. The ORA data are from the October 2026 release, pinned to repository commit d1b2ab5a7b05c96645f5d4afec7951fc912639e1. Financial support: Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation, project PID2023-138706NB-I00.

summary: This dataset accompanies the review article Linking World Models to Safe Embodied Intelligence: A Critical Review and Research Agenda . It contains the records behind the article's search, screening and source selection, and the data from the matched comparison reported in Section 6.3. Search. The exact query strings for the 15 database searches whose records were screened: four query families (R1, R2, I1 and W4) run on Scopus, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Guide to Computing Literature. They exported 6,714 records. The deposit also lists three broader pilot families (W1–W3) that were run but not adopted. Screening. One row for each of the 6,701 screened records, giving its identifier, title, year, DOI, the search or citation routes that found it, and the screening decision with its reason. A second table covers the 4,004 records kept after screening, linked to their full-text assessments where one exists. Selection. The register of the 178 cited references, with each one's role, the version examined and the pages inspected. Also included are the frozen selection record, the record of AI-assisted appraisal and the author's confirmations, the two targeted searches and the reference audit. Benchmark. The frozen episode inputs with their SHA-256 manifests, the separately written reference interpretation, the flat typed-contract comparator with its tests and results, all run records and timings, the deviation log and the recorded environment.

summary: Two Hamiltonian systems that share almost nothing in their physical origins turn out to behave identically once their local structure near a 2:1 internal resonance is examined. One system models a pair of flexural modes in a micromechanical resonator through coupled Duffing oscillators. The other models the stretch–bend Fermi resonance of a molecule such as carbon dioxide through a Morse oscillator coupled to a harmonic bend. Both possess an elliptic equilibrium, equal Krein signatures, a frequency ratio close to 2:1, and a cubic resonant coupling. These shared features place them in the same resonant normal-form type, a difference resonance that confines energy exchange rather than driving escape. On the conserved polyad fixed by an initial excitation that places nearly all the energy in the higher-frequency mode, the truncated normal form of any such system collapses to a one-degree-of-freedom problem that depends on only two numbers: a scaled detuning and a scaled anharmonic curvature. Consequently the largest fraction of energy that can be transferred to the lower mode is given by a universal curve whose edges are independent of the curvature. All of the necessary invariants are computed directly from each Hamiltonian before any trajectory is integrated. Numerical integration then confirms the predictions. When the curvature is small the systems follow the one-parameter curve; when it is large they follow the two-parameter curve to high accuracy. A beam whose quartic coefficient is deliberately softened until its curvature matches that of the molecular model reproduces the molecular exchange curve directly, even though the remaining normal-form coefficients differ. An ensemble of sixty randomly drawn members of the same type likewise collapses onto the appropriate universal curve. The residual discrepancy grows roughly linearly with excitation amplitude, as expected from the truncation of the normal form. Two controls mark the boundaries of the result. Reversing one Krein signature converts the same frequency window from bounded exchange into unbounded escape. Weak viscous damping reduces the transferred fraction in the manner predicted by a correspondingly damped reduced model. A quantum treatment of the truncated normal form introduces the polyad number as a third invariant; the lowest Fermi dyad therefore follows a distinct quantum curve rather than the classical one. The findings remain local, confined to two-mode models, and classical except where the quantum analogue is stated explicitly. Within those limits they demonstrate that a dimensionless exchange relation established for one physical system can be transferred to an unrelated system once both have been rescaled by invariants computed from their own Hamiltonians.
title: The Beam That Behaves Like a Molecule

summary: This record provides the complete reproducibility package for the manuscript: “A Smaller Drop Is Not Robustness: A Validation-Locked Cross-Pipeline and Independent-Cohort Evaluation of a Quantum Kernel for Chest X-ray Classification.” The study re-evaluates an apparent robustness advantage of a four-qubit ZZ-feature-map quantum support vector machine (QSVM-ZZ) for chest X-ray classification. The revised experimental design separates absolute target performance from internal-to-target degradation and addresses configuration-selection bias, limited random-seed inference, duplicate and provenance concerns, feature-compression effects, asymmetric feature encoding, prediction collapse, and lack of independent-cohort validation. Experimental scope The package contains reproducibility materials for three complementary evaluation settings: Source and internal evaluation: PneumoniaMNIST, derived from the Guangzhou/Kermany pediatric chest X-ray cohort. Cross-pipeline preprocessing-shift evaluation: original Kermany test images representing the same underlying cohort through a different preprocessing pipeline. Independent-cohort evaluation: the RSNA Pneumonia Detection Challenge / NIH Clinical Center chest radiograph cohort. The confirmatory low-dimensional benchmark uses a configuration selected from source validation data only and evaluates QSVM-ZZ against RBF-SVM, logistic regression and a compact MLP across ten fresh seeds. Additional analyses include wider classical feature representations, a symmetric π·tanh encoding control, prediction-collapse and near-collapse audits, strict one-to-one paired radiograph evaluation, and repeated fine-tuned ResNet18 experiments. Key contents The record includes: raw-image duplicate and provenance-audit outputs; perceptual-hash screening results; reconstructed group-aware source training and validation splits; high-confidence source-to-raw correspondence mappings; the corrected 554-radiograph one-to-one paired mapping; PCA explained-variance and compression-sensitivity analyses; validation-only QSVM configuration-selection results; ten-seed confirmatory predictions and performance metrics; exact seed-level sign-flip tests and Holm-adjusted statistical comparisons; classical π·tanh encoding-control results; exact-collapse and near-collapse audits; source-validation-selected wider classical reference results; grouped domain-classifier outputs; five-seed fine-tuned ResNet18 predictions, training histories and trained checkpoints; independent RSNA primary and secondary evaluation outputs; derived RSNA frozen-feature arrays; executable Kaggle/Jupyter notebooks; software-version and random-seed information; SHA-256 integrity manifests; and legacy exploratory QSVM/VQC outputs retained for transparency and provenance. Principal methodological finding The revised analysis shows that QSVM-ZZ can exhibit a smaller internal-to-target macro-F1 decline than a matched low-dimensional RBF-SVM, but that smaller decline does not constitute evidence of practically useful robustness. QSVM-ZZ remains near chance by AUROC on both the Kermany preprocessing-shift target and the independent RSNA cohort, and its absolute target advantage over matched RBF-SVM is not statistically established. Applying the same π·tanh feature squashing used by QSVM-ZZ to the classical RBF-SVM substantially reduces the absolute Kermany performance gap, indicating that the classical-to-quantum encoding contributes to the apparent stability. Wider classical representations and fine-tuned ResNet18 additionally demonstrate that conclusions drawn from a severely compressed four-dimensional benchmark should not be generalized to broader model classes. Data-use and redistribution statement This archive contains derived features, mappings, predictions, statistical results, trained model checkpoints, code and analysis outputs. It does not redistribute raw RSNA DICOM images or raw Kermany/PneumoniaMNIST source-i
title: Does a Smaller Performance Drop Really Mean Robustness? A Validation-Locked Evaluation of a Quantum Kernel for Chest X-ray Classification

F073 Biological Microenvironment Ionic Strength Coupling At The Limit — Investigates the coupling between ionic strength, interfacial noise, leachate mass and retained surface function. Unmodified and mature PEG-coated surfaces anchor the comparison; a concealed leachate challenge tests whether apparent electrical improvement actually reflects altered surface chemistry. F074 Nano-Interface Photothermal Side Effect Measurement At The Limit — Proposes assays for photothermal side effects at nano-interfaces, tracking leachate mass, functional retention and protein-corona turnover. Comparisons with unmodified and mature PEG controls, including hidden corona exchange, test whether apparent coating gains remain stable across specimens. F077 Microscale Interfacial-Molecular Selectivity At The Limit — Asks whether microscale interfaces achieve molecular selectivity beyond what changes in ligand loading or coating adhesion alone could explain. Surface coverage, adhesion energy and desorption rate are jointly assessed against ligand-matched covalent coatings under blinded delamination. summary: CronNet-Holo: A Unified Research Programme Author: Luis Morató de Dalmases Research Initiative: CronNet-Holo Initiative — Theory of Time Research Unit Version: 1.0 — November 2026 Document type: Research programme / preprint collection Language: English  Abstract This Zenodo record presents the complete CronNet-Holo research programme as a unified collection of manuscripts, technical specifications, and computational audits. The programme investigates a four-layer mathematical architecture for the relation between discrete geometry (the regular 600-cell), finite group representation theory (the binary icosahedral group 2I ≅ SL(2,5)), spectral operators, noncommutative geometry in the sense of Connes, and possible physical interpretations connected with M-theory and the Standard Model. The architecture is organized as: SFDG → Greg → SGUP 600 Cell → QSVG with two transversal modules: TELOS (teleological orientation and prioritization) PHYSCON (physical connection and testability). This record collects eleven documents and seven computational audit files: Manuscripts and specifications (PDFs): CronNet-Holo–Connes: Construction of a Triple Spectral Program TELOS and PHYSCON: Formal Definition of the Two Transversal Modules Spectral Frequency Data Layer and SFDG Annex G — FDL: Interface between Greg and the Frequency Data Layer CronNet-Holo H6 v9: Integral Four-Layer Architecture Regenerative Syntactic Grammar (Greg) — Version 5.1 Canonical Signatures of SER and CONFINAR Inverse Temporal Symmetry Hypothesis (H-STI) Temporal Reversal Operator: Representation Theory and the 53-Dimensional Sector Compression Grammar: M-Theory and Connes as Local Reflections CronNet-Holo–M-Theory Computational audits (PY and TXT): A. Geometric and Spectral Audit of the 600-Cell (H6 v5) B. Integral Audit 600-Cell / M53 C. SGUP 600-Cell Audit Throughout, the programme distinguishes definitions, exact mathematical identities, conditional propositions, computational results, hypotheses, conjectures, physical interpretations, and open problems. No claim is made that the programme proves the Riemann hypothesis, derives the Standard Model, or establishes an experimentally validated physical theory. 1. The Four-Layer Architecture 1.1 Canonical order The fundamental architecture of CronNet-Holo is the ordered composition SFDG → Greg → SGUP 600 Cell → QSVG. The four layers are necessary and non-interchangeable within the architectural design adopted in this programme. 1.2 Layer responsibilities     Layer Responsibility Main output SFDG Data governance, provenance, traceability Structured registry Greg Formal language and typed operations Typed expressions SGUP 600 Cell Geometric, combinatorial, and spectral construction Models, operators, spectra QSVG Geometric and spectral verification Certificates, invariants, relations 1.3 Transversal modules TELOS and PHYSCON are not additional layers. They are transversal modules that can interact with the four layers.     Module Responsibility Central question TELOS Orientation and prioritization What should we do next? PHYSCON Physical connection and testability What can we predict and test? 2. summary: This paper develops a scale-spanning account of latent vibration and frequency manifestation within Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM). It examines the relationship between complete latent vibration, the negative and positive displacement domains around the manifestable origin, and the eligibility of positive displacement for progression towards physical manifestation. The development distinguishes the complete latent-vibration interval from the directed displacement associated with manifestation, establishing the proposed Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck threshold relationships in terms of the Planck length. The analysis further develops phase-dependent frequency relations below the Planck threshold and considers the proposed frequency increments associated with the Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck domains. It then presents a state-dependent sequence of energy–frequency transformations across latent, phase, and manifested states, including the reverse progression associated with dissolution. Within this framework, frequency and displacement are treated as related physical parameters whose coefficients depend on the corresponding phase domain. The paper also distinguishes the phase-state potential-energy mass representation from the mass contribution associated with the manifested domain. It formulates the effective-mass relationship and separates this ECM representation from the distinct dark-energy-related mass representation. Taken together, these developments present an integrated theoretical description of latent vibration, manifestation eligibility, threshold transitions, energy–frequency relations, and mass-state transformations within the proposed ECM framework.
title: Complete Latent Vibration and Frequency Manifestation Eligibility in Extended Classical Mechanics

summary: This record contains the supplementary files of the systematic review "Sliding Mode Control of Quadrotor UAVs: A Systematic Review of Convergence Guarantees and Chattering Attenuation" (submitted to Aerospace Science and Technology). ESM_1_search_and_screening.zip - merged and de-duplicated record table (bibliographic data without abstracts), screening rules, every title/abstract screening decision with its reason code, the two validation samples, and the scripts used for de-duplication, screening and the statistics of the systematic map. ESM_2_extraction_sheet.xlsx - extraction sheet of the 2,358 studies of the systematic map, and the full-text evidence coding of the 57 studies selected for full-text analysis (45 included), with the passage on which each coded item is based and a codebook. ESM_3_benchmark_code_and_data.zip - MATLAB code and simulation data of the comparative benchmark of six sliding mode controllers on a 3DR Iris quadrotor model, and the scripts that generate the figures. ESM_4_supplementary_table_and_note.pdf - Supplementary Table S1 (analysis of SMC-based controllers) and Supplementary Note S1 (control laws and gains used in the benchmark).
tags: Sliding mode control; Quadrotor UAV; Systematic review; PRISMA; Fixed-time convergence; Arbitrary-time convergence; Chattering; Benchmark

The archive includes ms2's two git submodules at their pinned commits, since GitHub's own source archives omit submodules: orbit/ is Orbit from https://github.com/BenLangmead/runperm at commit bc4b455b04cca7c339b6b8be26caa9cfcd0cf0cc, and teratools/ is TeraTools from https://github.com/BenLangmead/TeraTools at commit de922b0331740569dbcd6a8b1b0b2ea47df14ee2. Build with make all and test with make test (see README.md). The benchmark workflow, run records and figures are in https://github.com/langmead-lab/ms2-experiments. Licenses: ms2's own source and the parts that follow TeraTools are under the MIT license; Orbit (orbit/) is under the GNU General Public License v3.0, so a built ms2 binary is distributed under the GPL-3.0. See LICENSE and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.
title: ms2: matching statistics and SMEMs on Orbit move structures (paper-v1)

summary: This archive holds the data and code behind the manuscript “Five Inexpensive Checks for Machine-Learned Enzyme Turnover-Number Predictors” by Fatih Aktas and Farida Rahayu. The protocol defines five checks for machine-learned predictors of the enzyme turnover number. They use supplied prediction columns and one measured panel. The five checks are a scale audit, the mutation-response ratio, a kinetics-untrained baseline floor, transfer to external data, and a calibration check. The protocol is applied to six published predictors. The data span 1,571 variants from 130 database-derived campaigns, 23,500 variants from eight deep mutational scans, and two panels of measured turnover numbers. The archive contains the analysis scripts, the JSON output of each script, the extracted datasets, the tables and figures, a README with the execution order, a REPRODUCE guide, and a dated pre-specification note. All kinetic measurements and all model predictions come from the EnzyArena benchmark (Zeng et al., bioRxiv 2026, doi:10.64898/2026.03.29.715152). No new measurements were made. The benchmark release is not redistributed here. Software: Python 3.13, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, RDKit 2026.9.1, Matplotlib 3.11.
title: Data and code for five checks on machine-learned enzyme kcat predictors

summary: Complete reproducibility materials for the manuscript “Auditing Unseen-Attack Transfer in Federated Intrusion Detection: A Controlled Leave-Family-Out Study Across Four NetFlow-v3 Captures.” The deposit contains two complementary archives. 03a_Supplementary_Material.zip contains the complete exploratory revision package, including the R0–R7 workflows, executed revision outputs, CPU diagnostics, statistical sensitivity analyses, convergence data, provenance records, verification scripts, amendments, manifests, and reproduction instructions. 03b_Supplementary_Original_Scores.zip contains the frozen original-study materials, including all 764 original job-score archives (665 main and 99 random-split jobs), raw result records, archived analysis code, and job identities. The original and revision analyses are explicitly distinguished. The revision materials do not replace or modify the frozen original prediction scores. SHA-256 manifests, coverage inventories, and verification scripts are included. The underlying NetFlow-v3 source datasets are not redistributed. The complete reproducibility package is publicly available through this version-specific Zenodo DOI. Identical archives accompany the journal resubmission.

summary: This dataset supports 121 benchmark tasks for evaluating coding agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment. It combines published tissue datasets and Albis simulations spanning serial-section alignment, cross-technology matching, robustness tests, and three-dimensional reconstruction. Compiled AnnData ( .h5ad ) files provide gene-expression measurements, spatial coordinates, and reference annotations where available. Each task is accompanied by instructions, input and output specifications, data provenance, and a defined scoring profile. The benchmark separates agent-visible inputs from reference information used for evaluation and compares submitted alignments with scripted implementations of published methods.
title: Spatial Transcriptomics Alignment Dataset for Agents

summary: How should complex chemical data be stored and communicated to meet chemists' different needs? Chemists identify, classify, describe, annotate and store their structures, and each need asks for something different. For atomically precise metal clusters (APMCs) and the cluster-assembled materials (CAMs) built from them, this deposit proposes a fourfold framework for their description, naming and identification: it writes each structure down once, in a standard descriptor format, and derives from it the names and identifiers that each need calls for. The problem. The same cluster appears as Au25, Au25(PET)18 or an acronym, and two Au38(PET)24 isomers are told apart by their discoverers' initials. Isomers, substitution sites, exchanged ligands and assemblies have no names. Databases hold coordinates but nothing searchable about core, staples, isomer or assembly. The InChI now encodes whole clusters, but not their handedness, and it does not yet describe crystals or cluster-assembled materials. The solution, a fourfold framework: describe once, derive the rest. APMC-META , the descriptor format: composition, core, surface motifs, ligands, symmetry, topology, isomerism, exchange, electrons, assembly and provenance, for describing and storing a cluster. APMC SYSNOM names for people, e.g. gold-25 18(2-phenylethane-1-thiolato) cluster(1−, (0/I), 8e−, Ih). APMC-ID labels for papers and tables, e.g. Au25(PET)18−–Ih. CluChI layered strings for machines and databases; reported with the InChI, they identify a cluster completely. The shortest complete form is a pair of keys: the CluChIKey at the level of description that makes the cluster unique, and the InChIKey of the whole structure. The framework is extensible: new descriptors enter through a versioned registry, and annotation never changes a key. summary: Fuente del Salín (Cantabria, Spain) is one of the few decorated caves where a large assemblage of hand stencils is associated with a Gravettian occupation, including a hearth and evidence of pigment processing. Using a 3D reconstruction of the cave’s Palaeolithic state, GIS-based measurements and multivariate statistics, we analysed the spatial organisation of its 55 hand stencils. All are located near the entrance, in accessible, visible spaces able to accommodate several people, unlike the only other motif, deeper in the cave. The assemblage nonetheless includes distinct spatial groups, compositions and unusual orientations. The hearth could have lit more than half of the hands, and both kernel density analysis and hierarchical clustering single out the group surrounding it. These results strengthen the hypothesis that the hands and the occupation were contemporaneous and, together with Gargas, suggest that hand stencils could be produced in spaces also used for everyday activities.
title: By the Light of the Fire: Characterisation and Spatial Organisation of the Hand Stencils at Fuente del Salín in Relation to their Archaeological Context
