summary: Pretrained vision models provide strong general-purpose representations, but in Domain-Incremental Learning (DIL), where the input distribution changes sequentially, adapting to new domains often degrades performance on previously learned ones. We observe that forgetting is not uniform across domains and classes and is not explained by training order alone. This motivates us to track each past domain-class concept individually. We use representation drift, defined as the deviation of a past concept's current representation from a fixed anchor, as a measurable surrogate for forgetting risk. The measured drift then serves two complementary roles. A consolidation loss assigns stronger preservation to high-drift pairs, while prototype construction down-weights highly drifted domains to reduce their influence on the class reference. Preservation is thus allocated by measured drift rather than assumed importance. To obtain this signal during training without storing past raw data, we repurpose a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA). For each domain-class pair, we store only a compact context summary in the backbone feature space and rerun it through the learned context-to-target relation to measure its drift from the fixed anchor. Across DomainNet, Office-Home, CORe50, and CDDB-Hard, our method sustains a strong accuracy-forgetting balance on every benchmark, using substantially less training memory than accuracy-competitive methods and the smallest storage among compared methods.
title: Drift-adaptive Representation Preservation for Domain-Incremental Learning

summary: Modern scientific and machine-learning applications compose many independently developed libraries. When these libraries run together, their independently managed runtimes can oversubscribe shared resources: using the same CPU cores, fighting over GPUs, or contending for memory bandwidth. Avoiding such contention requires careful configuration across library boundaries. Existing autotuners do not directly investigate what resources are shared between libraries, which runtime signals correlate with interference. As a result, they are inefficient for finding optimal configurations to mitigate contention. This paper presents SysPilot, a cross-library performance autotuning system based on Library Performance Contract (LPC). A Library Performance Contract captures a library's resource demands, assumptions, controls, and observability signals in LPCL, a specification language for describing library resource requirements. SysPilot synthesizes contracts from documentation and code artifacts, composes contracts from the libraries used by an application, derives resource-conflict hypotheses, profiles the application to validate those hypotheses, and selects candidate configurations. This design makes the Library Performance Contract a reusable unit of performance knowledge: a contract for a library can be reused across many applications that depend on that library. We evaluate SysPilot on a benchmark suite of cross-library contention scenarios. The results show that SysPilot matches the performance of autotuners that rely on application-specific manual information while retaining cross-application reuse. Compared with general-purpose autotuners such as OpenTuner and SMAC3, SysPilot improves benchmark performance metrics by up to an additional 38% over the best configuration found by these autotuners, while using 3x fewer runs.
title: SysPilot: Cross-Library Performance Autotuning via Library Performance Contracts

summary: Recent video world models allow users to explore generated environments through camera navigation. Continuous hand motion provides a fine-grained action channel for interacting with the people and objects encountered during exploration. We present TouchéWorld, a framework that integrates gesture-driven interaction into a camera-controlled video world model. Given an initial image and a scene-description prompt, the model generates video conditioned on temporally aligned camera and hand controls. We construct joint camera--hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment. Building on a pretrained camera-controlled world model, we combine spatial hand-skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation support chunk-level online generation, allowing users to update their controls based on generated visual feedback. We further introduce TouchéBench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera--hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Together, these components establish a framework for studying continuous exploration and hand-driven interaction within generative worlds.
title: TouchéWorld tech report : Towards Online Unified Camera--Hand Exploration in Generative Worlds

summary: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.
title: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement

summary: Public comment submitted to DICOM Working Group 32 on Supplement 253: Waveform Compression (Version 09, 2026-09-18), together with the benchmark it rests on. ITU-T T.261 / ISO-IEC 23003-8 ("H.BWC") is evaluated against the codec set of Buccino et al. 2023 (doi:10.1088/1741-2552/acf5a4) on Neuropixels 1.0 recordings at 384 channels and 30 kHz. The lossless results of that paper were reproduced first as a check (912 cells, paired per-recording median deviation 0.017 %, codec ranking 11/11), and T.261 was then added to the same protocol. The central finding is that the two obvious ways to qualify a lossy setting disagree with each other. On one simulated Neuropixels recording with ground truth, at matched compression T.261 preserves the average spike waveform better than WavPack Hybrid while adding six times as many spurious units above the lossless baseline (+30 against +5, on a baseline of 126). A lossy setting therefore cannot be qualified on waveform fidelity alone. The comment makes eight specific requests of WG-32 on that basis, including conveying the quantizer step rather than only a compression ratio, widening Relative Sample Times (which saturates at 71.6 minutes as VR UL), and using a 64-bit Basic Offset Table (32-bit offsets overflow after ~11 minutes of compressed data at 384 channels, and ~2.7 minutes on a 1,536-channel Neuropixels 2.0 Quad Base probe). Every quantitative claim derives from recorded computation rather than from prose: each measurement cell carries its own datalad run record naming the tool commit, input checksums and command line, and each sweep is re-runnable from the pinned tool commit. Funding. This work was supported by the NIH BRAIN Initiative under award R24MH117295 (NIMH), "DANDI: Distributed Archives for Neurophysiology Data Integration". The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health. AI assistance. The tooling, analysis scripts and the drafting of the report were produced with the assistance of Claude Code (Anthropic) under the author's direction and review; per-commit Co-Authored-By trailers record which model produced each commit. The quantitative claims derive from recorded computation, not from model output.
title: Benchmarking ITU-T T.261 against established codecs on extracellular electrophysiology, with a public comment on DICOM Supplement 253

summary: Reproducibility materials for "Operating Constraints Shape Portfolio Value in Phased Metro Flood Protection", version 1.3.0. This version supplements the previously published baseline archive (version 1.1.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22969483) with the analyses supporting the revised manuscript. The reproducibility addendum contains protocols, code, seeds, selected station sets, unrounded results, and numerical verification records for annualized design-storm appraisal, conditional position-severity stress tests, failure dependence and secondary closure variants, tail-sensitive objectives, budget comparisons, fragility likelihood weights, tail-extrapolation sensitivity, and information restrictions. Earlier results and protocols are retained. Separate files provide the current Supplemental Materials, its editable LaTeX source, a release README, and SHA-256 checksums. Historical scripts and earlier supplements inside the computational archives document earlier analyses; the separately supplied current supplement is the reference for the revised manuscript. The annualized quantity is the service deficit of an annual-maximum three-hour representative storm under a common exposure. Demand uses population as a proxy; station response, dependence, protection, and short-turn service are model assumptions. The packages document source data and third-party attribution.
title: Reproducibility materials for "Operating Constraints Shape Portfolio Value in Phased Metro Flood Protection"

summary: Understanding why source code is vulnerable is essential for developers to interpret vulnerability predictions, investigate potential security weaknesses, and make informed remediation decisions. Although transformer-based vulnerability detectors can identify potentially vulnerable code, existing explainability approaches remain predominantly \emph{attribution-centric}, highlighting influential code regions without adequately explaining the underlying vulnerability mechanisms or providing independently verifiable supporting evidence. This limits developers' ability to assess the credibility and practical relevance of generated explanations. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{Xgent}, a provenance-aware, multi-evidence explainability framework designed to support software vulnerability comprehension. Xgent integrates neural explanations, static-analysis findings, and retrieved vulnerability evidence through an agentic reasoning architecture to generate contextual explanations grounded in complementary evidence sources. We evaluate Xgent using canonical vulnerabilities, real-world vulnerability datasets, and defensive-code examples through a ten-configuration ablation study and a controlled user study involving 104 participants. Our evaluation examines explanation faithfulness, evidence grounding, provenance transparency, hallucination, evidence utilization, and developers' perceptions of explanation clarity, trustworthiness, and actionability. Results demonstrate improved explanation grounding, calibration, and evidence utilization, with a low hallucination rate, while the underlying detector's predictive performance remains statistically indistinguishable from the baseline (McNemar $p=0.22$). Participants also reported greater trust, perceived understanding, and actionability, with a strong preference for multi-evidence explanations over attribution-only alternatives. These findings highlight the potential of provenance-aware, evidence-grounded explanations to support developers in interpreting vulnerability predictions and understanding the reasoning behind identified security weaknesses.
title: Xgent: Provenance-Aware Multi-Evidence Explanations for Software Vulnerability Comprehension

summary: This deposit contains Stata replication code, execution instructions, and aggregate reference outputs for a study of public old-age pensions and private household transfers in Mexico, with comparative evidence from Chile. The analysis uses ENIGH 2008–2024 and CASEN survey microdata, which must be obtained from their original providers. The code reproduces the main empirical results and selected supplementary analyses. Additional Python-only analyses are not included. No individual- or household-level data are redistributed.
title: Replication code for public old-age pensions and private household transfers

summary: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models

summary: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.
title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?

summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $ε$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $ετ$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $ε$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.
title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions

summary: Algorithm-driven services, including search, recommendation, and advertising, rely on multi-stage model pipelines. While research prioritizes model optimization, post-deployment monitoring focuses on operational reliability. Yet operationally healthy systems may still produce poor-quality results, exposing a gap in existing evaluation and monitoring practices. However, a systematic problem formulation and benchmark for this task remain lacking. To bridge this gap, we formulate System Quality Diagnosis (SQD) for algorithm-driven services, a new task that extends quality evaluation beyond identifying poor outcomes to attributing their causes across system components. Focusing on industrial search, we propose WISE, an agentic framework for end-to-end quality diagnosis that discovers user-facing issues and traces their origins to underlying algorithmic components. To improve diagnostic reliability, we introduce ReTrace for constructing evidence-consistent trajectory supervision and Adaptive Harness-Policy Optimization (AHPO) for failure-guided optimization of the agent harness and model policy. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct WISE-BENCH, a real-world multimodal search benchmark that combines user-facing evidence, internal pipeline traces, and expert diagnosis annotations. Extensive experiments show consistent gains across model scales, with WISE achieving 75.20% end-to-end accuracy on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. In production, WISE supports quality auditing, online quality assurance, and model optimization, reducing diagnosis costs and improving downstream relevance models.
title: WISE: An Agentic Framework for Whole-page Multimodal Search Experience Attribution

summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents translate model outputs into consequential actions, turning indirect prompt injection into an execution-security problem. Existing defenses constrain tool calls, trajectories, or information flows, but often leave action semantics, state dependencies, and evidence relations implicit, limiting generalization across heterogeneous tools and complicating safe updates. We present \ours{}, a dynamic ontology-guided governance framework. \ours{} grounds heterogeneous calls in a shared semantic representation and combines an executable ontology with episode-level task state to derive deterministic ready, waiting, and forbidden decisions. A waiting decision identifies an unmet but recoverable obligation, enabling bounded replanning without expanding the agent's authorization boundary. \ours{} evolves its ontology offline from verified training executions. An offline LLM proposes instance-independent action--state axioms, which are accepted only if they address ontology errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen. We evaluate \ours{} on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn under benign and indirect prompt-injection settings. \ours{} achieves a 0\% attack success rate (ASR) across all three benchmarks while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines. These results show that explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking.
title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents

summary: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.
title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness

summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress on cross-modal reasoning tasks, yet they continue to suffer from hallucinations in long-chain reasoning processes. In this work, we revisit hallucination in MLLMs from the perspective of reasoning generation dynamics. We argue that entropy is not merely a static measure of uncertainty but a structured signal that reflects how modality information is integrated throughout decoding. Through systematic analysis, we identify two characteristic entropy patterns associated with hallucination behaviors: (1) a generally high-confidence regime corresponds to premature convergence to inappropriate multimodal interactions; and (2) local abrupt entropy transitions are associated with reasoning instability and hallucination onset. Building on these observations, we propose an entropy-aware self-introspective framework for MLLM reasoning. Our method continuously tracks entropy dynamics during decoding and performs targeted visual re-alignment when suspicious hallucination states are detected, encouraging the model to re-examine salient visual evidence at critical reasoning stages. Extensive experiments across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning nine distinct evaluation settings demonstrate that our approach delivers robust improvements in reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness, while providing new insights into the generation dynamics underlying MLLM failures. The code is available at: https://github.com/jden4524/SelfRetrospectiveDecoding.
title: Entropogram-guided Visual Realignment Decoding: Capturing the Rhythm of Multimodal Reasoning

summary: Deploying an explainable intrusion detection model from a validated laboratory setting into a forensic workflow requires guarantees that benchmarks do not test: that the certified model is the exact artifact applied to a case, that heterogeneous evidence can be classified reliably, and that every step is verifiable. We present MODEXRE, a forensic pipeline that extends a previously validated synthetic-data-trained XGBoost classifier with SHAP explainability (arXiv:2607.00763) into a dual-mode architecture: a Laboratory mode, where models are trained and certified on public and synthetic data, and a Formal mode, where a frozen, hash-verified model performs inference on case evidence under a SHA-256 hash-chained chain of custody. Suricata alerts, CEF firewall logs and packet captures are normalized through OCSF. Four design decisions, each triggered by an observed failure, shaped the architecture: a timestamp leak that inflated Kitsune performance (F1-macro 0.984, 0.662 after correction); a feature-coverage gap that made the 78-feature reference model misclassify a real SSH alert; causal temporal flow aggregation, which raised Kitsune multiclass F1-macro from 0.394 to 0.932; and a certification defect, exposed only by a real packet capture, whereby the pipeline had always trained a binary classifier. After correction, the same capture went from 100% of events flagged as malicious to 87% classified as Normal, with the scanning host identified as Reconnaissance. The default four-class certified model reaches F1-macro = 0.9538 on CICIDS2017-derived evidence; the recertified 18-category model reaches 0.6214, reflecting the real multiclass task. Chain-of-custody verification, model integrity hashing and per-prediction SHAP explanations are reported as measured outcomes.
title: Network Intrusion Forensic Detection System with Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Digital Chain of Custody

summary: Attracting features toward learned in-distribution (ID) regions is an intuitive strategy for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, but does such attraction improve detection? We investigate this question using class-conditioned Hamiltonian dynamics as a controlled testbed and identify an attraction-ranking mismatch: improving individual class-affinity scores need not improve the relative ordering of ID and OOD samples. Our analysis separates misalignment between the driving field and the detection score from ranking failure that persists even when they are aligned. An exact AUROC decomposition and a local boundary analysis identify relative score changes at the ID-OOD ranking boundary as the source of first-order AUROC change under regularity conditions. Experiments demonstrate that a score-aligned rule can improve performance on a held-out source validation split yet consistently degrade it after transfer, even without a single winning-class change. A separate perturbation study finds that near-boundary relative score changes track the direction of small AUROC changes in the tested settings. Finally, centroid approximation and shared scales connect the zero-step score to a static centroid family that includes the existing CTM detector. Together, these results explain why class attraction is insufficient to justify feature refinement and motivate evaluating its effect on the ranking boundary.
title: Attraction-Ranking Mismatch in Out-of-Distribution Detection: Theory and Evidence from Hamiltonian Feature Dynamics

summary: Abstract. Two Coulomb fields produce singular three-electron integrals that limited Hylleraas evaluations of lithium fine-structure operators. Two integrations by parts reduce the eight relevant operators to two inverse-square families and previously treated integrals. We give one-dimensional representations for their masters T₂, T₃, and alternative cube–square anchors C₂, C₃; C₃ is expressed in classical polylogarithms of weight at most three. Parity separates decoupled sectors from genuinely three-electron sectors. Exact rational reductions through index sum 32 use twelve sufficient masters at the tested exponent sets. Double screening and Gaussian coordinate integration determine these masters to sixty significant digits. Exact collection of the source functions controls cancellation near equal exponents at four tested separations; equal exponents use a separate exact reduction. Numerical comparisons cover 104 pre-specified recursive members and an independent direct sample of 136 decoupled members through index sum 32. Production-size basis matrix elements of P₄ and one component of P₁ agree by two methods to 41–45 digits. On one Intel Xeon Silver 4410Y machine, both families require 5.85–6.99 CPU hours per exponent set at the stated 64-digit output precision. Uniform error bounds, minimal master sets, and the uncovered lower integrals in some class-2 matrix elements remain open. This record holds the manuscript (version 11, revision 4; 38 pages), the verification bundle LITHIUM_QED_MASTER_P2_v11.zip (LaTeX source and PDF, the supplementary verification package with reference values, kernels, exact identities, the map from every statement to its source and the replay script run_checks.py , the claims ledger and the provenance of the manuscript; 3,050 files, checked by manifest.sha256 ), the clean arXiv LaTeX source, and SHA256SUMS.txt . README.md explains how to verify the files and run the checks; PAPER2_VERIFICATION/README.md inside the bundle is the entry point for the replay. Companion article: J. Matuzas, Elliptic structure of the singular three-electron Hylleraas integrals, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23858519. Generative-AI disclosure and author responsibility. ChatGPT-6 Pro (ChatGPT-5.6 Pro in parts of rounds 10 and 12; GPT-6 Astra Pro in writing the manuscript) was used for derivations, computations, and drafting; OpenAI Codex ran the production computations on a local server; Claude Opus 5.5 proposed several of the reduction steps and was used for independent re-derivation and audit of every increment. The author directed and audited the work throughout and takes full responsibility for the mathematics and the final text. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 81V45; Secondary 65D30, 65F35, 33B30, 33E05, 81-08.
title: Three-electron Hylleraas integrals with two inverse-square distances: exact reduction and high-precision evaluation for the fine structure of lithium

summary: Preprint, ChemRxiv, 30.08.2026. Abstract Air quality networks measure pollutant concentrations only at instrumented sites, leaving most locations unobserved. Graph-based virtual-node methods increasingly fill this gap, but are usually summarised by a single leave-one-station-out (LOO) R2 that leaves unstated where the model can be trusted and why it fails. Here, the operating envelope is the object of study. A graph attention network (GAT) combining multi-pollutant lags, ERA5 meteorology, MODIS aerosol optical depth, and land-use composition predicts daily-mean PM10 at unmonitored locations on the 18-station Styrian (Austria) network for 2020–2023. Under LOO cross-validation with disjoint years, the GAT reaches a median R2 of 0.52, seed-stable and ahead of Lagged-IDW (0.26), Lagged-Kriging (0.22), and Ridge-AR (0.45). At two stations whose PM10 distributions lie outside the training support, performance degrades sharply. Ablation and attribution trace the failure to one component: inverse-distanceweighted imputation of held-out lag features interacting with the persistence-residual head; graph topology is immaterial. An outlier-gated imputation policy raises pooled mean R2 from 0.31 to 0.38, node-masking training cuts per-station variance fourfold, and zeroing all auxiliary inputs lifts both outlier stations to positive R2: the partition is induced by the feature pipeline, not the architecture. The partition reproduces on NO2, and the model transfers to the 33-station Bavarian network (median R2 0.39, no negative folds). The outof-scope stations are clean-air sites under-represented in an urban-industrial network, and the worst is flagged in advance by a static-feature outlier detector: a deployable signal of where virtual-node estimates can be trusted and where the network must grow in regime diversity.
title: Graph attention networks for daily PM10 prediction at unmonitored European monitoring sites: operational scope, diagnostics, and outlier-robust training

summary: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.
title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents

summary: Pseudo-Jahn-Teller distortions can substantially alter singlet-triplet gaps, potentially reversing the predicted excited-state ordering in molecules proposed to exhibit inverted singlet-triplet (INVEST) gaps. In this study, we benchmark geometry optimization methods for 13 azaphenalenes against CCSD(T)-quality reference geometries, assessing their ability to reproduce symmetry lowering and its consequences for singlet-triplet gaps. Among the methods examined, $ω$B97M-D4 reliably describes the distorted geometries and corresponding gaps, whereas the commonly used methods B3LYP and MP2 retain high-symmetry structures, potentially leading to false-positive INVEST assignments. We further assess $ω$B97M-D4 geometries across 337 molecules comprising azaphenalenes, boron/nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and non-alternant hydrocarbons. Subsequent L-CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ calculations predict negative singlet-triplet gaps for 85 molecules and identify discrepancies with previously reported INVEST assignments. These findings demonstrate that the choice of geometry optimization method is crucial for reliable INVEST screening, particularly in systems susceptible to symmetry-breaking distortions.
title: When optimized geometries are not optimal: Implications for inverted singlet-triplet gap predictions

summary: Statistical models frequently employ nonlinear effects, interactions, and multiresolution basis expansions to represent complex relationships between predictors and responses. Determining the appropriate level of model complexity, however, remains a fundamental challenge. This paper introduces \textit{Inherited Local Shrinkage} (ILS), a Bayesian global-local shrinkage framework for adaptive functional form discovery that incorporates strong heredity among hierarchically related predictors. ILS propagates shrinkage through directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) encoding relationships among predictors, allowing increasingly complex terms to contribute only when supported by their simpler ancestors. This construction provides a common prior framework for a broad class of hierarchical regression models. We demonstrate its application to polynomial regression, as well as multiresolution modeling with two-dimensional Haar wavelet and eigenvalue-ordered spline (EVOS) bases. Although these examples illustrate specific basis systems, ILS is not tied to any particular basis construction and can be applied to any regression model in which relationships among predictors can be represented by a DAG, regardless of the graph's size or topology. Simulation studies demonstrate that ILS achieves competitive predictive performance relative to existing heredity-constrained methods while recovering underlying functional structure. Spatial applications further illustrate its ability to adaptively regulate model complexity across multiple resolutions, identifying where finer-scale detail is supported by the data. Together, these results establish ILS as a flexible framework for hierarchical complexity control and adaptive functional form discovery in Bayesian regression.
title: Inherited Local Shrinkage for Adaptive Functional Form Discovery

summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.
title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?

summary: We provide a description of general Newtonian cosmologies for collisionless matter in terms of an exact and dynamical volume partitioning of global realizations of Newtonian models. Employing the formalism for the description of cosmological backreaction, an interaction between the inhomogeneities of the formation of structures in the Universe and their average properties can be analyzed. Our results can be regarded as a tool for many potential applications in the context of Newtonian simulations, but they also provide an exact way to assume analytical properties of the universe models on regional scales in conformity with global integral constraints on their average properties. We discuss approaches in relation to `separate Universe conjectures' in the literature and examine their consistency with the exact partitioning framework. In particular, using the Average Expansion Rate Approximation (AvERA) as an example, we show that identifying locally assigned Friedmannian rates with physical regional expansion rates is constrained by the global Newtonian 3-torus condition. Alternatively, when the simulation cells are interpreted as non-material control volumes, Reynolds transport introduces mass flux and flux-backreaction terms, so that their dynamics is not in general that of independent Friedmann domains. We also discuss the corresponding consistency conditions for stable clustering prescriptions.
title: Cosmological Backreaction and the Separate Universe Conjecture: Dynamical volume partitioning of Newtonian cosmologies

summary: The continuous expansion of digital infrastructure, especially data centers, has imposed unprecedented, geographically concentrated stress on existing power grids. However, rigorous causal evidence quantifying how these facilities reshape local power-infrastructure supply remains limited. This study builds a comprehensive county-level US panel dataset spanning 2010-2024, uniquely integrating individual data center building footprints and power-plant additions. To mitigate endogeneity and high-dimensional confounding, this study deploys Double Machine Learning with five-fold cross-fitting, conditioning on county and year fixed effects alongside regional socioeconomic covariates. Baseline estimation identifies a significant positive causal effect robust across multiple rigorous specifications. The result holds following 1%-99% winsorization that downweights mega-clusters including Loudoun County: growth in data-center floor area drives meaningful increases in nearby power-generation capacity (ATE=1.982, P=0.000, CI: [1.25, 2.72]). Outcomes remain statistically significant using a one-year lagged treatment to address reverse causality, and are stable under state-level fixed-effect alternatives. An event-study framework augmented with historical agglomeration controls validates clear parallel trends and detects a sharp causal spike at t = 3, matching typical utility-scale grid-construction lead times. A placebo test further verifies these causal estimates cannot emerge from random chance. Substantial regional heterogeneity emerges: strong positive impacts concentrate in the West, while significant negative displacement-related effects appear within resource-constrained Northeastern counties. These results deliver timely insights for urban planners and energy regulators, stressing the importance of forward-looking grid-capacity investment to support ongoing digital transformation.
title: Data Center Agglomeration and Power Infrastructure Capacity in the United States

summary: When multi-agent systems act on the external world, a single agent's faulty output can spread across tasks before detection, creating a system-wide blast radius. Single-agent guardrails are confined to individual harnesses, while existing multi-agent controls either cancel only the faulty source and miss downstream consumers or halt and roll back the entire workflow at the cost of healthy work. We present Airlock, a multi-agent runtime and guardrail for selective post-alert fault containment. Its tree-structured runtime, EdgeCitadel, narrows permissions vertically from parent to child agents to establish node boundaries and control switches. Meanwhile, an append-only provenance DAG records cross-agent data consumption horizontally. Upon an alert, Airlock traces forward on this DAG to isolate tainted executions and pending actions, and backward to narrow root causes. At the site switches, a default full quarantine tier freezes affected branches without a solver, while an assured optimized cut tier uses fence-then-prune to enforce a deadline-aware minimum cut minimizing collateral disruption. Across 1,832 testbed runs, 161 physical smart-home LLM runs, and 24,266 simulation records, Airlock blocks all post-alert faulty actuations on our main testbed and smart-home grids with zero post-convergence leaks. Whereas native controls in A2A and LangGraph either contain at most 33.3% of faults or retain at most 16% of work without redo, Airlock retains +68 pp to +96 pp more healthy work, and its optimized cut retains +46 pp more than full quarantine under dense spread. These results show that co-designing runtime authority boundaries with online provenance enables surgical fault containment without sacrificing healthy work (code: https://github.com/EdgeCitadelTeam/EdgeCitadel).
title: Airlock: Bounding the Multi-Agent Blast Radius via Selective Online Containment

summary: IntroductionResilience is considered of high relevance when developing interventions to cope with stressful situations. Schools are one of the key settings to promote resilience among adolescents. The purpose of this cluster randomized controlled trial is to assess the effectiveness of an intervention in adolescents at risk, aged 12-to-15 years old, to increase resilience and emotional regulation strategies.MethodsThe recruitment period started in January 2022. Schools will be randomly allocated to control and intervention groups by an external researcher using computer-generated random numbers. The minimum sample size was estimated to be 70 participants per group. Primary health care nurses will carry out the intervention during the school period (January to June 2022). Students will follow a specific training consisting of six 55-min sessions, for 6 weeks. Each session will consist of 5 min of mindfulness, followed by 45 min of the corresponding activity: introducing resilience, self-esteem, emotional regulation strategies, social skills, problem-solving, community resources, social and peer support, and 5 min to explain the activity to do at home. Data will be collected at baseline, 6 weeks, and 24 weeks after the intervention. The child youth resilience measure-32 (CYRM-32) scale will be used to assess the effectiveness of the intervention. This study received a grant in June 2021.DiscussionThe intervention is intended to improve mental health through resilience. Different factors related to resilience will be promoted, such as self-esteem, emotional regulation, social and communication skills, problem-solving and peer support, among others. As it has been designed as a cluster-randomized school-based intervention, we will directly ameliorate the participation and engagement of the target population. With the present intervention, we expect to improve coping skills in adolescents by enhancing resilience capacities. Copyright © 2023 Llistosella, Torné, García-Ortiz, López-Hita, Ortiz, Herández-Montero, Guallart, Uña-Solbas and Miranda-Mendizabal.
title: Fostering Resilience in Adolescents at Risk: Study protocol for a cluster randomized controlled trial within the resilience school-based intervention

summary: Background The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) strategy to face the challenges of ageing societies. This strategy is focused on person centered care and the assessment intrinsic capacity (IC). Early identification of five domains of IC (cognition, locomotion, vitality, sensory (hearing and vision), and psychological) has been shown to be related with adverse outcomes and can guide actions towards primary prevention and healthy ageing. IC assessment proposed by the WHO ICOPE guidelines is composed by two steps: First, Screening for decreased IC by the ICOPE Screening tool; second, by the reference standard methods. The aim was to assess the performance of diagnostic measures (sensibility, specificity, diagnostic accuracy, and agreement of the ICOPE Screening tool) compared to the reference standard methods in European community-dwelling older adults. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of the baseline of the ongoing VIMCI (Validity of an Instrument to Measure Intrinsic Capacity) cohort study, which was carried out in Primary Care centers and outpatient clinics from 5 rural and urban territories in Catalonia (Spain). Participants were 207 community dwelling persons >= 70-year-old with Barthel >= 90, without dementia or advanced chronic conditions who provided their consent to participate. The 5 IC domains were assessed by the ICOPE Screening tool and the reference methods (SPPB, gait speed, MNA, Snellen chart, audiometry, MMSE, GDS5) during patients' visit. Agreement was assessed with the Gwet AC1 index. Results ICOPE Screening tool sensitivity was higher for cognition (0.889) and ranged between 0.438 and 0.569 for most domains. Specificity ranged from 0.682 to 0.96, diagnostic accuracy from 0.627 to 0.879, Youden index from 0.12 to 0.619, and Gwet AC1 from 0.275 to 0.842. Conclusion The ICOPE screening tool showed fair performance of diagnostic measures; it was helpful to identify those participants with satisfactory IC and showed a modest ability to identify decreased IC in older people with high degree of autonomy. Since low sensitivities were found, a process of external validation would be recommended to © 2023. The Author(s).
title: Identification of decreased intrinsic capacity: Performance of diagnostic measures of the ICOPE Screening tool in community dwelling older people in the VIMCI study

summary: Introduction: Basic life support training in school age is a topical issue because, with adequate training, any person can help save a life.Methods: Cluster clinical trial with data collection through an ad hoc self-administered, semi -structured questionnaire. The target population encompassed the students aged 4--6 years enrolled in 49 educational centres. The centres were randomly allocated to the intervention or control group. The intervention group was trained with the RCParvulari (R) methodology, consisting of theoretical and practical training on the first link of the chain of survival. The control group only received theoretical training. We evaluated participants before and immediately after the intervention and between 3 and 12 months post-intervention by means of the ques-tionnaire. We assessed the acquisition and retention over time of the knowledge and skills covered in the training compared to previous trainings in both groups.Results: A total of 1327 schoolchildren (79% of the target population) participated. The level of knowledge acquired immediately after training and after 3-12 months compared to baseline was significantly better (P <.001) in the intervention group than in the control group, both in early recognition and contacting of emergency services (112) and in remembering the "mouth -nose-eyes " mnemonic.Conclusions: The RCParvulari (R) methodology significantly contributed to an improved ability to recognize a possible medical emergency, start the chain of survival by alerting an adult and call the 112 emergency number in students in the last year of preschool education.
title: RCParvulari training: A basic life support training methodology applied to 5-year-old students: Effectiveness in a cluster-randomized clinical trail

summary: PREPRINT SUBMITTED TO RENEW 2026 CONFERENCE.   MoodyMarine is an open-access weakly nonlinear potential flow solver for wave-body and mooring interactions. In this study the capabilities of MoodyMarine for modeling tension-leg-platform (TLP) type floating offshore wind turbines (FOWT) is assessed. A TLP-type platform has been simulated for four wave cases of increase wave steepness and compared to experimental data measurements of surge, heave, pitch, and mooring-line tension. A qualitatively and quantitatively comparison has been carried out using the root-mean-square error (RMSE), the relative root-mean-square-error (RRMSE), and the correlation coefficient (R). A numerical calibration was carried out for the baseline wave condition showing that the required initial experimental mooring stiffness had to be reduced from K = 132N/mm to K = 50N/mm to ensure good agreement between experimental and numerical data. Pitch motion agreement improved significantly (88.4 % reduction in RRMSE), while surge responses experienced small variations since surge is dominated by wave excitation rather than tendon stiffness. Mooring line tensions showed only a small improvement, as the baseline tension errors were already low. For the rest of the validation cases MoodyMarine showed good agreement with the experimental data while keeping the computational time to 0.152 s of CPU time per 1 s of simulated time.
title: NUMERICAL VALIDATION OF A FLOATING OFFSHORE WIND TLP-TYPE PLATFORM USING MOODYMARINE

summary: The exponential increase in the number of people suffering chronic illness has become a problem for which healthcare services need a response. The inclusion of self-care and positive mental health as part of a strategy to promote health offers an opportunity for a reorganization oriented towards community spaces and group interventions. This study undertook the assessment of an intervention designed to optimize the agency of and capacity for self-care and positive mental health by utilizing activities drawn from the Nursing Intervention Classification (NIC), specifically from Field 3 (Behavioral), and organized as a program called PIPsE. A quasi-experimental design was prepared with an intervention group (n = 22) and a control group (n = 22), in a primary care center in the Barcelona metropolitan area. The instruments used were two ad hoc questionnaires to collect sociodemographic and satisfaction information and two scales: the Appraisal of Self-care Agency Scale (ASA) and the Positive Mental Health Questionnaire (PMHQ). The results obtained showed a significant increase in self-care capacity and both overall positive mental health and mental health by factors in the intervention group.
title: Nursing Intervention to Improve Positive Mental Health and Self-Care Skills in People with Chronic Physical Health Conditions

summary: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.
title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors

summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge

summary: We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks. LifeVal covers the most valuable life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate, representing over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories (e.g., managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, finding childcare). To construct our activity distribution, we conducted a new survey of willingness-to-pay for a digital superassistant across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referencing our results against the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) and the Multinational Time Use Study (Fisher et al., 2025). For the most valuable consumer activities, we recruited task creators to create AI evaluation tasks personalized using real ChatGPT conversations and memories, reference files, and personal context. Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year) and also write a rubric, ensuring that our evaluation measured the best personalized completion for that task. All tasks had to pass at least three rounds of human quality-control before acceptance into our final evaluation sets.
title: LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks

summary: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
title: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models

summary: Resource management for distributed edge networks hosting different services has been handled efficiently using Reinforcement learning (RL). Reward generalization in complex workflows is still an open issue within the RL realm. Therefore, this work proposes RAGAM-AI, a hybrid framework that combines the capabilities of RL algorithms and Generative-AI (Gen-AI) for powering an Agentic AI workflow that optimizes resource allocation at the Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) units. This framework further resolves the reward generalization issue by utilizing Large Language Model (LLM) for feedback. A Multi- Agent Soft-Actor Critic (MASAC) using MathΣtral as a reward oracle is implemented for managing resource allocations at the MEC. RAGAM-AI interprets system state information and evaluates multi-objective trade-offs guiding the resource orchestration loop over distributed edge server agents. The complexity of the framework is further brought down by incorporating surrogate reward model. The overall performance is evaluated against the single agent SAC, REINFORCE and random policies for benchmarking. On using RAGAM-AI, lower allocation deviations for CPU, memory and bandwidth resources are reported while minimizing the latency and data rate costs. A scalable AI as a feedback (AIAF) solution optimizing network resources with significant performance improvement is thus presented.
title: RAGAM-AI: A Hybrid Reinforcement Learning based Agentic approach powered by Generative AI for Edge Resource Management

summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.
title: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability

summary: Reconstructing cell lineages from 3D time-lapse microscopy requires distinguishing cell motion from division and inferring temporally consistent connections. When only a subset of cells is annotated, however, training procedures that treat unannotated regions as background or incorrect correspondences can be problematic. We propose a cell tracking pipeline that integrates detection from sparse annotations, calibration of candidate connections using image features, and joint selection of lineage graph events. For detection, we combine the outputs of 2.5D and 3D models trained to suppress erroneous background supervision at unannotated cells. We then calibrate ordinary link and division probabilities using motion features from dense flow, correspondence features from a learned cell-matching model, and features from models that identify cells immediately before division, dividing parents, and daughters immediately after division. Ordinary links, divisions represented as daughter pairs, and node inclusion are selected jointly under a surrogate objective derived from the evaluation metric, followed by gap filling and temporal coordinate refinement. The pipeline achieves an overall score of 0.9762 in 5-fold cross-validation on 199 videos from 2 zebrafish embryos. With candidates and calibrated values held fixed, joint selection outperforms a sequential method that allows replacement of existing divisions and reoptimization of ordinary links by 0.0105. The improvement arises primarily from division recovery.
title: Learning to Track Cells from Sparse Annotations in 3D Time-Lapse Microscopy

summary: Offline reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on a fixed pool of sampled responses and typically supervises every token of every response, although responses and tokens are not equally informative. We study which ones to supervise through the Gibbs-optimal policy of KL-regularized RLVR, which offline training targets, and measure the mismatch between a policy and this target with a bidirectional KL divergence. At the reference policy, this mismatch factorizes exactly and separates the two outcomes: correct responses contribute mainly through the forward term, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and incorrect responses through the reverse term, concentrated on the responses the policy generates often and on their high-probability tokens. Based on this analysis, we propose GIST (Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection), a two-level selection method that approximates these principles with signals available before training. GIST uses the sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy's mode, and it uses the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies. Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises the average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP for all three models under both objectives. In a controlled comparison on Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.
title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR

summary: BackgroundAn outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) occurred in young people from Catalonia (Spain) who travelled to Menorca (Spain) in summer 2021. This outbreak appeared when governments relaxed Covid-19 preventive measures: the mask usage and the opening of nightlife. It was related to a super-disseminating mass event: Sant Joan festivities in Ciutadella. The aim of this article is to describe an outbreak of COVID-19 in young people aged 17-19 years from Catalonia travelling to Menorca. MethodsThis is an observational study of a COVID-19 outbreak. The study population comprised Catalonian youth aged 17-19 years who travelled to Menorca from 15 June to 10 July. Epidemiological descriptive indicators were obtained. Descriptive and geographical statistics were carried out. Bivariate Moran's I test was used to identify spatial autocorrelation between the place of residence and deprivation. The outbreak control method was based on identifying and stopping chains of transmission by implementing the test-trace-isolate-quarantine (TTIQ) strategy. ResultsWe identified 515 confirmed cases infected in Menorca, 296 (57.5%) in girls and 219 (42.5%) in boys, with a total of 2,280 close contacts. Of them, 245 (10.7%) were confirmed as cases. The cases were diagnosed between 15 June and 10 July. None of the persons with confirmed infection died or required hospitalisation. The attack rate was 27.2%. There was an inverse relationship between deprivation and number of confirmed cases (p<0.005), there were clusters of confirmed cases in the most socioeconomic favoured areas. DiscussionThe outbreak is related with young people from socioeconomic favoured areas who travelled to Menorca in summer 2021. Failure to comply with preventive measures in binge-drinking events and during holidays may have favoured SARS-CoV-2 transmission. The interauthority coordination and establishment of a clear line of leadership allowed continuous communication between institutions, which were key to managing this complex COVID-19 outbreak.
title: A large outbreak of COVID-19 linked to an end of term trip to Menorca (Spain) by secondary school students in summer 2021

summary: This curated dataset contains locally available records from a postharvest dragon-fruit (pitaya) campaign: 311 original RGB JPEG images organized by storage day (0, 7, 14, 21, and 25), 193 macro-enabled electronic-nose exports, electronic-nose derived matrices, NIR response/analysis workbooks, and 26 readable chemometric and ANOVA reports. A SHA-256 file manifest is supplied for all 551 data files. The data are related to Ferreira et al. (2024), Deep computer vision system and explainable artificial intelligence applied for classification of dragon fruit (Hylocereus spp.) , published in Scientia Horticulturae . The publisher PDF is not included; the record links to the article DOI. The README and data dictionary identify critical provenance limits. summary: This deposit contains the data and the analysis code that reproduce the Methods and Results of a systematic review of polymer-based dental materials incorporating an engineered self-healing mechanism. The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework on 26 October 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QCZFY) before formal screening and before any data were extracted. The review separates three contrasts that the literature conflates under the single heading of healing efficiency: C-I, the baseline penalty of the self-healing material in its virgin state against a capsule-free control; C-II, the recovery of the repaired material against the same material in its virgin state; and C-III, the net position of the repaired material against a conventional material without a healing system. The effect measure is the log ratio of means, back-transformed to a ratio and a percentage. Contents. The extraction matrix holds 105 arm-level rows covering four studies and 17 harmonised outcomes, each row linked to the exact formulation of both arms, the source page and the provenance of the value. Four further tables record the full-text eligibility decisions for the 48 assessed reports, the re-screening of the 96 discarded reports against the registered criteria, the characteristics of the studies carrying extracted data, and the register of 16 departures from the registered protocol. The R pipeline recomputes the 89 arm-level contrasts, the three pre-specified contrasts, the efficient-frontier criterion, both manuscript figures and the main and supplementary effect tables. A validation script asserts 21 reported values and halts the pipeline on any mismatch. Reproduction. R 4.4 or later with the metafor package is the only requirement. Running "Rscript run_all.R" from the root of the package regenerates every output in a few seconds and writes a session record alongside them. Limits of these data. Sixty of the 105 rows derive wholly or partly from provisional single-reader readings of figure panels and were not validated by duplicate digitisation; the provenance columns identify them. Five contrasts have a mean of zero in the numerator or the denominator, so the ratio of means is undefined for them. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were not assessed. Arm-level data were extracted from four of the 39 included studies. Licensing. Data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; the code under R/, run_all.R and legacy/ is released under the MIT Licence.
title: Self-healing dental polymers: extraction matrix and analysis code for a systematic review with endpoint harmonisation

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: Description This repository contains the Python implementation, numerical experiments, analysis outputs, and figures associated with the manuscript Sharp Bounds for Raman Band-Area Ratios . The study investigates the identifiability of Raman band-area ratios under explicit constraints on baseline curvature, measurement noise, nonnegativity, and band-free anchor regions. Sharp identification intervals are computed using linear programming, while an analytical bound is used to examine the influence of spectral geometry and integration-window selection. The accompanying materials support the reported simulation studies, analytical-bound evaluations, semi-synthetic validation on measured backgrounds, and analysis of nitrate–nitrite mixtures. The original experimental Raman spectra are publicly available from Mendeley Data: https://doi.org/10.17632/cxf3zxsc3k.3 . Funding: This research received no external funding.
tags: Raman spectroscopy, Band-area ratios, Baseline correction, Identifiability, Linear programming, Python
title: harp Bounds for Raman Band-Area Ratios

summary: Proving an alternating-current optimal power flow solution globally ε-optimal usually takes a convex-relaxation solve per instance. Most of these solves can be reused. For a fixed multiplier, the box-constrained Lagrangian bound of a conic relaxation is affine in the load, so a multiplier computed once gives a lower bound at every load by an inner product. Where the relaxation's prices vary smoothly in few load directions, packing numbers in their number bound the size of a library from above and, under a curvature assumption, from below, and solving the relaxation only where the library falls short stays within the upper bound; where prices are constant within operating regimes, one multiplier per regime suffices. On eight benchmark systems of 14 to 500 buses, one multiplier per regime certifies nearly as many loads as a thousand, and a library used first makes an interior-point-plus-relaxation pipeline 3.0 to 15.2 times faster at ε = 0.5%, depending on the baseline configuration, and 8.9 times while proving both bounds. Grown this way over a year of hourly loads of a modified 2000-bus Texas grid, a library certified 98.2% of the hours with 252 solves.
title: Amortized and Rigorous Optimality Certificates for AC Optimal Power Flow via Load-Affine Dual Libraries

summary: LLMatter2D grounds pre-trained large language models (run locally through LM Studio, Ollama, or hosted APIs) in curated, citable data on two-dimensional materials: DFT electronic structure from C2DB, MC2D, 2DMatPedia and JARVIS-DFT, Wannier90 tight-binding models, geometry and ARPES observables. A hybrid retrieval layer (metadata filters plus embeddings) feeds the model, which answers with record-level citations. A generator built on the eleven Archimedean lattices proposes new 2D materials, screens them with nearest-neighbour tight-binding (flat bands, Dirac crossings) and exports structures for DFT validation. The package includes a benchmark comparing retrieval-augmented and closed-book answers.
title: LLMatter2D: retrieval-augmented LLM for the analysis and discovery of two-dimensional materials

summary: Code, data and outputs that reproduce a study of carbon embodied in China–EU trade and of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The archive covers three analyses: (1) CO2 embodied in China–EU27 trade, 2011–2022, from a global multi-regional input–output model (EXIOBASE 3.9.6, with release 3.8.2 for reconciliation and sensitivity); (2) China's potential CBAM certificate costs, 2026–2034; (3) EU27 imports from higher- and lower-carbon origins after CBAM reporting began, using a PPML triple-difference design on monthly Eurostat Comext data, January 2018 to July 2026. It contains the Python, R and Stata code, the analysis panel, derived input–output results, CBAM parameter files, codebooks, download manifests with checksums, and the output tables, figures and logs. The EXIOBASE 3.9.6 carbon multipliers and the ICAP daily price data are not included, in line with the source licences; the code to rebuild or process them is provided. Start with README_replication_archive.md. Code is released under the MIT licence and data under CC BY-SA 4.0 or CC BY 4.0, as set out in LICENSE.md.
title: Replication archive: Embodied CO2 in China–EU trade and early responses to the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism
