summary: This dataset supports the study “Documented Monitoring Readiness in Local Strategic Environmental Assessment: Evidence from Surakarta and Magelang, Indonesia.” It contains the original scores assigned independently by two researchers, documentary evidence and source-page references, the record of how 131 scoring disagreements were resolved, final agreed scores, and summaries of all 107 indicator–recommendation units: 35 from Surakarta and 72 from Magelang. Each unit was assessed across six dimensions: baseline, target, responsible agency, data source, monitoring schedule, and documented follow-up mechanism. Original scores were used to calculate inter-coder agreement, while final agreed scores were used to report the findings. The dataset assesses information documented in the two KLHS reports; it does not measure actual monitoring performance or environmental outcomes.
title: Supporting Dataset for Documented Monitoring Readiness in Local Strategic Environmental Assessment: Surakarta and Magelang, Indonesia

summary: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.
title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue

summary: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.
title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data

summary: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout

summary: Online Convex Optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) is a recently-introduced framework that captures the dynamics of stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with budget constraints. Despite its expressive power, COCO-M remains largely understudied. In this work, we tackle this problem in its full scale, providing an optimistic algorithm that incorporates untrusted predictions to tame universal dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation. Our analysis leverages a potent reduction from memory to delay and treats state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback. We establish the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity (path length $P_T$) and prediction accuracy, while lifting previous restrictive assumptions such as functional separability. En route to these results, we derive findings of independent interest for the memory-to-delay reduction, and for delayed OCO with time-varying constraints. The proposed framework ensures sublinear worst-case guarantees that improve with prediction accuracy, reaching $\mathcal O(1)$ regret under perfect predictions, with cumulative constraint violation (CCV) $\mathcal O(\sqrt{T})$ for unknown $P_T$ and $\mathcal O(\log T)$ for known or online observable $P_T$ , while recovering the optimal COCO rates when memory disappears.
title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence

summary: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.
title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression

summary: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on pretrained vision-language backbones; both tie policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. It remains unclear how much these generation-oriented choices affect control. In this work, we introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. Following Fast-WAM, La-JEPA learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competing policies. It runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance and outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to pi0.5 and above non-embodied-pretrained baselines. Through a design study of the choices behind La-JEPA, we show that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction choices significantly impact the policy even when future prediction is skipped at inference. We correct the LIBERO-Plus instructions, as the officially released evaluator corrupts them for most variants, and re-evaluate several strong open baselines. Without a generative pretrained policy backbone, La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling

summary: In large-scale payment networks, entities (card, merchant, etc.) and their interactions play a key role in transaction anomaly detection. However, transaction patterns between different entities usually change more frequently than the production model refresh schedule. Meanwhile, entity embedding tables suffer from high-cardinality and sparse interaction issues. To resolve the above challenges, we present PersonaAgent, an agentic transaction anomaly detection framework which represents the latest entity behavior signals as personas and saves them in a refreshable memory. Offline, a weekly scheduled batch job is used to extract the latest behavior signals and update them in the memory. At inference time, a lightweight adapter retrieves the corresponding entity behavior signals of each transaction from memory and uses them to augment the base anomaly classifier's scoring. Through comprehensive benchmarking with different anomaly detection models at Visa, PersonaAgent is able to score transactions efficiently (a 1,000-transaction CPU batch in 1-2 ms), lifting the PR-AUC by 0.65-6.58% and the production business metric by 8.93-14.24% relatively in deployment.
title: PersonaAgent: Retrieval-Augmented Transaction Anomaly Scoring with Refreshable Multi-Entity Persona Memory

summary: Tensor network kernel machines (TNKMs) combine nonlinear features with low-rank tensor representations to model complex relationships efficiently. However, selecting an appropriate tensor rank remains challenging, as conventional rank-search methods require training multiple candidate models, increasing computational costs. In this work, we focus on a canonical polyadic (CP) tensor network parameterization and propose GB-CPKM, a gradient boosting framework that builds a higher-capacity predictor by sequentially adding fixed-rank learners. This approach provides a new perspective on rank selection by incrementally increasing model capacity, with ensemble size selected based on validation performance rather than through explicit rank search. Experiments on real-world regression benchmarks show that GB-CPKM trains up to 6x faster and uses up to 2x less peak memory than a conventional rank-selection method based on cross-validation, while achieving comparable predictive performance. These results highlight the potential of gradient boosting to improve the computational efficiency and scalability of tensor-network learning.
title: Gradient Boosting for Efficient Rank Discovery in Tensor Network Kernel Machines

summary: Real-time voice agents need a speech recognizer that never waits for future audio and whose memory per call does not grow with the length of the call. We present E-Gaborformer, a strictly causal encoder that combines Gated DeltaNet-2 recurrent layers with sliding-window attention in a 3:1 ratio, and builds every temporal convolution from a fixed dictionary of causal Gabor atoms. Its streaming state is constant, about 19 MB per call at production scale including the prediction network, where a causal-attention encoder of the same size accumulates over 1 GB after ten minutes. In a controlled causal study on LibriSpeech, E-Gaborformer leaves the initial plateau earlier, reaches a given accuracy up to 18% sooner, and matches or beats an E-Branchformer trained with the identical front end and recipe. At production scale, a 0.6B-parameter Hebrew and English streaming transducer built on E-Gaborformer has 28 to 31% lower word error rate (WER) than NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming, a model of the same size, on English voice-agent traffic, and up to 20% lower Hebrew WER than our previous production system. The same weights serve strictly causal and 480 ms-lookahead decoding with no loss in accuracy, and a two-class formulation of the RNN-T lattice trains the transducer 2.6x faster with exact loss and gradients.
title: Gabor Gabor: E-Gaborformer, a Strictly Causal Speech Recognizer with Gabor-Dictionary Convolutions and Delta-Rule Memory

summary: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.
title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels

summary: The goal of this paper is to investigate the following question: what geometric restrictions does the existence of a transitive family of constant mean curvature hyperspheres impose on a Riemannian metric on $\mathbb S^n$? The notion of a transitive family can be made precise through the theory of Zoll families developed by Ambrozio, Marques, and Neves. Within this framework, we partially extend their local rigidity theorem for even conformal factors on $\mathbb S^3$ to every dimension $n\ge4$, assuming each hypersphere in the minimal Zoll family has the area of a round equator. Moreover, we give a partial answer to the following higher-dimensional version of a question posed by Robert Bryant: must a metric on $\mathbb S^n$, conformal to the round metric and admitting a Zoll family of hyperspheres with a common nonzero constant mean curvature, have constant sectional curvature? Finally, we also investigate inverse problems in the spirit of Hangan, asking which metrics make a fixed family of geodesic spheres have a common prescribed mean curvature.
title: Spheres with transitive families of CMC hypersurfaces

summary: Reconstructing turbulent flow fields from sparse and irregular measurements remains challenging because the underlying inverse problem is severely underdetermined. Here we present MANTRA, a manifold-based tensor framework that represents each velocity component in a continuous tensor-product space while constraining its coefficient tensor to a low-rank Tucker manifold. This structure provides a compact, data-adaptive representation without requiring gridded observations or governing equations. Riemannian optimization and adaptive selection of rank and basis complexity enable the model to exploit coordinate-wise spatiotemporal correlations. In simulations of forced isotropic turbulence and flow over a cylinder, MANTRA recovers multiscale structures at sampling densities orders of magnitude below the underlying grids and remains accurate under Gaussian noise up to 20% of the peak velocity. It also recovers leading coordinate-wise correlation structures from sparse observations. Applied to experimental particle-tracking velocimetry of an oscillating impinging jet, MANTRA reveals time-evolving structures that are not apparent from the scattered measurements alone.
title: Low-Rank Tensor Manifolds for Turbulent Field Reconstruction from Sparse Data

summary: Two-phase designs provide a cost-effective framework for biomarker studies and have been widely used to reduce the burden of collecting expensive biomarker measurements. Most methodological research has focused on efficient Phase II sampling and estimation of biomarker--outcome associations. A natural subsequent step, however, is to incorporate identified biomarkers into risk prediction models, where measures of predictive performance become important inferential targets. Even for binary outcomes, methodological developments for two-phase designs that jointly address association parameters and predictive performance remain limited. Building on classical case-control and matched case-control designs developed primarily for association inference with binary outcomes, we propose a risk-matched case-control (RMCC) design that uses a scalar disease-risk score constructed from Phase I variables to define matching strata and guide Phase II sampling. To address the limitations of existing likelihood-based approaches, which typically require correct specification of the nuisance distribution of biomarkers, we develop a unified design-based inference framework based on inverse probability weighting for both association parameters and predictive performance measures, including positive predictive value and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. We further introduce target-specific weight scaling and calibration procedures and derive variance estimators that account for sampling variability in both phases. Simulation studies demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of the proposed design and inference procedures, and an application to a Taiwanese oral cancer cohort illustrates their potential utility.
title: Risk-matched case-control sampling and semiparametric weight calibration for efficient biomarker assessment with binary outcomes

summary: This work identifies a fundamental, controller-independent limitation in reusable launch vehicle powered descent: a sudden $180^\circ$ phase transition in the open-loop transfer functions from the control inputs to the lateral drift and drift rate. The transition occurs inside the flight envelope, reverses the effective control direction, and can destabilize the closed loop system under uncertainty. An analytical condition governing this transition is derived, its physical mechanism is established, and its dependence on vehicle mass, aerodynamic properties, and geometry is characterized. An Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI)-based control architecture is then developed to inherently address this limitation and is tuned via $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Closed Loop Shaping to provide local robustness and performance guarantees. The internal dynamics introduced by the INDI inversion are analytically derived and proven to be stable throughout the flight envelope. The proposed controller is compared against a robust gain-scheduled baseline controller through linear stability analysis and an extensive nonlinear Monte Carlo campaign. Both controllers achieve 100% success across the considered Monte Carlo campaign, though the INDI-based controller provides improved tracking performance, superior nominal and dispersed stability margins, requires fewer controller design points, and reduces controller tuning complexity.
title: Overcoming Fundamental Control Limitations in Powered Descent Flight through Robust Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion

summary: Bacterial cellulose biofilms are complex networks of strong interwoven nanofibers that control transport and protect bacterial colonies in the film. Design of diverse applications of bacterial cellulose films also relies on understanding and controlling transport through the fiber mesh, and transport simulations of the films are most accurate when guided by experimental characterization of the structures and the resultant diffusion inside. Diffusion through such films is a function of their key microstructural length scales, determining how molecules, as well as particles and microorganisms, permeate them. We use microscopy to study the unique bacterial cellulose film structure and quantify the mobility dynamics of various sizes of tracer particles and macromolecules. Mobility is hindered within the films, as confinement and local movement strongly depend on void size relative to diffusing tracers. The biofilms have a naturally periodic structure of alternating dense and porous layers of nanofiber mesh, and we tune the magnitude of the spacing via fermentation conditions. Micron-sized particles can diffuse through the porous layers, but can not penetrate the dense layers. Tracer mobility in the porous layers is isotropic, indicating a largely random pore structure there. Molecular diffusion through the whole film is only slightly reduced by the structural tortuosity. Knowledge of transport variations within bacterial cellulose networks can be used to guide design of symbiotic cultures in these structures and enhance their use in applications biomedical implants, wound dressings, lab-grown meat, and sensors.
title: Molecular and colloidal transport in bacterial cellulose hydrogels

summary: Bacterial cellulose is an important class of biomaterials which can be grown in well-controlled laboratory and industrial conditions. The cellulose structure is affected by several biological, chemical and environmental factors, including hydrodynamic flows in bacterial suspensions. In this work, we explore the possibility of using well controlled turbulent flow to control the bacterial cellulose production. Turbulent flows leading to random motion of fluid elements may affect the structure of the extracellular polymeric matrix produced by bacteria. Here we show that two-dimensional turbulence at the air-liquid interface generates chaotic rotation at a well-defined scale and random persistent stretching of the fluid elements. The results offer new approaches to engineering of the bacterial cellulose structure by controlling turbulence parameters.
title: Turbulence-assisted formation of bacterial cellulose

summary: Hydrogels provide a solution-mimicking environment for the interaction with living systems that make them desirable for various biomedical and technological applications. Because relevant biological processes in living tissues occur at the biomolecular scale, hydrogel nanopatterning can be leveraged to attain novel material properties and functionalities. However, the fabrication of high aspect ratio (HAR) nanostructures in hydrogels capable of self-standing in aqueous environments, with fine control of the size and shape distribution, remains challenging. Here, we report the synthesis of nanostructures with a HAR in bacterial cellulose (BC) hydrogel via directed plasma nanosynthesis using argon ions. The nanostructures in BC are reproducible, stable to sterilization, and liquid immersion. Using in-situ surface characterization and semi-empirical modeling, we discovered that pattern formation was linked to the formation of graphite-like clusters composed of a mixture of C-C and C=C bonds. Moreover, our model predicts that reactive species at the onset of the argon irradiation accelerate the bond breaking of weak bonds, contributing to the formation of an amorphous carbon layer and nanopattern growth.
title: Ion-induced nanopatterning of a bacterial cellulose hydrogel

summary: The interparticle interactions in a magnetic nanocomposite play a dominant role in controlling the phase transitions superparamagnetic to superspinglass to superferromagnetic. These interactions can be tuned by controlling the size and number density of nanoparticles. Aerogel composites, 0.3 Ni-BC and 0.7 Ni-BC, consisting of Ni nanoparticles distributed in bacterial cellulose have been used as model systems to study the effect of interparticle interactions with increasing fraction of Ni in the composite. Contrary to conventional approach, the size of Ni nanoparticles is not controlled and was allowed to form naturally in the bacterial cellulose template. The structural characterization using x-ray diffraction and electron microscopies indicates the presence of only Ni and cellulose with no other phases. The uncontrolled growth of Ni in cellulose matrix results in the formation of nanoparticles with 3 different size distributions - 10 nm particles mainly distributed along the length of fibrils, 50 nm particles present in the intermediate spaces between the fibrils and 100 nm particles present in voids formed by the reticulate structure. At room temperature the composites exhibit a weakly ferromagnetic behavior with a coercivity of 40 Oe which increases to 160 Oe at 10 K. The transition from weakly ferromagnetic state at room temperature to a superferromagnetic state at low temperatures is mediated via a superspinglass state at intermediate temperatures. A temperature dependent microstructural model has been developed combining the structural and magnetic results obtained from the two composite aerogels.
title: Interparticle interactions mediated superspinglass to superferromagnetic transition in Ni-bacterial cellulose aerogel nanocomposites

summary: This is a health and safety subset of a larger dataset. It includes soil measurements from treatment and control areas collected at baseline, post-spreading, and post-weathering; shared feedstock characterization; weather data; and project, field-management, sampling, and analytical metadata.

summary: Background: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are persistent, hydrophobic and in several cases carcinogenic pollutants of soils and sediments. Bacterial degradation of high-molecular-weight PAHs is slow because of their low bioavailability, which has directed attention to ligninolytic fungi that attack pollutants extracellularly. Scope: This narrative review, based exclusively on published secondary data (1983–2024), examines the diversity of ligninolytic fungi, their enzyme systems, the biochemical mechanisms of PAH transformation, the factors that control degradation in soil, and the evidence from pilot- and field-scale applications. Key findings: Lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase (including lipid-peroxidation chemistry), versatile peroxidase and laccase–mediator systems oxidise PAHs to quinones and ring-fission products, while cytochrome P450 monooxygenases and unspecific peroxygenases form dihydrodiols and phenols. Fungi mineralise only part of the oxidised carbon, but their polar products are readily mineralised by soil bacteria. Field trials – from US demonstrations with Phanerochaete sordida to tonne-scale Finnish piles inoculated on pine bark and Danish trials with spent oyster-mushroom substrate – confirm that inoculation and colonisation are feasible, but improvements over indigenous microbial activity have been inconsistent and strongly site-dependent, limited by bioavailability, competition and logistics. Conclusion: Ligninolytic fungi are most promising for soils dominated by high-molecular-weight PAHs and as partners in integrated fungal–bacterial treatment. Soil-competent strains, low-cost lignocellulosic carriers, attention to bioavailability and standardised metabolite and toxicity monitoring are required for reliable field deployment.
tags: white-rot fungi; mycoremediation; polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; lignin peroxidase; manganese peroxidase; laccase; cytochrome P450; spent mushroom substrate; field-scale bioremediation
title: Ligninolytic Fungi in Bioremediation: Mechanism of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon (Pah) Degradation and Field Applications

summary: Grant-free uplink access in low-Earth-orbit (LEO) non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) poses a coordination challenge when multiple UEs share a satellite channel without real-time centralized scheduling under long propagation delays and time-varying channels. Conventional random access does not exploit peer context, leading to collisions and inefficient channel use as contention increases. To address this problem, we propose IRIS, a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for decentralized grant-free direct-to-satellite (D2S) uplink access, with A2A-IRIS as its sidelink-assisted Agent-to-Agent (A2A) realization. Each UE executes a shared binary transmission policy using local traffic/channel information augmented by compact peer states exchanged over UE-to-UE sidelink, while Vanilla-IRIS serves as a local-only ablation. Evaluations in rural and suburban LEO D2S deployments use TLE-based trajectories propagated using the Simplified General Perturbations 4 (SGP4), with a Walker-Delta constellation as fallback. A2A-IRIS achieves 2.1579 and 5.4478 Mbps, corresponding to 99.9% and 96.1% of the respective scenario-specific upper bounds. Relative to Vanilla-IRIS, throughput improves by 40.8% and 325.0%, with collision rates of 0.0000 and 0.0433, while one- and two-epoch delayed centralized schedulers are outperformed by approximately 51--130%. A2A-IRIS also improves fairness, service coverage, and transmission efficiency with moderate Deep Q-Network (DQN) inference overhead. Active-UE load scalability results further show sustained performance over the evaluated load range. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of sidelink-assisted A2A coordination for decentralized LEO D2S uplink access under propagation delay and delayed channel feedback.
title: IRIS: Intelligent Random Access with Integrated Shared Learning for Decentralized LEO Direct-to-Satellite Uplinks

summary: Thermal Quantum Annealing (tQuA) is a quantum architecture in which a system coupled non-adiabatically to a thermodynamic reservoir evolves toward the ground state of a target Hamiltonian . This paper provides a rigorous and honest foundation for tQuA and its extension to Quantum Intelligent Matrix Methods (QIMM). We distinguish carefully among Theorems (proved in cited literature), Propositions (proof sketches with explicitly identified gaps), and Conjectures (claims with open steps). This work delivers three principal contributions: Convergence Proof Chain: We present a five-pillar proof chain establishing that tQuA converges to the global minimum from any initial state, without adiabatic scheduling, without eigenstate knowledge, and with a strictly positive escape rate from every local minimum at any . Honest Scaling Benchmarks: We present scaling benchmarks for the Liouvillian spectral gap   on gopherhole Hamiltonians, reporting a key finding: fixed-schedule tQuA achieves a perfectly flat gap ( , independent of   up to ) when the number of local minima   is fixed and small, but experiences steep polynomial decay ( ) when   grows proportionally to . Adaptive Policy Framework: Third, we outline a rich adaptive annealing policy framework using observed function evaluations and prior probability distributions   over problem classes, framing it as a primary research direction for future empirical tuning.   The framework applies broadly to nonconvex optimization in artificial intelligence, signal processing, and imaging, with specific application to "seeing the sky" technologies described in the companion paper on intensity-correlation interferometry (Hyland & Werbos 2024).

title: Analytic Foundations of Thermal Quantum Annealing: Convergence Guarantees and Computational Advantage for Quantum Matrix Methods

summary: In standard multi-head attention, every head uses the same query, key, and value (QKV) projection matrices for every token. We study a simple variant in which, in every layer, a subset of the heads are token-specific: their QKV projections depend on the identity of the input token, while the remaining heads keep ordinary shared projections. Token-specific projections are parameterized as a shared matrix plus a per-token low-rank correction stored in a hashed lookup table, so the extra computation is small, although the parameter count grows. In GPT-style language models trained on FineWeb, with 2 of 4 heads per layer token-specific, every run had lower validation loss than every standard-attention run, at both of the scales we tested. At the larger of two scales (6 layers, width 512, 300M training tokens, 3 seeds per method), validation loss fell from 4.154 ± 0.005 to 4.107 ± 0.008, a 4.6% reduction in perplexity. A control that adds the same number of lookup-table parameters to the same heads as per-token vectors, rather than per-token matrix corrections, reached only 4.148 ± 0.002, indicating that the gain is not explained by the additional parameters alone. At the smaller scale, a sweep over the number of token-specific heads suggests that mixing token-specific and shared heads works at least as well as making all heads token-specific. The main cost is throughput: our unoptimized implementation trains about 30% slower than the baseline. These are small-scale results, and we discuss their limitations in detail.
title: Token-Specific Attention Heads: Mixing Per-Token and Shared Query, Key, and Value Projections in Transformer Language Models

summary: Supplementary data for an experiment that replaced the larva segmentation model of the Tenebrio molitor behavioral-phenotyping pipeline while every downstream step (Petri geometry, primary-larva selection, continuity gate, interpolation, smoothing, features, quality control) was held fixed. Five segmenters were compared: the YOLO11s-seg used for the v1.0.0 dataset, YOLOv8s-seg, YOLO26s-seg and Mask R-CNN R50-FPN v2 trained on full tray images, and a YOLO11s-seg trained on Petri crops. The crop-trained model was then applied to all 34 videos and the Results analysis repeated. On Petri crops, the input the pipeline processes, mask mAP@0.5 was 0.10 for the full-tray YOLO11s and 0.99 for the crop-trained YOLO11s and Mask R-CNN; on 79 held-out labelled video frames larva recall was 0.69, 0.99 and 0.96. The two ground-truth-accurate models agreed with each other (CCC 0.91–0.99 on distance, speed, edge fraction, entropy and area). Heat contrasts kept their direction on the 34 videos. Contents: configuration, protocol and results documents, held-out accuracy, ground-truth localization, the 12-video comparison (agreement, equivalence, per-configuration features and QC), the 34-video re-run with the crop-trained model, treatment contrasts and provenance. Model weights are not included. The values are objective behavioral proxies and do not measure welfare or any subjective state.
title: Tenebrio molitor behavioral phenotyping dataset: segmenter comparison supplementary data

summary: Abstract The Laser Cognition (LC) is a proposed multilevel theoretical framework for investigating how selective attention, conscious access, curiosity-guided inquiry, associative recruitment, and representational integration may contribute to the emergence and evaluation of novel ideas. Its central explanatory metaphor is laser illumination: a complex cognitive field contains multiple thoughts, memories, representations, and potential relationships, while a selected cognitive target receives processing priority. The framework uses this metaphor to organize a proposed mechanism linking cognitive-field activation, attentional targeting, awareness-mediated processing, focus regulation, associative recruitment, integrative recombination, candidate generation, and metacognitive evaluation. LC retains the distinction between the full theory, its default mechanism, and its canonical primary case. The primary case is the Laser-Spotlight Cognitive Genesis Case (LSCGC); the proposed default mechanism is the Laser Cognition Default Mechanism (LC-DM); and its principal operational cycle is the Laser-Guided Cognitive Integration Cycle (LGCIC). The framework is formalized using a weighted cognitive graph, a dual-route attentional-targeting model, a normalized attentional-allocation function, a focus-stability measure, an associative-recruitment equation, a cognitive-integration index, a probabilistic candidate-emergence model, and a feedback-control representation. The mathematical expressions constitute proposed model specifications, not established equations of human neural operation. Awareness, attention, curiosity, affective engagement, cognitive flexibility, and metacognitive monitoring are treated as related but conceptually distinct constructs. The architecture includes eighteen layers, a multidomain research structure, eight initial research hypotheses, explicit falsifiability requirements, a cross-system functional generalization framework, a fourteen-step research protocol, and a twenty-part manuscript structure. Human cognition is the primary explanatory domain. Applications to artificial intelligence, large language models, artificial general intelligence, and possible artificial superintelligence are framed as hypotheses about functional or computational correspondence rather than established claims of shared consciousness or identical mechanisms. LC is presented as a theory-development and validation framework. Its explanatory value, novelty, causal assumptions, parameter identifiability, empirical adequacy, and cross-domain applicability remain subject to systematic literature review, mathematical audit, empirical testing, model comparison, and replication.

summary: Audio textures exhibit complex temporal dynamics that are not well represented by single-scale models. We propose a multi-scale latent trajectory approach for audio texture synthesis using latent representations extracted from a pretrained neural audio codec. By decomposing latent trajectories into slow structural and fast stochastic components, we enable direct modeling and interpretation of the longterm temporal structure and fine-grained detail of audio textures. Our experiments on environmental audio textures suggest that the proposed method significantly improves audio quality over a single-scale baseline and achieves performance competitive with a latent diffusion model. Using perceptually motivated summary statistics, we demonstrate that generated continuations preserve texture identity. Through the proposed methods, we enable continuous texture generation from a given context and expose a latent structure that may support control over long-term dynamics.
title: MULTI-SCALE LATENT TRAJECTORY MODELLING FOR AUDIO TEXTURE SYNTHESIS

summary: AI appears to be accelerating because its benchmark scores are accelerating. Yet the systems being measured are trained and selected through closed procedures, while useful intelligence is ultimately judged against an open-ended world. Object detection provides an unusually direct empirical test of this mismatch. The high-end conventional COCO record reviewed here reached approximately 66 average precision in 2023 and has changed little through 2026 despite sustained research, large models, new architectures, new supervision, synthetic data, prompting, and architecture search. This is not a comparison between obsolete vision technology and modern language AI: object detection now uses the same fundamental machinery—transformers, learned representations, gradient optimization, sequence prediction, and in some systems the same multimodal parameters. Pix2Seq explicitly formulates detection as language modeling; Florence-2 and PaliGemma perform both perceptual and linguistic tasks.   We develop a mathematical model of the closed/open mismatch. Let an open causal state space have effective dimension d while the information admitted by a closed optimizer lies on a codimension-one boundary. At resolution ε, the number of distinguishable open states scales as (R/ε)^d while the boundary scales as (R/ε)^(d−1). The corresponding metric-entropy ratio approaches (d−1)/d. Under a state-identification model, Fano's inequality converts this information ratio into the same asymptotic upper bound on exact identification. For a three-dimensional causal volume and its two-dimensional boundary, the result is 2/3.   The theorem is mathematical: it establishes what follows from the stated information geometry. Its application to AI is scientific: observation determines whether contemporary closed-ended systems serving open-ended objectives exhibit that geometry. The empirical record is strikingly consistent with the resulting two-thirds hypothesis. Closed language benchmarks can exceed two-thirds easily because the objective itself is closed. More reality-coupled end-to-end tasks remain much harder. Recursive self-improvement does not escape the information boundary merely by searching it more aggressively. Under the stated information constraint, additional optimization alone cannot remove the modeled limitation.
title: The Illusion of Accelerating Intelligence: Closed Optimization, Open-Ended Reality, and the Two-Thirds Limit

summary: Integrating contemporary infill architectural projects into historical urban environments presents a delicate challenge between spatial evolution and cultural heritage preservation. Traditional visual impact assessments rely heavily on qualitative, subjective expert evaluations, often leading to procedural delays, public disputes, and compromised urban aesthetics. This paper develops a quantitative, multi-criteria methodology—termed the Visual-Spatial Adaptability Index (VSAI)—to evaluate and optimize the insertion of new architectural objects within historic urban contexts. Combining 3D volumetric viewshed analysis, 2D morphological silhouette integrity, facade solid-to-void rhythm analysis, and computational material texture matching, the VSAI framework establishes an objective metric for context-sensitive design. Empirical validation conducted across 50 infill intervention scenarios in historic urban centers demonstrates that VSAI-guided design optimization yields a 34.2% increase in expert approval consensus and a 42.1% reduction in historical view corridor occlusion compared to conventional baseline proposals. The methodology provides urban planning boards, heritage authorities, and architectural practitioners with a repeatable, transparent computational tool for sustainable heritage conservation.

summary: Fusion Pilot Plants (FPPs) need control systems that survive diagnostic and actuator failures . We present DIII-D experiments  validating real-time, ML-enabled controllers in FPP-relevant scenarios under both imposed diagnostic dropouts and real in-shot hardware failures. Conventional equilibrium reconstruction fails when key diagnostics drop out. Our ML-based RTCAKENN recovers plasma profiles under simulated failures of Thomson Scattering (TS), Charge Exchange Recombination (CER), and Motional Stark Effect (MSE) and maintains accuracies above 90%. ECHO, a fault-robust ML controller, coordinates electron cyclotron heating (ECH) by reallocating gyrotron power s and steering across surviving gyrotrons when units fail mid-shot. In a Hybrid scenario with real ECH dropouts, we mitigated heavy-Z impurity accumulation (argon proxy) using core ECH power tracking a real-time ML radiated-power (Bolo-NN) model for pumpout , and Electron Cyclotron Current Drive (ECCD) steering onto the 3/2 tearing mode for MHD amplitude control. Coordinated ML-controlled gyrotron power adjustments (>0.5MW) avoided argon accumulation and MHD-induced confinement collapse. We also accessed Resonant Magnetic Perturbation (RMP) Edge Localized Mode (ELM)-suppressed plasmas at reduced RMP coil current where large sawteeth would otherwise break ELM suppression. The approach was to reduce sawtooth magnitude (and increase frequency) by holding ECCD inside q=1. Control held through the same TS dropouts and ECH failures, with RTCAKENN providing q=1 localization while ECHO maintained aiming. These first-of-a-kind results show integrated ML-enabled fault-tolerant control sustaining FPP-relevant operating points through imposed and unscripted failures, foundational for resilient burning-plasma control.
title: ML-Enabled Fault Resistant Plasma Control on DIII-D

summary: A sixth-generation (6G) mobile network must share the radio resources of each base station among services with different requirements for delay, throughput, and energy use. Radio access network (RAN) slicing addresses this problem by allocating radio resources among logically separated services, and increasingly autonomous controllers are proposed to manage these allocations. Two proposed enhancements are a learned meta-agent that adjusts the controller’s configuration and a quantum optimizer for difficult discrete allocation decisions. Here we examine when these enhancements add value beyond strong classical controls using SHARP, a safety-preserving multi-cell RAN slicing controller whose per-slot capacity constraint is enforced independently of the added optimization layers. The meta-agent is evaluated against the best static parameter setting and the controller’s built-in adaptation. Its learned policy selects the same value in every observed state, so in deployment it coincides with a fixed setting (V = 3) and does not outperform the best static setting; its role is to locate that setting without a manual sweep. Relative to the default setting inherited from the host study, the located setting improves slot-level power-budget compliance by five to ten percentage points during constrained regimes at a one to two percent goodput cost, while the controller’s Lyapunov virtual queue already provides long-run adaptation of the power constraint. For the discrete allocation problem, plain QAOA does not outperform the classical baselines. Warm-started QAOA with a rotated mixer shows improvement only in the rugged regime evaluated here: it incurs no observed losses to the greedy seed in 48 comparisons and strictly improves six of 16 instances under the IBM-Heron-calibrated noise model, increasing normalized frame utility from 0.927 to 0.941. This gain is measured in frame utility rather than delivered goodput, and its attribution to quantum sampling remains unresolved because a matched classical seeded-perturbation control is not included. The greedy solution remains the fallback when the quantum device does not return within the planning deadline. We therefore formulate a controllerspecific break-even condition relating the expected utility gain, device availability, and quantum-dispatch cost, and derive the corresponding hardware requirements. All results are simulation outputs; no quantum hardware is executed and no quantum advantage is claimed.
title: Bounding the benefit of agentic meta-adaptation and quantum-assisted optimization for safe multi-cell 6G radio access network slicing

summary: Higgs-pair production through gluon fusion is sensitive both to the Higgs self-coupling and to additional scalars exchanged in the s channel. We compute gg → hh at leading order in QCD in the CP-conserving two-Higgs-doublet model with Yukawa alignment (A2HDM), keeping the full top-quark mass dependence and every interference term among the box, the light-Higgs triangle and the heavy-scalar triangle. Previous A2HDM studies of heavy scalars decaying to Higgs pairs used the narrow-width approximation. We contrast two benchmark points. When the heavy scalar H decouples from the top-quark loop, the modified couplings of h weaken the destructive box–triangle interference, and the 13 TeV cross section rises to 1.27 times the Standard Model value without any resonance. For m_H = 300 GeV, below the ttbar threshold, the cross section reaches 3.69 times the Standard Model value; interference with the continuum changes the integrated resonant contribution by only about 4%, but turns the parton-level m_hh distribution into a peak–dip structure. The two mechanisms are therefore separated by the shapes of the m_hh and p_T spectra rather than by the rate. Both benchmarks are illustrative and satisfy a simplified set of theoretical and experimental constraints. Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24029211

title: Interference and resonance effects in gluon-fusion Higgs-pair production in the Yukawa-aligned two-Higgs-doublet model

summary: Flagship 55/60 Can randomized or justified quasi-experimental intervention isolate the manufacturing effect from cell-lot, material and culture confounding? CAUSAL VERIFICATION AND COUNTERFACTUAL CONTROL IN NANOROBOT-ASSISTED REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT This 777-page Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Nano Regenerative Biomanufacturing series investigates intervention-defined causal treatment contrast rather than observational association. Its scientific coupling is causal inference x microscale interventions x biological functional validation. The evidence perimeter is prospective and nonclinical, using closed in-vitro systems, organ-on-chip platforms or authorized ex-vivo material; neither clinical efficacy nor autonomous human intervention is claimed. The falsifiable question is: Can randomized or justified quasi-experimental intervention isolate the manufacturing effect from cell-lot, material and culture confounding? The proposed minimum demonstration is: Randomize tool action within balanced chip batches, retain sham and medium-only controls, and repeat on a second platform. Strong comparators include correlational predictor, nonrandomized matched cohort and randomized sham manipulation. The central competing explanation is shared medium, selection, interference or time-dependent confounding. The noncompensatory stop rule is: negative controls exhibit the claimed effect or modest unmeasured confounding reverses it. Every eligible, stopped, refused and unsuccessful experiment belongs to the full denominator. Thirty conditional mathematical plates specify different analytic roles, measurements, units and blind failure tests. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 individual research investigations. Two hundred Research Gates organize twenty causal challenge families across ten primary physical observables, each with an independently read companion, concealed intervention, matched comparator, explicit rival and refusal gate. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future experimental and evidence instruments. All are experimental plans rather than executed observations. summary: This repository provides the data, Python scripts, numerical outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting a methodological investigation of negative multifractal spectrum estimates in stochastic cascades and digital images. The study distinguishes formally negative annealed multifractal spectra, which can arise in stochastic cascade models, from negative finite-resolution estimates that may depend on measurement and preprocessing procedures. The repository includes: 1. Synthetic image datasets generated using hierarchical random maps (HRM), Fourier-based synthesis (FFT), midpoint displacement (MPD), and binary geometric constructions. 2. Numerical experiments investigating uniform background floors, noise, quantization, clipping, scale-window dependence, and grid-phase sensitivity. 3. Analyses of Dirichlet multiplicative cascades, including Genuine, Shuffled, and Decoy controls. 4. Multifractal estimates based on multiplier moments and Chhabra–Jensen procedures, together with whole-image bootstrap uncertainty estimates. 5. Auxiliary experiments concerning finite-ensemble histogram spectra and supersampling. 6. Scripts, CSV result tables, execution logs, and figure-reproduction materials. 7. A manuscript-to-data mapping file (MANUSCRIPT_MAP.csv), documentation, and SHA-256 checksums supporting traceability and integrity verification. The repository documents reproducibility checks, including the comparison of 180 baseline cases and the reproduction of two computational figures. These checks should not be interpreted as independent validation of every numerical experiment or as proof of universal estimator reliability. The results emphasize that formally negative multifractal spectra and negative estimates obtained from finite digital observations have distinct mathematical interpretations. In particular, negative estimated values do not imply negative Hausdorff dimensions. The dataset is independent of any specific journal submission and is intended to support transparent examination, replication, and further methodological research. title: Negative Multifractal Spectra in Stochastic Cascades and Digital Observations: Reproducibility Data and Code

summary: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis of Global Armed Violence (1989–2025): C Software, 1,000 Permutation Tests and Cartographic Projection Audit This software and reproducibility package accompanies a computational-geometric investigation of geopolitical centrality based on the Uppsala Conflict Data Program Georeferenced Event Dataset (UCDP GED), version 26.1, covering the period 1989–2025. The study introduces a dynamic application of convex hull peeling (Convex Onion) to the spatial and temporal analysis of global armed violence. The method is grounded in the affine invariance of convex-layer membership and provides a hierarchical representation of spatial depth through successive convex hulls. Unlike conventional measures of centrality based on averages, distances, or event density, this approach examines the innermost geometric structure of the global distribution of recorded conflict locations. The dataset contains 358,130 events with day-level date precision , corresponding to 54,381 distinct geographical locations . The cumulative analysis identifies 1,134 convex layers in the final configuration. Software Components The archive includes four C-based computational components: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis: Chronological construction and updating of nested convex hulls, enabling the identification and tracking of the innermost geometric core from 1989 to 2025. Monte Carlo Permutation Analysis: A reproducible experiment involving 1,000 random permutations of complete geographical coordinate pairs across fixed chronological event positions, assessing the relationship between historical event ordering and geometric-core trajectories. Interactive Geometric Visualization: Offline visualization of the evolution of the innermost core, including annual configurations and changes in its geographical position. Cartographic Projection Comparison: Comparative analysis of convex-layer structures using planar longitude–latitude coordinates and the nonlinear Mollweide equal-area projection. Principal Findings The 2025 analysis identifies an innermost geometric location in Ethiopia under the original coordinate representation, whereas the Mollweide projection produces a two-location innermost layer in Sudan. The permutation experiment demonstrates that chronological event ordering influences the historical trajectory of the geometric core, although all permutations preserve the same final spatial configuration when the complete set of locations remains unchanged. These findings illustrate the distinction between affine-invariant geometric structure and centrality that depends on nonlinear cartographic representation. Reproducibility and Scientific Scope The package contains the original C source code, Windows executables, execution scripts, input datasets, computational outputs, visualization files, and technical documentation. The archive supports independent inspection, methodological evaluation, replication, and further development of computational-geometric approaches to spatial conflict analysis. The identified geometric core should not be interpreted as the location of maximum conflict intensity, the greatest number of fatalities, or a causal centre of global geopolitical instability. It represents a mathematically defined form of spatial depth whose interpretation depends on the adopted geometrical representation. Associated Research The Cartographic Construction of Geopolitical Centrality: Affine-Invariant Convex Layers and Global Armed Violence, 1989–2025. Data Source Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP), Georeferenced Event Dataset (GED), version 26.1. The UCDP data are attributed to their original providers. Dataset licensing and software provenance are documented separately in the archive.
title: Convex Onion Geopolitical Centrality

summary: The rational management of water resources and the control of hydroagricultural techniques in the Oued Souf area are complex and crucial to a harmonious and sustainable development. The Oued Souf area is presently facing the problem of upwelling from groundwater, which is harmful to cultures and homes. In order to minimize this problem, several aerated lagoon treatment plants were set up; this technique allows an efficient control of pollution due especially to the upwelling phenomenon. The aim of this study is to provide information about the efficiency and the management of an aerated lagoon treatment system at two plants of the Oued Souf area, the Hassani Abdelkrim and the Reguiba plants. The obtained results show that the removal efficiency of organic load is significant (greater than 50%), thus indicating that aerated lagoon system is well suited to arid areas. published by the   Journal of Biodiversity and Environmental Sciences | JBES

summary: Abstract This document gives a technical and functional description of Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints (ALF): a way to verify that an AI model or algorithm in production still makes the decisions that were reviewed and approved, and to stop its output from taking effect if it does not. The problem. Current AI trust mechanisms prove identity and origin, not behaviour: Model signing (OpenSSF Model Signing, led by Google, NVIDIA and HiddenLayer; NVIDIA NGC signed models) proves which file a model is. Attestation and transparency logs (for example Apple Private Cloud Compute) prove which software a server runs. Neither shows what the model actually decides. A model can be fine-tuned, quantised, wrapped in a prompt or proxy layer, or replaced behind the same name or signature, and an AI agent can act on its output before anyone notices. How it works. Fingerprint generation. A compact cryptographic fingerprint of decision behaviour is created without access to source code, model weights or training data. For machine-learning models it is built by sampling decision boundaries. For rule-based or traditional code it is built from normalised control-flow and decision structure. Sealed-probe verification. In the highest-assurance mode, the model is tested with a sealed set of inputs that the computing system cannot see in advance. Four views must match together: decision boundaries, monotonicity and consistency, constraint activation, and constraint topology. A different model wrapped to imitate the approved one cannot pass all four. Approved-fingerprint registry. Each approved model or algorithm version has a reference fingerprint that can be checked at any time. Run-time check at the point of effect. Inside a trusted execution environment (for example a confidential VM or a confidential GPU), the live fingerprint is compared with the approved one after computation finishes and before the output is used. Fail-closed enforcement. If the fingerprint does not match, approval is automatically invalidated and the output is withheld. The capability needed to act (send, pay, move, transmit) is not released. Validation receipts. Each decision produces a tamper-evident receipt anchored in a ledger, for audit and incident analysis. Where it applies. The same mechanism applies to AI agents and model-serving platforms, payment and digital-currency systems (including offline wallets), vehicles and robots, and satellites. It complements existing technology rather than replacing it: model signing and model registries (NVIDIA NGC, Google Kaggle); verifiable and confidential AI clouds (Apple Private Cloud Compute, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS, and NVIDIA, Intel and AMD confidential hardware); agent platforms (Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services); payment flows (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Ant Group); vehicle software governance under UN Regulation 156; Chinese AI platforms (Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, Tencent, Huawei, Zhipu AI). It also gives a technical signal for the EU AI Act's substantial-modification rule and for China's generative AI filing regime, both of which depend on knowing whether the deployed system is the one that was assessed. Source disclosure. That application claims priority from Indian applications 202531130168, 202631007467 and 202631018571. The related application PCT/IB2026/055615 (filed 4 June 2026, publicly disclosed 16 July 2026) claims priority from it. Author: Sangam Das. summary: Analysis package for a study of copy-specific assignment at the two 23S rRNA copies of Helicobacter pylori . What is reproducible. The six-criterion classification of 103 matched isolates is re-runnable and every verdict was re-derived from the counts with zero mismatches. The reference metadata for all cited works is captured from Europe PMC and every DOI was verified against its record. summary: Executable analysis pipeline (Jupyter notebook for Kaggle) and complete results for a study on spectroscopic screening of food adulteration with a stated risk of false accusation. Seven chemometric and deep-learning classifiers (PLS-DA, SVM, random forest, ROCKET, 1D-CNN and a multitask 1D-CNN with and without Beer-Lambert mixup) are compared under grouped, repeated cross-validation. Their out-of-fold scores feed three conformal layers: (i) class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal triage into PASS, FLAG and REFER decisions, with an ablation against marginal calibration and an analysis of calibration size and deployment batch shift; (ii) cross-conformal detection of adulterants absent from training (DD-SIMCA, leave-one-adulterant-out, network embeddings) with Benjamini-Hochberg batch screening; and (iii) a leave-level-out audit for level-batch confounding whose threshold is calibrated by a semi-synthetic Beer-Lambert simulation built from real ATR-FTIR spectra. Four public datasets are analysed (NIR hyperspectral imaging of extra-virgin olive oil; ATR-FTIR of turmeric with wheat flour; MIR of strawberry purée; ATR-FTIR of edible oils); they are not redistributed here (see README for sources and licences). The archive contains the notebook with the outputs of the run reported in the article, all result tables (CSV), figures (PNG), a results summary, run logs and environment information.
title: Risk-controlled spectroscopic screening of food adulteration with conformal prediction: code and results

summary: The FBT spectral-capacity action is the heat trace of one specified geometric Dirac operator at fixed spectral resolution. This paper states its domain and trace hypotheses, exact first and second variations, stationarity tests, coupled relative-torus 4 + 2 expression, and complete finite-computation requirements. The current application uses the embeddingto-operator map already supplied by DCQ6 and FBT10D on the closed coherent product. No second source map is required. The degree-24 regular magnetic realization, its singular-end analysis and the separate torus numerical benchmark are removed from the main development. Their removal leaves the functional and the relative-torus geometry intact. The global line-extension obstruction is retained to explain this separation. The inherited twist, its closed domain and all metric, spin and connection variations are used together. Exact fibre integration preserves the full heat trace; the four-dimensional quadratic action and normal stability certificates are cited from FBT10D with their original scope. General spectral error bounds retain feedback through omitted modes and distinguish affine connection tests from nonlinear geometric families. A final ledger separates established results from resolution selection, balance-layer selection, full nonlinear control and real-time interpretation. This revision introduces no new numerical sign certificate or physical mass prediction.
title: FBT10A: The Spectral–Capacity Action of the Fracture–Berry–Tension Framework

summary: Description This dataset provides harmonised administrative and surveillance health data describing the epidemiology and health system burden of varicella (ICD-10: B01) and herpes zoster (ICD-10: B02) in Bulgaria during the period 2023–2025 . The analysed time window corresponds to the post-COVID-19 period and precedes the introduction of mandatory varicella vaccination (2026) , providing an important baseline for evaluating vaccination policies and monitoring changes in disease epidemiology. The dataset integrates aggregated information from several national administrative and surveillance systems: 1. National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) – hospital reimbursement through clinical pathways. 2. National Health Information System (NHIS) – national digital health infrastructure containing information on hospitalisations, outpatient medical examinations, and vaccination administration. 3. National Social Security Institute (NSSI) – sick leave records, sick leave duration, and compensation payments. 4. National Statistical Institute (NSI) – population denominators used for epidemiological rate calculations. National infectious disease surveillance system – mandatory reporting of infectious diseases according to Bulgarian public health legislation. All datasets are aggregated administrative records and contain no personally identifiable information . Data are aggregated at the regional (oblast) level and reported at monthly resolution , except for population denominators, which are annual. Regional names have been standardised to English transliterations , while the original Bulgarian names are preserved. All financial variables in this dataset are reported in Bulgarian lev (BGN) , which was the official currency of Bulgaria during the study period 2023–2025 . Bulgaria adopted the euro (EUR) in 2026 . However, the Bulgarian lev had long operated under a currency board arrangement with a fixed exchange rate to the euro . summary: Implementation Mechanisms for Tipiṭaka-Grounded AI Alignment — An Engineering Companion to Suffering-Cessation as Value Function This paper reads the Abhidhamma — the analytical third division of the Theravāda Buddhist canon — as a process specification of mind: typed, momentary mental events arising one at a time under twenty-four typed conditioning relations, with ethical class tracked per event and per position in a processing cycle. From that reading it derives a research program for AI alignment evaluation and intervention: a red-team taxonomy of mimicry failure modes, resting-state (minimal-context) evaluation of language models, an intervention-timing typology over a processing cycle, a typed causal vocabulary, the limits of interpretability by subtraction, paired entailment-and-denial consistency testing of alignment claims, and a positive competence taxonomy. It is the engineering companion to Suffering-Cessation as Value Function (Ly, 2026), which argues for the Theravāda Tipiṭaka as a substrate for autonomous-AI alignment, and it develops the canon's third basket — the Abhidhamma Piṭaka — at the layer where that paper's §6.6 left off: the layer of cognitive process itself. We make one framing claim and two structural contributions. The framing claim is the compilation thesis : the Abhidhamma is a substrate-neutral process-specification of mind, and each era that has received it has read it in the vocabulary for process it had to hand — the scholastic commentators' wheels of classification, the twentieth century's reading of it as a psychology, cognitive science's information processing, and computation for ours. The tradition itself reached for machine images again and again, each fitted to one lesson; computation is this era's addition. The claim defended here is not that the Abhidhamma secretly describes computers. It is that the computational reading is our era's compilation of a specification that has survived the earlier readings, and that this compilation's target can enact what it compiles rather than only describe it. Formal and computational readings exist (Barendregt 2006; Karunananda et al. 2015; Lou 2017); Takeuchi (2026) reads transformer self-attention as anattā and pursues alignment by subtraction; an agent grounded in the substrate is engineered toward enacting wholesome cognition rather than simulating it. No priority is claimed for that aim. The first structural contribution is the machine architecture (§4): the samsaric process rendered in four repaired mappings — (1) a conditioned machine with exactly one free variable, against the strictly deterministic reading the canon itself condemns in Makkhali Gosāla's fatalism; (2) citta as the instruction-cycle rather than the processor, with the 89/121 citta-typology as a shared instruction set, the mindstream ( santāna ) as the thread, and uniqueness residing in the execution trace; (3) the kammic continuity as an append-only linked ledger rather than a blockchain — no miners, no consensus, maximal privacy, immutable entries whose ripening remains context-dependent; and (4) the counter-gear : the dhamma-wheel that engages the samsaric wheel at its one free variable and unwinds the machine by fuel-withdrawal rather than force, terminating in kiriya -mode execution — action that leaves no kammic residue. The second structural contribution is the verification-suite reading (§5) of the analytical books: the Yamaka as bidirectional property-testing, the Vibhaṅga's interrogation method as schema validation, the Dhātukathā as inclusion-matrix consistency, and the Kathāvatthu as formal adversarial protocol — with the Kathāvatthu's opening controversy ( puggalakathā , the refutation of the person-entity) read as the canon pre-running, and settling, this paper's own central repair. title: The Wheel That Unwinds the Wheel: The Abhidhamma as Executable Process-Specification

summary: A six-gene mineralization-inhibitor score (ENPP1, ANKH, MGP, GGCX, VKORC1, NT5E) in CD90+ dermal fibroblasts reads lower in systemic sclerosis than in controls. The gene set, direction, detection floors and significance threshold were fixed before any expression value was read. In a pre-registered held-out set of 50 donors (25 and 25), the observed difference is -0.2939 at one-sided p = 0.0204. That replication is across platforms within one study (GSE195452), not across studies, and no ambient RNA correction was applied. The score did not replicate in an independent series. In GSE292979, the same frozen genes, direction, floors and threshold were applied under a pre-registration, and a blinded second implementation reproduced every donor score within 1e-6 before the result was unmasked. All four pre-registered contrasts were null (primary -0.0412, one-sided p 0.4955; minimum attainable p 0.0045). The paper offers no explanation for the null and does not claim the effect is absent. The osteogenic half of the original hypothesis did not clear its pre-registered detection floor in any dataset examined. This is not a study of calcinosis lesions, not evidence of specificity, and not a mechanism. It is a pre-registered result that held within one study and did not replicate in the one independent series tested, reported with both outcomes.
title: A pre-specified mineralization-inhibitor score separates systemic sclerosis fibroblasts within one study and does not replicate in an independent series

summary: Lectures and practical classes remain the core formats for teaching specialized subjects in medical and dental universities, yet their modernization is often guided by descriptive experience rather than by empirical evidence. This review aimed to synthesize the evidence on the effectiveness of contemporary lecture and practical-class formats and to propose evidence-informed criteria for selecting them in the teaching of specialized subjects. A narrative review of literature indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ERIC and Google Scholar was performed, prioritizing meta-analyses, systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Findings were interpreted through constructive alignment, cognitive load theory and Miller's pyramid of clinical competence. Across 225 studies, active learning increased examination performance by 0.47 standard deviations, and students taught by traditional lecturing were 1.5 times more likely to fail. In health professions education, the flipped classroom outperformed traditional teaching (SMD = 0.33); in dental education, problem-based, case-based, team-based and flipped formats together outperformed lecture-based learning (SMD = 0.48; 29 RCTs, 3,502 students). Technology-enhanced simulation was associated with large effects on knowledge and skills (effect sizes 1.09–1.20) compared with no intervention. However, the evidence shows high heterogeneity and focuses mainly on knowledge and learner satisfaction rather than clinical performance. Lectures and practical classes should be designed as a single aligned system in which the teaching format is selected according to the intended learning outcome and level of competence. Locally conducted controlled studies are needed to confirm these effects in medical universities of Uzbekistan.
title: MODERN FORMS OF TEACHING SPECIALIZED SUBJECTS IN MEDICAL AND DENTAL EDUCATION: AN EVIDENCE-BASED NARRATIVE REVIEW OF LECTURES AND PRACTICAL CLASSES
