summary: STARLI | FLAGSHIP 13 FISSION Bioelectric and Quantum Signal Science | Flagships 151–160 / 300 Author: 33  |  White Rainbow Epoch  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2 This ten-volume collection investigates physically traceable bioelectric sensing, cell-membrane-potential readout, neural-field magnetometry, electrically guided microrobotic navigation, extracellular field metrology, noise separation, dynamic tracking, interface safety, spatial field reconstruction and electrical–mechanical multimodal identification. The common challenge is to distinguish real biological or phantom source physics from electrode polarization, ionic screening, induced electromagnetic pickup, motion artifact, thermal drift and inverse-model bias. Each English monograph uses 777 individually numbered pages: 30 candidate mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 one-page research investigations, 200 Research Gates with six detailed second-pass annotations, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Together these ten books contain 7,770 pages, 300 mathematical plates, 820 chapters, 4,100 investigation pages, 2,000 research gates and 330 prospective research instruments, protocols or successor objects. Ten independent research directions F151 | NANO-QUANTUM BIOELECTRIC-FIELD SENSING AT THE LIMIT — Separates calibrated local electric-field amplitudes from ionic screening, source geometry, electrode polarization, optical and mechanical interference by phantom-based blinded reference measurements. F152 | MICROSCALE NONINVASIVE CELL-MEMBRANE-POTENTIAL READOUT AT THE LIMIT — Treats noninvasive cell-membrane voltage as an inverse measurement problem; tests capacitive loading, optical reporting lag, transmembrane polarity, geometry and membrane-surrogate leakage against direct voltage truth. F153 | QUANTUM MAGNETOMETRY AND NEURAL ELECTRICAL SIGNAL COUPLING AT THE LIMIT — Compares magnetometer responses to independently known neural-like current sources while testing coil leakage, cross-axis sensitivity, gradiometer common-mode noise, timing uncertainty and localization ambiguity. F154 | NANOROBOTIC LOCAL BIOELECTRIC NAVIGATION AT THE LIMIT — Studies whether local electric cues direct bounded microrobotic paths rather than passive advection, electroosmosis, mechanical channel constraints or unreported magnetic control. F155 | EXTRACELLULAR ELECTRIC FIELD QUANTUM METROLOGY AT THE LIMIT — Builds traceability for extracellular electric-field and electrode polarization measurement, with complex impedance, source loading, SI units, shared calibration covariance and reference transfer. F156 | MICROSCALE BIOELECTRIC SIGNAL NOISE SEPARATION AT THE LIMIT — Disentangles bioelectric signals from mains interference, cable motion, thermal and Johnson noise, spectral leakage, common-mode drift, classifier bias and unequal optical/energy budgets. F157 | QUANTUM SENSOR BIOELECTRIC DYNAMIC TRACKING AT THE LIMIT — Tests dynamic tracking error against concealed moving-source truth, incorporating phase unwrap, bandwidth, tracking latency, source overlap, blank events and quantum/coherence limits. F158 | NANOROBOTIC BIOELECTRIC INTERFACE SAFETY AT THE LIMIT — Examines temperature rise, electric charge, interface Faradaic reactions, shear, optical exposure, chemical leachate, membrane surrogate breakdown and independently witnessed hard-stop states. F159 | MICROFLUIDIC BIOELECTRIC SIGNAL SPATIAL RECONSTRUCTION AT THE LIMIT — Studies the identifiability of current-source location in microfluidic conductors, including ill-posed inverse maps, anisotropic ionic conduction, missing electrodes, 3D depth and boundary effects. F160 | BIOELECTRIC AND MECHANICAL SIGNAL MULTIMODAL IDENTIFICATION AT THE LIMIT — Separates causally applied mechanical strain from electrical source signals in multimodal experiments, including piezoelectric coupling, mechanical resonance, pressure-dependent contact,

Each English monograph uses 777 individually numbered pages: 30 candidate mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 one-page research investigations, 200 Research Gates with six detailed second-pass annotations, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Together these ten books contain 7,770 pages, 300 mathematical plates, 820 chapters, 4,100 investigation pages, 2,000 research gates and 330 prospective research instruments, protocols or successor objects. Ten independent research directions F151 | NANO-QUANTUM BIOELECTRIC-FIELD SENSING AT THE LIMIT — Separates calibrated local electric-field amplitudes from ionic screening, source geometry, electrode polarization, optical and mechanical interference by phantom-based blinded reference measurements. F152 | MICROSCALE NONINVASIVE CELL-MEMBRANE-POTENTIAL READOUT AT THE LIMIT — Treats noninvasive cell-membrane voltage as an inverse measurement problem; tests capacitive loading, optical reporting lag, transmembrane polarity, geometry and membrane-surrogate leakage against direct voltage truth. F153 | QUANTUM MAGNETOMETRY AND NEURAL ELECTRICAL SIGNAL COUPLING AT THE LIMIT — Compares magnetometer responses to independently known neural-like current sources while testing coil leakage, cross-axis sensitivity, gradiometer common-mode noise, timing uncertainty and localization ambiguity. F154 | NANOROBOTIC LOCAL BIOELECTRIC NAVIGATION AT THE LIMIT — Studies whether local electric cues direct bounded microrobotic paths rather than passive advection, electroosmosis, mechanical channel constraints or unreported magnetic control. F155 | EXTRACELLULAR ELECTRIC FIELD QUANTUM METROLOGY AT THE LIMIT — Builds traceability for extracellular electric-field and electrode polarization measurement, with complex impedance, source loading, SI units, shared calibration covariance and reference transfer. F156 | MICROSCALE BIOELECTRIC SIGNAL NOISE SEPARATION AT THE LIMIT — Disentangles bioelectric signals from mains interference, cable motion, thermal and Johnson noise, spectral leakage, common-mode drift, classifier bias and unequal optical/energy budgets. F157 | QUANTUM SENSOR BIOELECTRIC DYNAMIC TRACKING AT THE LIMIT — Tests dynamic tracking error against concealed moving-source truth, incorporating phase unwrap, bandwidth, tracking latency, source overlap, blank events and quantum/coherence limits. F158 | NANOROBOTIC BIOELECTRIC INTERFACE SAFETY AT THE LIMIT — Examines temperature rise, electric charge, interface Faradaic reactions, shear, optical exposure, chemical leachate, membrane surrogate breakdown and independently witnessed hard-stop states. F159 | MICROFLUIDIC BIOELECTRIC SIGNAL SPATIAL RECONSTRUCTION AT THE LIMIT — Studies the identifiability of current-source location in microfluidic conductors, including ill-posed inverse maps, anisotropic ionic conduction, missing electrodes, 3D depth and boundary effects. F160 | BIOELECTRIC AND MECHANICAL SIGNAL MULTIMODAL IDENTIFICATION AT THE LIMIT — Separates causally applied mechanical strain from electrical source signals in multimodal experiments, including piezoelectric coupling, mechanical resonance, pressure-dependent contact, timing and domain shifts. Evidence and research limitations All effects and formula adaptations are research hypotheses or proposed model applications, not completed experiments. The scientific protocols are confined to synthetic electrical phantoms, traceable nonclinical test systems and authorized ex-vivo material, where applicable. Published work on NV-sensor arrays, nanodiamond materials and optical magnetometry supports comparator methodology, not these new flagship outcomes. Each volume calls for resource-matched classical baselines, frozen blinded challenges, orthogonal measurement, raw failure records and explicit termination criteria. Independent specialist verification of causal novelty, complete dimensional derivations, biological relevance and reference-to-claim fit remains outstanding. Join the STARLI Research Community Explore more than 100 interdisciplinary research themes and follow the evolving STARLI Research Gate community: https://zenodo.org/communities/starli-research-gate/

The scientific protocols are confined to synthetic electrical phantoms, traceable nonclinical test systems and authorized ex-vivo material, where applicable. Published work on NV-sensor arrays, nanodiamond materials and optical magnetometry supports comparator methodology, not these new flagship outcomes. Each volume calls for resource-matched classical baselines, frozen blinded challenges, orthogonal measurement, raw failure records and explicit termination criteria. summary: Code, input-distribution parameters, and all Monte Carlo and sensitivity outputs for the manuscript "A multilayer probabilistic influence model of train driver human error probability and system-level failure probability: Monte Carlo simulation and input-factor sensitivity analysis" (submitted to Reliability Engineering & System Safety). summary: We propose the interrogative investment hypothesis: the basic interrogative forms can serve as units for describing how individuals come to differ in cognitive competence. These forms fall into two levels. Questions of object (what, where, who, when, how many) carve reality into aspects; questions of reason (how, why) relate these aspects and underlie methods of inquiry such as the historical and scientific methods. Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences offers a rich description of these differences; we propose a complementary developmental mechanism that may help explain how its profiles take shape. In line with Hayes's (1962) motivational-experiential theory of intelligence, we suggest that its domains are strengthened, at least in part, through investment. A spontaneous preference for one kind of question draws attention and time toward it; because time is scarce, this produces cumulative practice, growing competence and increasing reward, which strengthens the preference in turn. We discuss where such preferences may come from: inherited dispositions, early ability, the answers children receive, and culture. Hayes's experience-producing drives were never operationalised; we suggest that question preferences could provide one possible behavioural indicator of them. We propose a simple task to capture these preferences, a pilot study with explicit criteria for failure, and five testable predictions. Finally, we draw implications for education: questions show where a child's attention goes before competence is visible, one object can be taught through many questions, and the way adults answer may shape which questions grow. The proposal is theoretical; no data have been collected.   Version 5. Adds a section on the origins of question preferences with a fifth prediction, a pilot study with criteria for failure, and a section on implications for education.

summary: Code and derived data for the measurement of Monte Carlo ensembles of a fire-front-oriented wildfire cellular automaton on commodity processors. The record contains the benchmark harnesses for the synthetic and the real-domain families, the scenario module that declares the landscape parameters, the workload profiler, the framework-cost and contention harnesses, the analysis script that derives the paper's analytical results from the measured tables, the exported Eastern Hills fuel raster, and every measured table behind every reported figure, including the per-round and per-replicate records and not only the summaries. The README inside the archive lists every script and every table with its purpose, and carries a glossary of the Spanish column names the tables use. What changed in version 2.3.0 This version adds 1 script and 2 tables, and changes no earlier number. run_combined_benchmark.py measures the ensemble with distribution over actors and the algebraic reduction of the propagator applied together, on the same two real domains, seeds and horizons as the published harness, with the final state of every replicate checked against the reference formulation. On the full Eastern Hills domain the 16-replicate ensemble goes from 1,504.1 s on 1 worker with the reference formulation to 23.5 s on 16 workers with the reduced one, a 63.9-fold gain. The tables are combined_benchmark.csv and combined_rondas.csv . The internal draft desc_actual.txt left in the previous archive is removed. What changed in version 2.2.0 This version carries the measurement that changed what the article claims, and it retracts no earlier number. The record now compares four formulations of the same transition rule, not three. run_propagator_comparison.py measures the reference formulation, which convolves the whole grid once per emitting cell, the algebraic reduction, the full-grid sweep and a genuine front restriction, all on the same trajectory of each scenario and all verified to produce the same state hash. propagador_frente_real.py is that front restriction, the formulation the two earlier versions of the article discussed without ever having measured. The result is that the formulation every benchmark in this study was measured against is the slowest of the four, by 15 to 732 times. Each entry of that table is now the median of five takes with its range , except the reference column on the two largest scenarios, where one take costs minutes. The ranges matter, since the three cheap formulations are timed in tenths of a second and a single take there does not separate a real difference from the variation of the machine. The same harness measures the ensemble on the fastest formulation, so the parallel gain can be read against a competent serial baseline as well as against the slow one. An earlier execution warmed two workers instead of all sixteen and understated the gain by a factor of 1.6 to 3.4; the deposited harness warms the whole pool and the withdrawn figures are kept in data/calentamiento_retirado.log . The run log of every measurement now travels inside the archive beside the table it produced. What changed in version 2.1.0 Version 2.1.0 added measurements and closed gaps that version 2.0 had declared open, retracting no earlier measurement. The extreme scenario moved from 1 measurement round to 3, so its speedup rests on a reproducible measurement rather than on a single observation. The lockstep verification of the algebraic reduction was extended to the full horizon each domain runs, 1,016 steps on the El Cable sector and 400 on the Eastern Hills, at a Hamming distance of 0 on the state grid and on the moisture field at every step, and the counted gain of the reduction rose accordingly because the earlier truncation had measured the fire only while its front was at its narrowest. summary: Claims about acoustic keystroke side channels, attacks that infer typed content from the sound of a keyboard, are difficult to compare because studies differ in recording conditions, data splits, and how defenses are tested. This paper presents OpenKeystroke, an open source research platform for authorized acoustic side-channel experiments and privacy-defense evaluation. The platform measures how much class information survives in short acoustic transients, and how much signal transformations (defenses) reduce it, under a strict evaluation protocol: session, device, and environment-disjoint splits with leakage checks, train-only fitting of preprocessing statistics, validation-only model selection, cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired comparisons across repeated seeds. Defenses are labelled effective only when they produce a significant accuracy drop, over at least three seeds, against both a static attacker and an adaptive attacker who knows the defense is applied. The platform ships eight classification models and six defenses behind one experiment lifecycle shared by a command line interface, a Python API, and an interactive dashboard. On a synthetic benchmark, headline accuracy degrades materially under domain shift, and several defenses that appear strong against a static attacker largely fail against an adaptive one, which is exactly the gap the platform exists to expose. OpenKeystroke operates only on predefined, non-sensitive acoustic categories in controlled or explicitly consented data. It does not reconstruct typed text, passwords, or messages.
title: OpenKeystroke: An Open Research Platform for Acoustic Side-Channel Experiments and Privacy-Defense Evaluation

summary: The triangular Lagrange point of the restricted three-body problem and the radial motion of a charged particle in a Penning trap are both equilibria held at a maximum of an effective potential by a gyroscopic force. Each possesses one mode of negative energy, and each loses linear stability when its two frequencies collide—one at Routh’s mass ratio, the other at the trapping limit. Both systems belong to a single family of planar gyroscopic Hamiltonians. On every level of the conserved angular-momentum invariant, the degree-four normal form of any member at such a collision coincides with the reduced Hamiltonian of an axisymmetric Penning trap whose detuning is shifted by a term proportional to the invariant and whose quartic coefficient is fixed by a single normal-form invariant. On the level containing orbits that start at rest, this reduction yields closed-form laws for the largest excursion, the escape threshold, and the escape time. These laws depend only on the sign of the quartic coefficient and on scaled variables. At the triangular point the coefficient is positive, placing the collision in the soft class: orbits remain confined after stability is lost, with an excursion that grows like the square root of the distance past the critical value. Direct integration confirms the soft law to a fraction of a percent at the smallest detunings tested. Two traps whose quartic coefficient matches that of the triangular point reproduce the same law. Traps with the opposite sign escape at the predicted threshold and in the predicted times. A randomized ensemble of members confirms the classification by the sign of the coefficient. Two further results hold for every member of the family. Before the collision the linear transient gain is exactly the inverse square root of the frequency splitting. With isotropic velocity damping the first-order growth rates depend only on the undamped frequencies, and at the collision they scale with the square root of the damping rate. The first of these explains earlier reports of apparent escape just below Routh’s value as ordinary linear transients that reach a fixed radius. The second recovers the classical magnetron-instability formula as a special case. The results are local, planar, and classical. What transfers between the asteroid and the trap is the normal-form dynamics on each level of the invariant, the transient gain, and the damped linear rates. What does not transfer without further work is the behaviour beyond the normal-form neighbourhood, where the gravitational terms of every order cause the triangular point to deviate from any purely quartic trap.
title: An Asteroid in a Penning Trap

At the triangular point the coefficient is positive, placing the collision in the soft class: orbits remain confined after stability is lost, with an excursion that grows like the square root of the distance past the critical value. Direct integration confirms the soft law to a fraction of a percent at the smallest detunings tested. Two traps whose quartic coefficient matches that of the triangular point reproduce the same law. Traps with the opposite sign escape at the predicted threshold and in the predicted times. A randomized ensemble of members confirms the classification by the sign of the coefficient. Two further results hold for every member of the family. Before the collision the linear transient gain is exactly the inverse square root of the frequency splitting. With isotropic velocity damping the first-order growth rates depend only on the undamped frequencies, and at the collision they scale with the square root of the damping rate. The first of these explains earlier reports of apparent escape just below Routh’s value as ordinary linear transients that reach a fixed radius. The second recovers the classical magnetron-instability formula as a special case. The results are local, planar, and classical. What transfers between the asteroid and the trap is the normal-form dynamics on each level of the invariant, the transient gain, and the damped linear rates. What does not transfer without further work is the behaviour beyond the normal-form neighbourhood, where the gravitational terms of every order cause the triangular point to deviate from any purely quartic trap.
title: An Asteroid in a Penning Trap

summary: GLIAG essay, Geology, Minerals & Petroleum of Suriname, Revision 1.1 (7 November 2026). Every barrel of oil in the Golden Lane sits in sand that was once a mountain on the Guiana Shield. The essay follows two billion years of Suriname's geology in six acts: the Trans-Amazonian ocean floor and island arc (2.18–2.13 Ga), collision and orogenic gold (2.13–2.06 Ga), the Bakhuis ultrahigh-temperature granulites (2.07–2.05 Ga), the felsic flare-up (1.99–1.95 Ga), the Roraima sandstone and the quiet craton (1.87–1.0 Ga), and the opening of the Atlantic that built the Golden Lane turbidite fans. It links each map unit to its mineral system (gold at Rosebel, Merian and Overman; plateau and coastal bauxite; Cu–Ni–Cr, Li–Sn–Ta–Be and Nb–REE occurrences; Tambaredjo heavy oil; Golden Lane light oil) and discusses the shield-to-slope source-to-sink system. It closes with a FACT · MISSING · GLIAG JUDGEMENT · TRIGGER evidence register, a glossary, a references annex and an amendment register. Revision 1.1 corrects the provenance reading of Girault et al. (2023): their Early Cretaceous Demerara Plateau zircons are mainly Pan-African–Brasiliano and sourced from the French Guiana margin, so the shield origin of the Late Cretaceous Golden Lane sands is presented as a working hypothesis supported by Roddaz et al. (2021). Literature-based interpretation for education and research; not a resource assessment or investment advice. Location: Zoetermeer & Paramaribo. Text-and-data mining reserved under Art. 4(3) Directive (EU) 2019/790 and Art. 15o Dutch Auteurswet.
title: Suriname: a Palimpsest of Two Billion Years

summary: This repository contains the analytical datasets, Python scripts, numerical outputs, plots and reproducibility documentation accompanying the manuscript Can strontium isotopes track changing mobility patterns? Evidence from La Tène Central Europe. The repository is intended to support transparent evaluation, replication and further comparative research on Iron Age mobility, life histories and the relationship between human movement and regional geological environments. The repository supports reproduction of the downstream statistical analyses, including: Cemetery-level isotope distributions and local/non-local classifications. Individual-level mobility estimates using two complementary classification rules: Rule A (any sampled tooth potentially non-local) and Rule B (one predefined permanent reference tooth). Mixed-effects logistic models evaluating chronological, demographic and burial material-group associations while accounting for repeated teeth from the same individual. Sensitivity analyses, paired-tooth comparisons and reconstruction of childhood strontium exposure histories. Cross-cemetery isotope comparisons and relationships between lithological diversity and strontium variability at 1, 5, 10 and 20 km spatial scales. Reproducible analytical plots and numerical verification against the published supplementary results.
title: Strontium isotopes and mobility in La Tène Central Europe: analytical data, Python code and reproducibility materials

summary: This dataset provides the numerical inputs, source code, reference results, and reproduction workflow accompanying “Light in Light Bubbles — Gravitational Light in the Phraqtal Field” ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23652779 ). Version 2.0 preserves the numerical baseline of version 0.2: stationary-core calculations, regime-channel coupling, integrated gravitational-source calculations, static three-knot comparisons, constrained-curvature diagnostics, and analytical examples for tension-front energy, arrival geometry, and conditional golden-ratio relations. Original numerical programs, input fields, parameters, dependencies, and comparison tolerances remain unchanged. The historical Google Colab replay of October 27, 2026, passed 11 comparison groups and 3,055 checks within the declared tolerances. Its verification records are retained as historical evidence, not presented as a newly executed version-2.0 numerical replay. The extension adds the complete expanded German manuscript and 110 finite exact algebraic controls for magnetic twist organization, the constitutive magnetization readout, source variations, and a conditional magnetic–gravitational response. These controls distinguish directed organization from quadratic source contributions and retain the direct source term in the response calculation. No new core, regime-chain, numerical field-response, or physical-time field-evolution calculations were performed for this extension. The magnetic readout remains an explicit constitutive model choice; its physical calibration and validation against measurements remain open. The algebraic controls do not establish a measured magnetic response or derive the numerical value of Newton’s gravitational constant. The single-cell Colab notebook defaults to integrity checks and the new algebraic extension. Replaying the historical numerical calculations is optional. Release instructions and the new executable interface are in English. The expanded manuscript is in German; the original English manuscript is also retained. The package includes checksums, claim-to-material mappings, and separate historical and extension verification records.
title: Light in Light Bubbles — Reproduction Data and Code for Gravitational Light in the Phraqtal Field

summary: When a phone fails and its owner keeps the messaging account running on a second device, the account's history can end up in two archives, each intact and each missing what the other holds. We call this Temporal Communication Fragmentation (TCF), a loss by non-union: no message is deleted, but the platform offers no operation that joins the two halves. WhatsApp's own documentation states that old and new chats cannot be merged. We define TCF by three jointly necessary and sufficient conditions and specify CARTA 1.1, a framework for reconstructing one archive from several. CARTA is an output contract owed to a reader who cannot check the result. Records that cannot be read unambiguously are quarantined with a typed reason, and a report gives each record's provenance, the conflicts and deduplication ambiguities found, and every setting used. We evaluated a reference implementation, CHAMP-Pipeline, on synthetic fragment sets with known ground truth. With its declared date inference it reproduced the ground truth in all 4,500 configurations of a parameter sweep; the invariants and the predicted outcome held in all 5,000 random configurations of two to four fragments; and reconstruction stayed exact at one million messages. A zone-offset advisory, frozen before testing, flagged all 2,800 misdeclared zones in a designed test of overlapping fragment pairs and 1,470 of 1,542 in random configurations, and raised false alarms in 2 of 600 correctly declared runs. A systematic search found 60 chat-merging tools; none fully provides more than 2 of the five output properties CARTA specifies. With a fragment's time zone left undeclared, every benchmarked tool and CHAMP-Pipeline produce the same duplicated and misdated records, and only CHAMP-Pipeline's report says so. All data are synthetic; no real archive has been reconstructed.
title: When Chats Split Apart: Formalizing Temporal Communication Fragmentation and the CARTA Reconstruction Framework

summary: Version 4.0.0 provides code and numerical evidence supporting manuscript V13, "Auditing Integrity Enforcement in Biometric Verification". It contains the unchanged original service, a separately identified strict verification path, portable execution and reanalysis, two paired five-seed campaigns with FaceNet and OpenCV SFace, target-attributed offline audit, structural checks, measured HTTP latency and authenticated-log scaling, scientific figures and Appendices A-F. Each backend has 4,840 scored responses across four configurations. Each configuration has 1,100 specified fault attempts; detected/enforced counts are 51/51 (minimal), 400/400 (conventional subset), 650/550 (full original) and 1,100/1,100 (strict). Clean requests and two trust-boundary negative-control classes are reported separately. The primary records retain coarse collector flags; final analysis explicitly attributes the B10 composed log-rollback alarm to the targeted history. Raw primary responses are unchanged, and collection-time analysis is preserved. The current strict path has 620 complete scored normal-return traces. The median paired strict-minus-minimal latency is 173.90 ms for FaceNet and 83.35 ms for SFace on the recorded CPU host. The study evaluates one application family and a selected scenario set under trusted application code, keys and reference state. It does not establish population attack probabilities, production-cloud security, presentation liveness, durable distributed state or hostile-host attestation. The separately implemented auditor is part of the same AI-assisted study, not an independent laboratory replication. Earlier historical campaigns and engineering pilots are not pooled with the new experiments. No source photographs, reusable biometric vectors, pretrained weights, private keys or private author contact sheet are included. Inputs are acquired separately from documented upstream sources and identified by SHA-256. AT&T Laboratories Cambridge is acknowledged. summary: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) to infer particle formation rate J(t) and size-dependent growth rate GR(d, t) from parallel differential mobility analyzer (DMA) particle size distribution counts measured in the CERN CLOUD (Cosmics Leaving OUtdoor Droplets) chamber experiments. The PINN is trained on measured counts and constrained by the aerosol general dynamic equation (GDE), with nucleation expressed as a boundary flux at 1.7 nm. For baseline benchmark comparison, the notebook also includes a Python re-implementation of the Julia-based extended Kalman filter and fixed-interval smoother from Ozon et al. (2021). Both methods are evaluated on four simulated cases with known truth (0000_00 to 0000_03) and the three CLOUD experiments (1802_01, 1952_02, 1906_03). For the CLOUD runs, results are compared with the independent PSM (J) and INSIDE (GR) estimates reported in the paper. BAYROSOL 1.1 data is downloaded directly from Zenodo within the notebook (Ozon, Stolzenburg and Dada, 2021, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4450492 , MIT license), so no additional data files are appended.

summary: Pre-specified reanalysis of public human arteriovenous fistula single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE305423) along with bulk RNA-sequencing data (GSE220796, GSE119296). The repository contains the analysis pipeline, fixed random seed (2611), pinned environment, all result tables cited in the article, and a numeric-provenance assertion script that re-derives every number quoted in the manuscript from the result files. Main findings: apparent transcriptional signatures of maturation failure are dominated by changes in cell composition (including ambient-RNA-driven artefacts) rather than cell-intrinsic reprogramming; myofibroblast abundance, fate bias and matrisome programmes are unchanged within the detectable effect range.
title: Analysis code for: Cell composition accounts for much of the transcriptomic difference between failed and matured human arteriovenous fistulas

summary: STARLI | FLAGSHIP 13 FISSION Bioelectric and Quantum Signal Science | Flagships 151–160 / 300 Author: 33  |  White Rainbow Epoch  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2 This ten-volume collection investigates physically traceable bioelectric sensing, cell-membrane-potential readout, neural-field magnetometry, electrically guided microrobotic navigation, extracellular field metrology, noise separation, dynamic tracking, interface safety, spatial field reconstruction and electrical–mechanical multimodal identification. The common challenge is to distinguish real biological or phantom source physics from electrode polarization, ionic screening, induced electromagnetic pickup, motion artifact, thermal drift and inverse-model bias. Each English monograph uses 777 individually numbered pages: 30 candidate mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 one-page research investigations, 200 Research Gates with six detailed second-pass annotations, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Together these ten books contain 7,770 pages, 300 mathematical plates, 820 chapters, 4,100 investigation pages, 2,000 research gates and 330 prospective research instruments, protocols or successor objects. Ten independent research directions F151 | NANO-QUANTUM BIOELECTRIC-FIELD SENSING AT THE LIMIT — Separates calibrated local electric-field amplitudes from ionic screening, source geometry, electrode polarization, optical and mechanical interference by phantom-based blinded reference measurements. F152 | MICROSCALE NONINVASIVE CELL-MEMBRANE-POTENTIAL READOUT AT THE LIMIT — Treats noninvasive cell-membrane voltage as an inverse measurement problem; tests capacitive loading, optical reporting lag, transmembrane polarity, geometry and membrane-surrogate leakage against direct voltage truth. F153 | QUANTUM MAGNETOMETRY AND NEURAL ELECTRICAL SIGNAL COUPLING AT THE LIMIT — Compares magnetometer responses to independently known neural-like current sources while testing coil leakage, cross-axis sensitivity, gradiometer common-mode noise, timing uncertainty and localization ambiguity. F154 | NANOROBOTIC LOCAL BIOELECTRIC NAVIGATION AT THE LIMIT — Studies whether local electric cues direct bounded microrobotic paths rather than passive advection, electroosmosis, mechanical channel constraints or unreported magnetic control. F155 | EXTRACELLULAR ELECTRIC FIELD QUANTUM METROLOGY AT THE LIMIT — Builds traceability for extracellular electric-field and electrode polarization measurement, with complex impedance, source loading, SI units, shared calibration covariance and reference transfer. F156 | MICROSCALE BIOELECTRIC SIGNAL NOISE SEPARATION AT THE LIMIT — Disentangles bioelectric signals from mains interference, cable motion, thermal and Johnson noise, spectral leakage, common-mode drift, classifier bias and unequal optical/energy budgets. F157 | QUANTUM SENSOR BIOELECTRIC DYNAMIC TRACKING AT THE LIMIT — Tests dynamic tracking error against concealed moving-source truth, incorporating phase unwrap, bandwidth, tracking latency, source overlap, blank events and quantum/coherence limits. summary: STARLI | FLAGSHIP 13 FISSION Ten Research Design Monographs | Flagships 141-150 / 300 Author: 33  |  White Rainbow Epoch  |  Research Design Working Edition v1.2 This ten-volume STARLI series examines trustworthy AI-assisted micro/nanorobotic experiments and nano-quantum measurement systems. The common research question is how to bind physical observation, decision authority, calibration uncertainty, and independently reconstructable evidence without mistaking computational confidence for experimental proof. Each volume is a 777-page English, nonclinical prospective research design containing 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 separately paginated research studies, 200 Research Gates with six mechanistic annotations, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Across the ten volumes, the collection contains 300 research plates, 820 chapters, 4,100 study pages, 2,000 Research Gates, and 330 Phoenix candidates. Research scope by flagship F141 | Microrobotic Autonomous Control Authority Envelope at the Limit — Defines physical authority envelopes for microrobotic control, including credential expiry, actuator veto, permission transfer, and independently observed safe stopping. F142 | AI Nano-Quantum System Trustworthy Refusal Decision at the Limit — Studies when an AI-guided nano-quantum system must refuse action, separating calibrated abstention from indiscriminate rejection and unsafe confidence. F143 | Microscale Autonomous Experimental Design at the Limit — Examines autonomous microscale experimental design under specimen, information, energy, and permission budgets, with causal identification and independent replication. F144 | AI Quantum Sensing Uncertainty Calibration at the Limit — Investigates calibration of quantum-sensing uncertainty, including shared drift, covariance, phase ambiguity, photon budgets, and fair classical comparisons. F145 | Nanorobotic Closed-Loop Control Replayability at the Limit — Tests whether nanorobotic closed-loop decisions can be replayed from raw sensor data, actuator histories, calibration versions, and unselected failures. F146 | AI-Driven Microscale Active Sampling at the Limit — Designs AI-driven active sampling experiments that jointly measure analyte recovery, physical disturbance, resource cost, and contamination under blinded controls. F147 | Nano-Quantum System Human Review Mechanism at the Limit — Evaluates human review of nano-quantum decisions through signed authority, contradictory permissions, case-level uncertainty, and independent physical vetoes. F148 | AI Autonomous Research Agent Safety Boundary at the Limit — Defines safety boundaries for autonomous research agents across instrument access, sample authorization, unsafe tool composition, and immutable evidence. F149 | Microrobotic Autonomous System Interlaboratory Generalization at the Limit — Tests transfer of frozen microrobotic protocols between laboratories with different geometries, materials, calibration trees, operators, and failure environments. F150 | AI Nano-Quantum Trustworthy Autonomous Laboratory at the Limit — Integrates sample custody, microrobotic actuation, quantum/classical readouts, controlled autonomy, human oversight, and cross-site evidence reconstruction. Scientific boundary and publication status These books provide falsifiable research questions, candidate mathematical models, prospective blinded tests, competing explanations, negative-result criteria, and successor research interfaces. They do not report performed experiments or establish clinical efficacy, autonomous deployment safety, or quantum advantage. Independent expert verification of physical assumptions, formula applicability, all bibliographic relationships, and the scientific independence of closely related designs remains necessary. The common research question is how to bind physical observation, decision authority, calibration uncertainty, and independently reconstructable evidence without mistaking computational confidence for experimental proof. Each volume is a 777-page English, nonclinical prospective research design containing 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 separately paginated research studies, 200 Research Gates with six mechanistic annotations, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Across the ten volumes, the collection contains 300 research plates, 820 chapters, 4,100 study pages, 2,000 Research Gates, and 330 Phoenix candidates. Research scope by flagship F141 | Microrobotic Autonomous Control Authority Envelope at the Limit — Defines physical authority envelopes for microrobotic control, including credential expiry, actuator veto, permission transfer, and independently observed safe stopping. F142 | AI Nano-Quantum System Trustworthy Refusal Decision at the Limit — Studies when an AI-guided nano-quantum system must refuse action, separating calibrated abstention from indiscriminate rejection and unsafe confidence. F143 | Microscale Autonomous Experimental Design at the Limit — Examines autonomous microscale experimental design under specimen, information, energy, and permission budgets, with causal identification and independent replication. F144 | AI Quantum Sensing Uncertainty Calibration at the Limit — Investigates calibration of quantum-sensing uncertainty, including shared drift, covariance, phase ambiguity, photon budgets, and fair classical comparisons. F145 | Nanorobotic Closed-Loop Control Replayability at the Limit — Tests whether nanorobotic closed-loop decisions can be replayed from raw sensor data, actuator histories, calibration versions, and unselected failures. F146 | AI-Driven Microscale Active Sampling at the Limit — Designs AI-driven active sampling experiments that jointly measure analyte recovery, physical disturbance, resource cost, and contamination under blinded controls. F147 | Nano-Quantum System Human Review Mechanism at the Limit — Evaluates human review of nano-quantum decisions through signed authority, contradictory permissions, case-level uncertainty, and independent physical vetoes. F148 | AI Autonomous Research Agent Safety Boundary at the Limit — Defines safety boundaries for autonomous research agents across instrument access, sample authorization, unsafe tool composition, and immutable evidence. F149 | Microrobotic Autonomous System Interlaboratory Generalization at the Limit — Tests transfer of frozen microrobotic protocols between laboratories with different geometries, materials, calibration trees, operators, and failure environments. F150 | AI Nano-Quantum Trustworthy Autonomous Laboratory at the Limit — Integrates sample custody, microrobotic actuation, quantum/classical readouts, controlled autonomy, human oversight, and cross-site evidence reconstruction. Scientific boundary and publication status These books provide falsifiable research questions, candidate mathematical models, prospective blinded tests, competing explanations, negative-result criteria, and successor research interfaces. They do not report performed experiments or establish clinical efficacy, autonomous deployment safety, or quantum advantage. Independent expert verification of physical assumptions, formula applicability, all bibliographic relationships, and the scientific independence of closely related designs remains necessary. summary: STARLI | F131–F140 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · AI-Guided Micro/Nanosystems, Sampling and Validation Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.1 / Gate Annotation v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview These ten STARLI flagship monographs form an AI, nanosystems and microfluidic research-design collection in the second volume of the Flagship 13 Fission atlas. The studies connect adaptive sampling, counterfactual inference, autonomous calibration, hybrid physical-learning models, failure prediction, interpretable quantum sensing, closed-loop latency, multi-agent coordination, external digital-twin validation and biological signal drift. Each volume defines a prospective measurement target and competing explanation. No result is claimed to be experimentally demonstrated. The collection contains ten separately authored 777-page English working editions: 300 prospective mathematical plates, 820 chapter openers, 4,100 separately paginated study positions, 2,000 Research Gates with six annotation fields per Gate, and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. These counts describe the publication structure, not validated scientific novelty. A companion publication ZIP includes the ten original PDFs and ten per-book Zenodo introductions. The Ten Research Directions F131  AI-Driven Microfluidic Sampling Strategy Optimization At The Limit — Examines recoverable analyte as a fraction of input under fixed sampling resources. Expert tuning with equal trials is the comparator; hidden human intervention is the rival. Blind recovery audits and out-of-distribution refusal test whether AI planning adds genuine value. F132  Nano-Quantum System Counterfactual Inference At The Limit — Tests held-out, intervention-specific counterfactual prediction error while retaining constraint-violation safeguards. Frozen open-loop policies anchor comparison; training-test leakage and nonreplayable observation-to-action chains can invalidate apparent autonomy. F133  AI-Driven Microrobotic Autonomous Calibration At The Limit — Uses blind-standard calibration bias after autonomous correction as a physical measurement target. Preregistered experimental design is the baseline. Extra experimental trials and any action outside the authority envelope defeat a claimed improvement. F134  Microscale Physical Model and Neural Network Coupling At The Limit — Challenges coupled learning and physical models against independently measured conservation residuals under withheld shifts. Matched expert tuning and hidden manual intervention are alternative explanations; unsafe confidence outside the tested domain is a stop condition. F135  AI-Driven Nanoscale Sampling Failure Prediction At The Limit — Proposes prospective fault warning lead time, in seconds, at a fixed false-alarm rate. Frozen open-loop policies and unselected failure cases distinguish early warning from hindsight leakage. Recovery outcomes and complete action replay remain necessary. F136  Quantum Sensor Interpretable AI At The Limit — Asks whether AI explanations agree with mechanism-specific physical ablations, rather than merely producing plausible narratives. The proposed witness is an agreement fraction, with counterfactual error and calibrated sensing as safeguards. More experimental trials are a competing account. F137  Microrobotic Closed-Loop Control Latency At The Limit — Measures the full sensor-to-physical-action delay, in seconds, inside a declared operating envelope. Expert-tuned controls under matched resources establish the comparison. Hidden human intervention and high-confidence out-of-domain action must be ruled out. F138  AI Multi-Agent Sampling Mission Coordination At The Limit — Evaluates calibration-adjusted joint sampling mission completion as a fraction under fairness and safety vetoes. Frozen open-loop coordination and identical observation

summary: Reproducibility materials for "Operating Constraints Shape Portfolio Value in Phased Metro Flood Protection", version 1.3.2. This version adds Supplemental Notes A–E to the original Supplemental Materials. The combined PDF contains 40 pages: the original 33-page material with Tables S1–S35, Figs. S1–S4, and Supplementary Methods, followed by seven pages of additional data and operating evidence, identification checks, sequencing comparisons, annualization sensitivities, and tail diagnostics. The first 33 pages and their numerical results are unchanged from version 1.3.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23969774). The unchanged computational addendum contains protocols, code, seeds, selected station sets, unrounded results, and verification records. It supplements the baseline analysis (version 1.1.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22969483). The original LaTeX source archive constructs the original 33-page part; the editable Word source for the appended seven-page Notes is supplied separately. A release README and SHA-256 checksums document the complete file set. The annualized quantity represents the service deficit of an annual-maximum three-hour representative storm under a common exposure; it is not calibrated cumulative passenger loss. Population is a demand proxy. Station response, dependence, protection, and short-turn service are model assumptions. Source attribution and the original license terms are retained.

This version adds Supplemental Notes A–E to the original Supplemental Materials. The combined PDF contains 40 pages: the original 33-page material with Tables S1–S35, Figs. S1–S4, and Supplementary Methods, followed by seven pages of additional data and operating evidence, identification checks, sequencing comparisons, annualization sensitivities, and tail diagnostics. The first 33 pages and their numerical results are unchanged from version 1.3.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23969774). The unchanged computational addendum contains protocols, code, seeds, selected station sets, unrounded results, and verification records. It supplements the baseline analysis (version 1.1.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22969483). The original LaTeX source archive constructs the original 33-page part; the editable Word source for the appended seven-page Notes is supplied separately. A release README and SHA-256 checksums document the complete file set. The annualized quantity represents the service deficit of an annual-maximum three-hour representative storm under a common exposure; it is not calibrated cumulative passenger loss. Population is a demand proxy. Station response, dependence, protection, and short-turn service are model assumptions. Source attribution and the original license terms are retained.

summary: This package contains the Python code used to obtain, process, and analyze the data for the article "Coca, Armed Violence, and Drug Seizures in Colombia: Spatial and Temporal Evidence on Territorial Security". The study examines how coca cultivation, recorded armed violence, and drug seizures were related across 1,121 Colombian municipal units between 2020 and 2024, with an extended window from 2016. It combines spatial autocorrelation analysis (global and local Moran statistics with permutation inference and false discovery rate control) with Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood models that include municipality and year fixed effects. Data. The package does not redistribute data. All inputs are public official sources downloaded by the code itself: - Coca area by municipality (Ministry of Justice and Law / UNODC Integrated Illicit Crops Monitoring System, datos.gov.co). - Homicides, terrorism acts, cocaine and coca base seizures, and manual eradication (Ministry of National Defense, datos.gov.co). - Presumed homicides, definitive figures (National Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, datos.gov.co). - Armed conflict events (National Center for Historical Memory, SIEVCAC, datos.gov.co). - PDET municipalities (Territorial Renewal Agency, datos.gov.co). - Population projections, census-based poverty index, and 2023 municipal boundaries (DANE). The download script records the access date and SHA-256 hash of every file. Open-data portals are updated continuously, so later downloads may include revised records. The analyses reported in the article used files downloaded on November 7, 2026. Contents: - scripts/01_download.py: downloads the official datasets. - scripts/02_inspect.py: audits the raw files (structure, periods, codes, units, duplicates). - scripts/03_build_panel.py: builds the municipality-year panel (DANE DIVIPOLA codes, 2015–2024) and a data-quality report. - scripts/04_spatial_prep.py: prepares municipal geometries and spatial weights (queen contiguity and six nearest neighbors). - scripts/05_analysis.py: descriptive statistics, spatial autocorrelation, fixed-effects Poisson models, robustness checks, and seizure analyses. - scripts/08_revision_analyses.py: contrasts for concrete changes in coca area, exploratory equivalence tests, within/between (correlated random effects) models, first-difference models, extended-window sensitivity, and sample composition. - scripts/10_revision2_analyses.py: composition of the armed conflict event index, contiguity-constrained spatial clusters for robust inference, and alternative population specifications. - requirements.txt and README.md: software requirements and run instructions. Usage. Install Python 3.12 and the packages in requirements.txt, then run the scripts in numerical order from the package folder. Results are written as CSV files to results/ and logs to logs/. Inference is descriptive and associational. The code does not identify causal effects.

summary: Physically Anchored Multi-Resolution Neural Operator Framework for Flood Inundation Prediction Initial research release of the multi-resolution neural operator framework for high-resolution flood inundation prediction. This release includes the source code for the coarse-scale Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), terrain-aware Neural Residual Magnifier, physics-anchored reconstruction, and supporting training and inference utilities. The implementation supports three flood inundation case studies: Neuse River flooding, Fall River Lake dam-break, and Chowilla floodplain. Datasets and pretrained models: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23990987 The source code and associated research data are provided to support reproducibility and further research on neural operator-based flood inundation prediction.
title: AMBehroozi/Flood_Neural_operator: Physically Anchored Multi-Resolution Neural Operator Framework for Flood Inundation Prediction

summary: Overview Part 20 of 20. This is version 2 of the dataset. The source list, the tar file names and the split into parts are the same as in version 1. All images were generated again with a new model, EBGSv2. The dataset contains 2,981,033 synthetic Euclid VIS images. Each image corresponds to one source in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. The sources lie in the Euclid DR1 footprint, and most of them are BGS Bright and BGS Faint photometric targets. The model input is the DESI r- and z-band cutout. Changes from version 1 Item Version 1 This version Model EBGS: trained on DESI–Euclid cutout pairs centred on BGS targets (66,359 training pairs) EBGSv2: trained on patches cut from full Euclid Q1 MER tiles (not centred on galaxies) PSF conditioning None DESI r- and z-band PSF size as input; Euclid PSF fixed to one reference PSF Sampling 10 reverse steps; 3 trajectories share the first 70% of the steps and then run independently; the released image is the mean of the 3 trajectories 50 reverse steps; one trajectory HDUs Prediction, DESI_IMG, PREDICTION_STD Prediction, DESI_IMG; no PREDICTION_STD WCS None In both HDUs Noise model None Parameters in the header give a 1σ uncertainty for each pixel File organisation The dataset has 1,235 tar archives, grouped by HEALPix pixel (nside = 64, NESTED ordering). The archive names, the sources in each archive and the part that holds each archive are the same as in version 1. Each archive holds flat FITS files named <RA>_<DEC>.fits , in decimal degrees. This record holds 52 archives with 127,059 files, covering RA 349.8° to 99.9° (across RA = 0) and Dec −66.8° to −35.7°. Metadata files in this record: checksums.tsv : size, SHA256, MD5 and number of files for all 1,235 archives. ebgsv2_nfe50_index.csv and ebgsv2_nfe50_index.fits : one row per archive, with sky range, list of HEALPix pixels, part number and checksums. record_20_archives.txt : the archives in this record. ebgsv2_nfe50_files.csv.gz : one row per file (file name, RA, Dec, archive, part). Finding the archive for a sky position (same as version 1): import healpy as hp pix = hp.ang2pix(64, ra_deg, dec_deg, nest=True, lonlat=True) # find the row of the index whose hp64_nested_pixels column contains pix Model and generation settings The model is an Image-to-Image Schrödinger Bridge (I2SB). It starts from the DESI r-band image and is conditioned on the DESI z-band image. The training data come from 304 Euclid Q1 MER tiles. A further 16 tiles were used for validation and 24 tiles were held out for testing. None of these 40 tiles was used in training. The training target is the background-subtracted MER VIS mosaic (BGSUB). The generated images have the same pixel units, with an AB zero point of 24.6. We use the EMA weights at training step 68,931. This checkpoint has the lowest reduced χ² on the validation set. DESI PSF conditioning : the r- and z-band PSF FWHM come from the PSFSZ_R and PSFSZ_Z keywords of the DESI cutout header and enter the model as constant maps. If a cutout has no such keywords, we use the median of its PSFSIZE map. The values used are stored in the DPSF_R and DPSF_Z keywords of each file. Euclid PSF conditioning : all sources use the same reference PSF, the median stack of the Q1 test-set PSFs (header keyword PSFMODE = 'ref'). summary: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) to infer particle formation rate J(t) and size-dependent growth rate GR(d, t) from parallel differential mobility analyzer (DMA) particle size distribution counts measured in the CERN CLOUD (Cosmics Leaving OUtdoor Droplets) chamber experiments. The PINN is trained on measured counts and constrained by the aerosol general dynamic equation (GDE), with nucleation expressed as a boundary flux at 1.7 nm. For baseline benchmark comparison, the notebook also includes a Python re-implementation of the Julia-based extended Kalman filter and fixed-interval smoother from Ozon et al. (2021). Both methods are evaluated on four simulated cases with known truth (0000_00 to 0000_03) and the three CLOUD experiments (1802_01, 1952_02, 1906_03). For the CLOUD runs, results are compared with the independent PSM (J) and INSIDE (GR) estimates reported in the paper. BAYROSOL 1.1 data is downloaded directly from Zenodo within the notebook (Ozon, Stolzenburg and Dada, 2021, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4450492 , MIT license), so no additional data files are appended.
title: PINN Inference of Aerosol Formation and Growth Rates from CLOUD Chamber Data

summary: Pre-specified reanalysis of public human arteriovenous fistula single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE305423) along with bulk RNA-sequencing data (GSE220796, GSE119296). The repository contains the analysis pipeline, fixed random seed (2611), pinned environment, all result tables cited in the article, and a numeric-provenance assertion script that re-derives every number quoted in the manuscript from the result files. Main findings: apparent transcriptional signatures of maturation failure are dominated by changes in cell composition (including ambient-RNA-driven artefacts) rather than cell-intrinsic reprogramming; myofibroblast abundance, fate bias and matrisome programmes are unchanged within the detectable effect range.
title: Analysis code for: Cell composition accounts for much of the transcriptomic difference between failed and matured human arteriovenous fistulas

summary: STARLI | F131–F140 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · AI-Guided Micro/Nanosystems, Sampling and Validation Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.1 / Gate Annotation v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview These ten STARLI flagship monographs form an AI, nanosystems and microfluidic research-design collection in the second volume of the Flagship 13 Fission atlas. The studies connect adaptive sampling, counterfactual inference, autonomous calibration, hybrid physical-learning models, failure prediction, interpretable quantum sensing, closed-loop latency, multi-agent coordination, external digital-twin validation and biological signal drift. Each volume defines a prospective measurement target and competing explanation. No result is claimed to be experimentally demonstrated. The collection contains ten separately authored 777-page English working editions: 300 prospective mathematical plates, 820 chapter openers, 4,100 separately paginated study positions, 2,000 Research Gates with six annotation fields per Gate, and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. These counts describe the publication structure, not validated scientific novelty. A companion publication ZIP includes the ten original PDFs and ten per-book Zenodo introductions. The Ten Research Directions F131  AI-Driven Microfluidic Sampling Strategy Optimization At The Limit — Examines recoverable analyte as a fraction of input under fixed sampling resources. Expert tuning with equal trials is the comparator; hidden human intervention is the rival. Blind recovery audits and out-of-distribution refusal test whether AI planning adds genuine value. F132  Nano-Quantum System Counterfactual Inference At The Limit — Tests held-out, intervention-specific counterfactual prediction error while retaining constraint-violation safeguards. Frozen open-loop policies anchor comparison; training-test leakage and nonreplayable observation-to-action chains can invalidate apparent autonomy. F133  AI-Driven Microrobotic Autonomous Calibration At The Limit — Uses blind-standard calibration bias after autonomous correction as a physical measurement target. Preregistered experimental design is the baseline. Extra experimental trials and any action outside the authority envelope defeat a claimed improvement. F134  Microscale Physical Model and Neural Network Coupling At The Limit — Challenges coupled learning and physical models against independently measured conservation residuals under withheld shifts. Matched expert tuning and hidden manual intervention are alternative explanations; unsafe confidence outside the tested domain is a stop condition. F135  AI-Driven Nanoscale Sampling Failure Prediction At The Limit — Proposes prospective fault warning lead time, in seconds, at a fixed false-alarm rate. Frozen open-loop policies and unselected failure cases distinguish early warning from hindsight leakage. Recovery outcomes and complete action replay remain necessary. F136  Quantum Sensor Interpretable AI At The Limit — Asks whether AI explanations agree with mechanism-specific physical ablations, rather than merely producing plausible narratives. The proposed witness is an agreement fraction, with counterfactual error and calibrated sensing as safeguards. More experimental trials are a competing account. F137  Microrobotic Closed-Loop Control Latency At The Limit — Measures the full sensor-to-physical-action delay, in seconds, inside a declared operating envelope. Expert-tuned controls under matched resources establish the comparison. Hidden human intervention and high-confidence out-of-domain action must be ruled out. F138  AI Multi-Agent Sampling Mission Coordination At The Limit — Evaluates calibration-adjusted joint sampling mission completion as a fraction under fairness and safety vetoes. Frozen open-loop coordination and identical observation

summary: This package contains the Python code used to obtain, process, and analyze the data for the article "Coca, Armed Violence, and Drug Seizures in Colombia: Spatial and Temporal Evidence on Territorial Security". The study examines how coca cultivation, recorded armed violence, and drug seizures were related across 1,121 Colombian municipal units between 2020 and 2024, with an extended window from 2016. It combines spatial autocorrelation analysis (global and local Moran statistics with permutation inference and false discovery rate control) with Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood models that include municipality and year fixed effects. Data. The package does not redistribute data. All inputs are public official sources downloaded by the code itself: - Coca area by municipality (Ministry of Justice and Law / UNODC Integrated Illicit Crops Monitoring System, datos.gov.co). - Homicides, terrorism acts, cocaine and coca base seizures, and manual eradication (Ministry of National Defense, datos.gov.co). - Presumed homicides, definitive figures (National Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, datos.gov.co). - Armed conflict events (National Center for Historical Memory, SIEVCAC, datos.gov.co). - PDET municipalities (Territorial Renewal Agency, datos.gov.co). - Population projections, census-based poverty index, and 2023 municipal boundaries (DANE). The download script records the access date and SHA-256 hash of every file. Open-data portals are updated continuously, so later downloads may include revised records. The analyses reported in the article used files downloaded on November 7, 2026. Contents: - scripts/01_download.py: downloads the official datasets. - scripts/02_inspect.py: audits the raw files (structure, periods, codes, units, duplicates). - scripts/03_build_panel.py: builds the municipality-year panel (DANE DIVIPOLA codes, 2015–2024) and a data-quality report. - scripts/04_spatial_prep.py: prepares municipal geometries and spatial weights (queen contiguity and six nearest neighbors). - scripts/05_analysis.py: descriptive statistics, spatial autocorrelation, fixed-effects Poisson models, robustness checks, and seizure analyses. - scripts/08_revision_analyses.py: contrasts for concrete changes in coca area, exploratory equivalence tests, within/between (correlated random effects) models, first-difference models, extended-window sensitivity, and sample composition. - scripts/10_revision2_analyses.py: composition of the armed conflict event index, contiguity-constrained spatial clusters for robust inference, and alternative population specifications. - requirements.txt and README.md: software requirements and run instructions. Usage. Install Python 3.12 and the packages in requirements.txt, then run the scripts in numerical order from the package folder. Results are written as CSV files to results/ and logs to logs/. Inference is descriptive and associational. The code does not identify causal effects.
title: Replication code: coca cultivation, armed violence, and drug seizures in Colombian municipalities, 2016–2024

summary: Overview Part 20 of 20. This is version 2 of the dataset. The source list, the tar file names and the split into parts are the same as in version 1. All images were generated again with a new model, EBGSv2. The dataset contains 2,981,033 synthetic Euclid VIS images. Each image corresponds to one source in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. The sources lie in the Euclid DR1 footprint, and most of them are BGS Bright and BGS Faint photometric targets. The model input is the DESI r- and z-band cutout. Changes from version 1 Item Version 1 This version Model EBGS: trained on DESI–Euclid cutout pairs centred on BGS targets (66,359 training pairs) EBGSv2: trained on patches cut from full Euclid Q1 MER tiles (not centred on galaxies) PSF conditioning None DESI r- and z-band PSF size as input; Euclid PSF fixed to one reference PSF Sampling 10 reverse steps; 3 trajectories share the first 70% of the steps and then run independently; the released image is the mean of the 3 trajectories 50 reverse steps; one trajectory HDUs Prediction, DESI_IMG, PREDICTION_STD Prediction, DESI_IMG; no PREDICTION_STD WCS None In both HDUs Noise model None Parameters in the header give a 1σ uncertainty for each pixel File organisation The dataset has 1,235 tar archives, grouped by HEALPix pixel (nside = 64, NESTED ordering). The archive names, the sources in each archive and the part that holds each archive are the same as in version 1. Each archive holds flat FITS files named <RA>_<DEC>.fits , in decimal degrees. This record holds 52 archives with 127,059 files, covering RA 349.8° to 99.9° (across RA = 0) and Dec −66.8° to −35.7°. Metadata files in this record: checksums.tsv : size, SHA256, MD5 and number of files for all 1,235 archives. ebgsv2_nfe50_index.csv and ebgsv2_nfe50_index.fits : one row per archive, with sky range, list of HEALPix pixels, part number and checksums. record_20_archives.txt : the archives in this record. ebgsv2_nfe50_files.csv.gz : one row per file (file name, RA, Dec, archive, part). Finding the archive for a sky position (same as version 1): import healpy as hp pix = hp.ang2pix(64, ra_deg, dec_deg, nest=True, lonlat=True) # find the row of the index whose hp64_nested_pixels column contains pix Model and generation settings The model is an Image-to-Image Schrödinger Bridge (I2SB). It starts from the DESI r-band image and is conditioned on the DESI z-band image. The training data come from 304 Euclid Q1 MER tiles. A further 16 tiles were used for validation and 24 tiles were held out for testing. None of these 40 tiles was used in training. The training target is the background-subtracted MER VIS mosaic (BGSUB). The generated images have the same pixel units, with an AB zero point of 24.6. We use the EMA weights at training step 68,931. This checkpoint has the lowest reduced χ² on the validation set. DESI PSF conditioning : the r- and z-band PSF FWHM come from the PSFSZ_R and PSFSZ_Z keywords of the DESI cutout header and enter the model as constant maps. If a cutout has no such keywords, we use the median of its PSFSIZE map. The values used are stored in the DPSF_R and DPSF_Z keywords of each file. Euclid PSF conditioning : all sources use the same reference PSF, the median stack of the Q1 test-set PSFs (header keyword PSFMODE = 'ref'). Sampling : one sample per source, 50 reverse steps, no steps shared with other samples. The random seed is 1024 plus the list index of the first file in the batch, so the results are reproducible. summary: Event-level Sentinel-2 burned-area dataset of western Canada and the results of a leave-one-province-out benchmark of fourteen segmentation configurations (revised study, version 2.0). Contents: 135 windows of about 20 x 20 km at 10 m in Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan (120 windows centred on large fires of 2022-2024 and 15 fire-free windows), each a single post-fire Sentinel-2 Level-2A scene stacked as nine layers (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, NDVI, NBR, NDMI; GeoTIFF, 32-bit float) with a reference raster derived from the National Burned Area Composite (burned / unburned / ignored) and a no-data mask; the window manifest with scene provenance (product identifiers, processing baseline, clear and masked fractions, fire identifiers); the fold file of the three leave-one-province-out folds (training, validation and test role of every window); the per-window results of every configuration and label-free rule; and the predicted burned-unburned maps of all 1,890 window-model pairs. Code, environment specification and summary tables are in the companion GitHub repository; the trained models are in a separate Zenodo record. Sources: Copernicus Sentinel-2 data (ESA), National Burned Area Composite (Natural Resources Canada, Canadian Forest Service; Open Government Licence - Canada). Files. data_postfire_AB.tar, data_postfire_BC.tar, data_postfire_SK.tar (one per province, 45 windows each, 6.9-7.1 GB each): for every window <window_id>_S2.tif (nine layers, float32, masked pixels NaN), <window_id>_label.tif (0 unburned, 1 burned, 255 ignored) and <window_id>_scl.tif (scene classification layer), plus manifest.csv. data_prefire_AB.tar, data_prefire_BC.tar, data_prefire_SK.tar (6.8-6.9 GB each): the pre-fire scene of every window used by the dNBR baselines, <window_id>_S2pre.tif and <window_id>_scl_pre.tif, plus manifest_prefire.csv. predicted_maps.tar.gz (74 MB): the predicted burned-unburned maps of the 1,890 window-model pairs, maps/<run>/<window_id>_pred.tif (8-bit). results_and_manifests.zip : the per-window results of every configuration and label-free rule, the summary tables, the run ledger and both manifests. burned-area-segmentation-western-canada-v2.0.zip : snapshot of the companion repository at tag v2.0 (code, fold file, manifests, per-window results, tables). SHA256SUMS_release.txt : SHA-256 of every file in this record and in the checkpoint record. Companion to the manuscript "Remote sensing of burned-area delineation with Sentinel-2: a leave-one-province-out multi-model semantic segmentation benchmark across western Canada" (M. S. Khan, H. Afzaal, G. S. Randhawa, A. A. Farooque; in revision at Computers & Geosciences).
title: Sentinel-2 burned-area segmentation benchmark for western Canada (v2.0): dataset, reference rasters, fold file, per-window results and predicted maps

summary: We determine the complete equal-reference Umegaki relative-entropy contraction coefficient of every finite-dimensional quantum channel. For its unnormalized Choi matrix J, let H be the largest output subspace with ℂⁿ ⊗ H ⊆ supp J, and let M(ρ) be the compression to H of Tr_A[(ρᵀ ⊗ I)J⁺]. The coefficient is 1 − min_ρ Tr_H M(ρ)⁻¹, with the minimum set to zero when H = {0}. A Kraus cancellation inequality gives the upper bound, and a weighted trace-zero operator basis gives matching faithful pairs with both marginals equal and reference dimension n². The complementary coefficient has a reciprocal radius formula, a finite semidefinite representation, and an exact product law. Strict contraction is equivalent to a nonzero completely positive replacer minorant. The formula also gives the exact coefficient of depolarizing channels throughout their physical parameter range. The general matching family has vanishing input divergence; its logarithmic rate is pointwise for a fixed faithful input density, with separate finite-accuracy bounds for optimization and conditioning. A different construction retains any prescribed positive limiting divergence when the coefficient is one. This cannot hold universally: a complete nonlinear bound for binary symmetric channels forces every maximizing sequence to lose input divergence, regardless of reference dimension. The positive construction still has vanishing trace distance and exponentially small regularization; no fixed-error or capacity conclusion follows. A visual guide records the mathematical routes, proof dependencies, and provenance of the result.

The coefficient is 1 − min_ρ Tr_H M(ρ)⁻¹, with the minimum set to zero when H = {0}. A Kraus cancellation inequality gives the upper bound, and a weighted trace-zero operator basis gives matching faithful pairs with both marginals equal and reference dimension n². The complementary coefficient has a reciprocal radius formula, a finite semidefinite representation, and an exact product law. Strict contraction is equivalent to a nonzero completely positive replacer minorant. The formula also gives the exact coefficient of depolarizing channels throughout their physical parameter range. The general matching family has vanishing input divergence; its logarithmic rate is pointwise for a fixed faithful input density, with separate finite-accuracy bounds for optimization and conditioning. A different construction retains any prescribed positive limiting divergence when the coefficient is one. This cannot hold universally: a complete nonlinear bound for binary symmetric channels forces every maximizing sequence to lose input divergence, regardless of reference dimension. The positive construction still has vanishing trace distance and exponentially small regularization; no fixed-error or capacity conclusion follows. A visual guide records the mathematical routes, proof dependencies, and provenance of the result.

summary: Does the governance of climate money behave like the governance of a ration card? The Map of Maps of Governance (Tailwinds 2026-02) proposed seven rules for how success and failure move through Indian institutions. This companion to Tailwinds 2026-10 takes the rules out of India for the first time and tests them, in a registered analysis, on the full portfolio of the Green Climate Fund (372 projects, frozen 12 October 2026). Three rules could be tested on the Fund's records; four were declared untestable before any result was seen. One rule holds. Islands: work moved out of the routine, high-discretion track succeeds, and projects on the Fund's Simplified Approval Process reach first disbursement 5.4 months sooner than regular proposals (8.8 against 14.1 months; 90 percent interval −7.3 to −2.9), in every run. Two rules fail. Downhill: delay does not fall harder on the most vulnerable countries (+0.6 months, −2.0 to 2.8). Broker: international intermediaries do not carry more of the money where vulnerability is higher; they carry about four-fifths of it everywhere (79.6 against 81.4 percent). The fast lane is faster, and it is not fairer: inside it, the most vulnerable third of countries waits 1.4 months longer than the least, against 0.2 months on the regular track. The rules travel in part. Where they fail, they fail for a reason the map can use: between countries, a fund's queue runs through its intermediaries, which serve every country alike. The tail that Downhill predicts lies inside countries, where the Fund's record cannot see.
title: The fast lane and the long chain: Why the Green Climate Fund's simplified track speeds money to the ground but does not make it fairer, and what the Map of Maps of Governance learns from its first test outside India

The fast lane is faster, and it is not fairer: inside it, the most vulnerable third of countries waits 1.4 months longer than the least, against 0.2 months on the regular track. The rules travel in part. Where they fail, they fail for a reason the map can use: between countries, a fund's queue runs through its intermediaries, which serve every country alike. Evaluation-only configurations. The pipeline now evaluates a config with no model when it enables baselines explicitly, scoring those alone. summary: The 42 trained model checkpoints of the leave-one-province-out burned-area segmentation benchmark for western Canada (revised study, version 2.0): fourteen configurations (U-Net, DeepLabV3, PSPNet and DeepLabV3+ with ResNet-50 encoders, UPerNet with a ConvNeXt-T encoder, SegFormer MiT-B2, SAM-LoRA ViT-B, Mask2Former Swin-L, Prithvi-EO-2.0 300M fully fine-tuned and with LoRA adapters, TerraMind-1.0 base, and the plain-cross-entropy contrast of U-Net, DeepLabV3 and PSPNet) trained once in each of the three folds F-AB, F-BC and F-SK on single post-fire Sentinel-2 scenes with National Burned Area Composite reference labels. Each checkpoint (best validation epoch, PyTorch state dictionary) comes with its run configuration, normalisation statistics, training log and SHA-256 checksum. The dataset, fold file and results are in a separate Zenodo record; the code that loads and applies the checkpoints is in the companion GitHub repository. Files. <run>_best.pt for the 42 runs (<configuration>_F-AB, _F-BC and _F-SK; the suffix _C2 marks the plain-cross-entropy contrast runs), 98 MB to 1.3 GB each and 16.1 GB in total: PyTorch checkpoints holding the model state dictionary, the epoch and the validation score of the best epoch. run_folders.zip : config.json (all arguments and the training, validation and test window lists), norm_stats.json, log.csv (per-epoch log) and ledger.json of every run, and run_ledger.csv (best validation F1, epochs, SHA-256 of the checkpoint, finishing time, wall time, GPU). burned-area-segmentation-western-canada-v2.0.zip : snapshot of the companion repository at tag v2.0, whose models.py builds each architecture and whose eval.py loads a checkpoint and predicts a window. SHA256SUMS_release.txt : SHA-256 of every file in this record and in the dataset record. Companion to the manuscript "Remote sensing of burned-area delineation with Sentinel-2: a leave-one-province-out multi-model semantic segmentation benchmark across western Canada" (M. S. Khan, H. Afzaal, G. S. Randhawa, A. A. Farooque; in revision at Computers & Geosciences).
