summary: Medical microbiology occupies an unusual position in the medical curriculum: its objects are almost never seen directly, yet graduates must reason about them from stains, colonies, reaction patterns, and laboratory reports. Methodological guidance in Uzbekistan and the wider Russian-language literature typically responds with lists of criteria for choosing teaching technologies. This article argues that such lists, however sound their individual items, conceal a structural problem, because they treat criteria of different logical kinds as if they could be traded against one another. Using a conceptual model-building design, the study derives eight selection criteria from the literature, sorts them into three tiers (non-compensatory gates, discipline-specific epistemic criteria, and calibration criteria) and applies an explicit 0–2 affordance appraisal to ten teaching technologies. Two of the eight criteria proved relational: they describe a match between a technology and an outcome or a cohort and cannot be scored as properties of the technology. Of the 60 attributable judgements, 26 were conditional rather than direct. Additive totals favoured case analysis, problem-based tasks, and laboratory work, yet only concept mapping and comparison tables cleared both the feasibility and the assessability thresholds unconditionally. The resulting coupling principle holds that a technology chosen for its inferential demand should be paired with one that leaves an assessable trace. The model is offered as an analytic proposal for empirical testing, not as evidence of differential effectiveness.
title: TEACHING THE INVISIBLE: A CONSTRAINT-FIRST DECISION MODEL FOR SELECTING PEDAGOGICAL TECHNOLOGIES IN MEDICAL MICROBIOLOGY

Of the 60 attributable judgements, 26 were conditional rather than direct. Additive totals favoured case analysis, problem-based tasks, and laboratory work, yet only concept mapping and comparison tables cleared both the feasibility and the assessability thresholds unconditionally. The resulting coupling principle holds that a technology chosen for its inferential demand should be paired with one that leaves an assessable trace. The model is offered as an analytic proposal for empirical testing, not as evidence of differential effectiveness.

summary: Replication code for the reanalysis reported in the Nature Food manuscript "Strong El Nino events and thin inventories drive concentrated tropical crop losses and uneven world price transmission". Added frontend/scripts/copy-data.mjs calls an optional, product-owned module frontend/scripts/copy-data.product.mjs once, after the declared files are copied into the rebuilt overlay, with { derived, out, repo, readiness } ( readiness is the parsed readiness document or null ). It returns { copied, absent, problems } , arrays of strings: the paths (relative to public/data ) it copied, the paths it leaves out as declared absent (each printed as a WARN line), and the problems that stop the build. No module: the output is that of 0.15.004. frontend/src/lib/copy-data.test.ts , a base test of the script (it says "A product takes this file verbatim"): one case per behaviour above. Changed tests/adversarial/test_base_tests_0_15_003.py : a base script is a frontend/scripts/*.mjs that is not a *.product.mjs . summary: Encounters among heterogeneous epistemic–praxis systems can expose differences in evidence, interpretation, and practical capacities . Some differences become consequential gaps relative to specified concerns; others sustain complementary ways of knowing . This paper develops a provisional account of generative translation through which situated encounters may enable new meanings and, under more demanding conditions, enduring changes in interpretive or practical capacities . A comparative philosophical analysis draws on hermeneutics, semiotics, pragmatism, social epistemology, evolutionary coordination, and procedural justice while preserving their distinct commitments . The discussion distinguishes representational correspondence, practical reconstruction, and generative translation, then separates interpretive affordance from realized meaning, retained capacity, recurrent convention, and possible normative recognition . Each transition requires different evidence; ordinary learning, resource changes, incentives, and institutional interfaces provide competing explanations for apparent co-evolution . Ethical evaluation concerns task-appropriate fidelity, opportunities for participation and refusal, authority over classifications, affected interests, and the review of consequential decisions . Ceva’s interactive justice and Eglash and Garvey’s generative justice inform distinct aspects of the inquiry, with questions of cross-category standing remaining open to separate justification . Constructed cases and proposed research designs indicate ways to evaluate and challenge the framework . The contribution is an integrative research programme connecting translation-mediated meaning formation with causal scrutiny and ethical responsibility .
title: How Meaning Grows Across Epistemic Gaps: A Discussion of Generative Translation and Its Ethics

summary: Data and code for computational prioritization of MYB–NFIB and MYBL1–NFIB junction peptides in adenoid cystic carcinoma. The primary analysis screens 284 public RNA-sequencing libraries and evaluates 3,746 observations representing 3,122 peptide–HLA pairs from 63 reconstructed contexts. Same-observation affinity-percentile and unflanked eluted-ligand rank cutoffs of ≤2% select 57 pairs (34 sequences) supported by 27 libraries, including an 11-pair provisional testing panel. The corrected analysis uses a consistent donor-frame translation rule. A separately reported HLA suffix-relaxed analysis evaluates 7,370 observations and selects 111 pairs, including a 26-pair sensitivity panel. Normal-peptide controls, native-flank comparisons, source annotations, conditional donor-support analyses and reconstruction checks retain their respective scopes; the resource does not provide complete native-context scoring of every normal-control combination or definitive donor attribution. This package includes the checked manuscript and supplement with updated public data links, 133 scientific tables with a 135-sheet workbook, figures, analysis code, saved prediction outputs and reproduction checks. Scientific data, code and outputs are unchanged from the clean 5 November package. Licensed executables, model weights, bulk sequencing reads and accession-linked genetic comparisons are not redistributed. Predictions prioritize experimental testing.
title: Selecting MYB–NFIB and MYBL1–NFIB junction peptides for experimental testing in adenoid cystic carcinoma

summary: Event-level Sentinel-2 burned-area dataset of western Canada and the results of a leave-one-province-out benchmark of fourteen segmentation configurations (revised study, version 2.0). Contents: 135 windows of about 20 x 20 km at 10 m in Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan (120 windows centred on large fires of 2022-2024 and 15 fire-free windows), each a single post-fire Sentinel-2 Level-2A scene stacked as nine layers (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, NDVI, NBR, NDMI; GeoTIFF, 32-bit float) with a reference raster derived from the National Burned Area Composite (burned / unburned / ignored) and a no-data mask; the window manifest with scene provenance (product identifiers, processing baseline, clear and masked fractions, fire identifiers); the fold file of the three leave-one-province-out folds (training, validation and test role of every window); the per-window results of every configuration and label-free rule; and the predicted burned-unburned maps of all 1,890 window-model pairs. Code, environment specification and summary tables are in the companion GitHub repository; the trained models are in a separate Zenodo record. Sources: Copernicus Sentinel-2 data (ESA), National Burned Area Composite (Natural Resources Canada, Canadian Forest Service; Open Government Licence - Canada). Files. data_postfire_AB.tar, data_postfire_BC.tar, data_postfire_SK.tar (one per province, 45 windows each, 6.9-7.1 GB each): for every window <window_id>_S2.tif (nine layers, float32, masked pixels NaN), <window_id>_label.tif (0 unburned, 1 burned, 255 ignored) and <window_id>_scl.tif (scene classification layer), plus manifest.csv. data_prefire_AB.tar, data_prefire_BC.tar, data_prefire_SK.tar (6.8-6.9 GB each): the pre-fire scene of every window used by the dNBR baselines, <window_id>_S2pre.tif and <window_id>_scl_pre.tif, plus manifest_prefire.csv. predicted_maps.tar.gz (74 MB): the predicted burned-unburned maps of the 1,890 window-model pairs, maps/<run>/<window_id>_pred.tif (8-bit). results_and_manifests.zip : the per-window results of every configuration and label-free rule, the summary tables, the run ledger and both manifests. burned-area-segmentation-western-canada-v2.0.zip : snapshot of the companion repository at tag v2.0 (code, fold file, manifests, per-window results, tables). SHA256SUMS_release.txt : SHA-256 of every file in this record and in the checkpoint record. Companion to the manuscript "Remote sensing of burned-area delineation with Sentinel-2: a leave-one-province-out multi-model semantic segmentation benchmark across western Canada" (M. S. Khan, H. Afzaal, G. S. Randhawa, A. A. Farooque; in revision at Computers & Geosciences).

summary: We determine the complete equal-reference Umegaki relative-entropy contraction coefficient of every finite-dimensional quantum channel. For its unnormalized Choi matrix J, let H be the largest output subspace with ℂⁿ ⊗ H ⊆ supp J, and let M(ρ) be the compression to H of Tr_A[(ρᵀ ⊗ I)J⁺]. The coefficient is 1 − min_ρ Tr_H M(ρ)⁻¹, with the minimum set to zero when H = {0}. A Kraus cancellation inequality gives the upper bound, and a weighted trace-zero operator basis gives matching faithful pairs with both marginals equal and reference dimension n². The complementary coefficient has a reciprocal radius formula, a finite semidefinite representation, and an exact product law. Strict contraction is equivalent to a nonzero completely positive replacer minorant. The formula also gives the exact coefficient of depolarizing channels throughout their physical parameter range. The general matching family has vanishing input divergence; its logarithmic rate is pointwise for a fixed faithful input density, with separate finite-accuracy bounds for optimization and conditioning. A different construction retains any prescribed positive limiting divergence when the coefficient is one. This cannot hold universally: a complete nonlinear bound for binary symmetric channels forces every maximizing sequence to lose input divergence, regardless of reference dimension. The positive construction still has vanishing trace distance and exponentially small regularization; no fixed-error or capacity conclusion follows. A visual guide records the mathematical routes, proof dependencies, and provenance of the result.
title: Exact Complete Relative-Entropy Contraction of Finite Quantum Channels

The work proposes physical test designs, not observed new laws, clinical results or experimentally established quantum advantages. Two five-theme research units contain ten English 777-page working editions: 300 mathematical model plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study designs, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Research Unit I · F221–F225 F221  OPTICAL PHASE CONTROL AND MICROSCALE LOCALIZATION AT THE LIMIT — Challenges interferometric optical-phase localization with independently registered fiducials, wavefront reversals, detector reference drift and photon-matched free-space baselines. Reports phase and position residuals alongside photothermal rise; apparent field enhancement is not by itself a localization gain. F222  NANOMATERIALS QUANTUM DEFECT ENGINEERING AT THE LIMIT — Tests defect creation, charge states, spin coherence, surface passivation and unselected emitter yield against a geometry-matched classical materials stack. summary: The 42 trained model checkpoints of the leave-one-province-out burned-area segmentation benchmark for western Canada (revised study, version 2.0): fourteen configurations (U-Net, DeepLabV3, PSPNet and DeepLabV3+ with ResNet-50 encoders, UPerNet with a ConvNeXt-T encoder, SegFormer MiT-B2, SAM-LoRA ViT-B, Mask2Former Swin-L, Prithvi-EO-2.0 300M fully fine-tuned and with LoRA adapters, TerraMind-1.0 base, and the plain-cross-entropy contrast of U-Net, DeepLabV3 and PSPNet) trained once in each of the three folds F-AB, F-BC and F-SK on single post-fire Sentinel-2 scenes with National Burned Area Composite reference labels. Each checkpoint (best validation epoch, PyTorch state dictionary) comes with its run configuration, normalisation statistics, training log and SHA-256 checksum. The dataset, fold file and results are in a separate Zenodo record; the code that loads and applies the checkpoints is in the companion GitHub repository. Files. <run>_best.pt for the 42 runs (<configuration>_F-AB, _F-BC and _F-SK; the suffix _C2 marks the plain-cross-entropy contrast runs), 98 MB to 1.3 GB each and 16.1 GB in total: PyTorch checkpoints holding the model state dictionary, the epoch and the validation score of the best epoch. run_folders.zip : config.json (all arguments and the training, validation and test window lists), norm_stats.json, log.csv (per-epoch log) and ledger.json of every run, and run_ledger.csv (best validation F1, epochs, SHA-256 of the checkpoint, finishing time, wall time, GPU). burned-area-segmentation-western-canada-v2.0.zip : snapshot of the companion repository at tag v2.0, whose models.py builds each architecture and whose eval.py loads a checkpoint and predicts a window. SHA256SUMS_release.txt : SHA-256 of every file in this record and in the dataset record. Companion to the manuscript "Remote sensing of burned-area delineation with Sentinel-2: a leave-one-province-out multi-model semantic segmentation benchmark across western Canada" (M. S. Khan, H. Afzaal, G. S. Randhawa, A. A. Farooque; in revision at Computers & Geosciences).
title: Sentinel-2 burned-area segmentation benchmark for western Canada (v2.0): trained model checkpoints

summary: Medical microbiology occupies an unusual position in the medical curriculum: its objects are almost never seen directly, yet graduates must reason about them from stains, colonies, reaction patterns, and laboratory reports. Methodological guidance in Uzbekistan and the wider Russian-language literature typically responds with lists of criteria for choosing teaching technologies. This article argues that such lists, however sound their individual items, conceal a structural problem, because they treat criteria of different logical kinds as if they could be traded against one another. Using a conceptual model-building design, the study derives eight selection criteria from the literature, sorts them into three tiers (non-compensatory gates, discipline-specific epistemic criteria, and calibration criteria) and applies an explicit 0–2 affordance appraisal to ten teaching technologies. Two of the eight criteria proved relational: they describe a match between a technology and an outcome or a cohort and cannot be scored as properties of the technology. Of the 60 attributable judgements, 26 were conditional rather than direct. Additive totals favoured case analysis, problem-based tasks, and laboratory work, yet only concept mapping and comparison tables cleared both the feasibility and the assessability thresholds unconditionally. The resulting coupling principle holds that a technology chosen for its inferential demand should be paired with one that leaves an assessable trace. The model is offered as an analytic proposal for empirical testing, not as evidence of differential effectiveness.
title: TEACHING THE INVISIBLE: A CONSTRAINT-FIRST DECISION MODEL FOR SELECTING PEDAGOGICAL TECHNOLOGIES IN MEDICAL MICROBIOLOGY

summary: Version 5.1.0 reproducibility package for “Feasibility and Portability of Model-Based Duty-Cycle Grades for Marine Fuel Cells” by Eun-Hye Park, Hyo-Chan Kwon and Eun-Joo Park. This complete archive contains executable Python sources, synthetic inputs, frozen computational protocols, numerical tables, selected actual simulated waveforms, first-party figures, provenance and independent numerical checks. It preserves all 827 files of the version-5 numerical baseline at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24037253 and adds 16 disclosure and verification files. No scientific model, input, physical threshold, representative selection or original numerical result is changed. New in v5.1: - Complete five-setting, eight-seed stationary non-Gaussian diagnostic results for 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1 Hz plus exact identity transfer, with signed prediction-error means and seed ranges for both telegraph processes and their phase-randomized controls. At 0.01 Hz, the symmetric and asymmetric telegraph mean errors are +94.2606% and +120.1515%. These separate periodic distribution tests are counterexamples to a general Gaussian absolute-increment accuracy claim, not error bounds for physically screened voyages or estimates of physical aging error. - Explicit calculation conventions: 131,072 samples at 4 Hz, the ideal continuous transfer on the periodic Fourier grid, all circular one-second increments at a 0.25-second stride, and no final voyage-reporting Butterworth filter. The final constrained grades continue to use directly evaluated voyage increments and dwell times. - A fresh isolated execution of the unchanged diagnostic. Its 160 raw rows, 20 summary rows and metadata matched the baseline byte for byte; independent reaggregation from the raw moments had a maximum discrepancy of 1.11e-16 in fractional prediction error. - Clarified field-evidence wording: MS Mariella supports ferry installation and ship-network commissioning tests; the separate Pa-X-ell land-module aging observation is not an at-sea aging slope. - Explicit remaining limitations: universal single-coordinate EMS sufficiency and measured aging equivalence are not established; compatible empirical marine coefficient calibration, confidence intervals and covariance are unavailable; the original PLECS project remains unavailable, and no new OpenModelica/PLECS execution has been performed. Start with README_v5_1.md and ADDENDUM_v5_1_EN.md or ADDENDUM_v5_1_KO.md. Run “python -B verify_v5_1.py” for file integrity. Run “python -B disclosure_v5_1/reproduce_diagnostic.py --scratch ../diagnostic_fresh” for a fresh diagnostic; the scratch directory must be new and outside the extracted archive. Integrity checks do not execute scientific calculations. Original numerical exceptions, failure records and previous-version metadata remain preserved. Publication-status clarification: this ZIP is deposited byte-for-byte as prepared before publication. The “local submission supplement”, “no new DOI” and null publication-identifier statements in README_v5_1.md, release_metadata_v5_1.json and the two ADDENDUM_v5_1 files record that preparation-time state. This Zenodo version publishes those identical v5.1 bytes and supersedes only that historical publication-status wording. The version-5 DOI above continues to identify the earlier numerical baseline; the DOI assigned to this record identifies this version-5.1 archive. The record’s current access and publication state are authoritative. Scope: finite synthetic computational assessment under a phenomenological scalar loss index, a lossless battery and reduced oxygen dynamics. No measured vessel dataset, physical stack-aging validation, hardware qualification or universal grade claim is supplied. Manuscripts, response letters and third-party full papers or standards are excluded; included PDF files are first-party computational figures and overviews. License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.
title: Reproducibility package for Feasibility and Portability of Model-Based Duty-Cycle Grades for Marine Fuel Cells

This complete archive contains executable Python sources, synthetic inputs, frozen computational protocols, numerical tables, selected actual simulated waveforms, first-party figures, provenance and independent numerical checks. It preserves all 827 files of the version-5 numerical baseline at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24037253 and adds 16 disclosure and verification files. No scientific model, input, physical threshold, representative selection or original numerical result is changed. New in v5.1: - Complete five-setting, eight-seed stationary non-Gaussian diagnostic results for 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1 Hz plus exact identity transfer, with signed prediction-error means and seed ranges for both telegraph processes and their phase-randomized controls. At 0.01 Hz, the symmetric and asymmetric telegraph mean errors are +94.2606% and +120.1515%. These separate periodic distribution tests are counterexamples to a general Gaussian absolute-increment accuracy claim, not error bounds for physically screened voyages or estimates of physical aging error. - Explicit calculation conventions: 131,072 samples at 4 Hz, the ideal continuous transfer on the periodic Fourier grid, all circular one-second increments at a 0.25-second stride, and no final voyage-reporting Butterworth filter. The final constrained grades continue to use directly evaluated voyage increments and dwell times. - A fresh isolated execution of the unchanged diagnostic. Its 160 raw rows, 20 summary rows and metadata matched the baseline byte for byte; independent reaggregation from the raw moments had a maximum discrepancy of 1.11e-16 in fractional prediction error. - Clarified field-evidence wording: MS Mariella supports ferry installation and ship-network commissioning tests; the separate Pa-X-ell land-module aging observation is not an at-sea aging slope. - Explicit remaining limitations: universal single-coordinate EMS sufficiency and measured aging equivalence are not established; compatible empirical marine coefficient calibration, confidence intervals and covariance are unavailable; the original PLECS project remains unavailable, and no new OpenModelica/PLECS execution has been performed. Start with README_v5_1.md and ADDENDUM_v5_1_EN.md or ADDENDUM_v5_1_KO.md. Run “python -B verify_v5_1.py” for file integrity. Run “python -B disclosure_v5_1/reproduce_diagnostic.py --scratch ../diagnostic_fresh” for a fresh diagnostic; the scratch directory must be new and outside the extracted archive. Integrity checks do not execute scientific calculations. Original numerical exceptions, failure records and previous-version metadata remain preserved. Publication-status clarification: this ZIP is deposited byte-for-byte as prepared before publication. The “local submission supplement”, “no new DOI” and null publication-identifier statements in README_v5_1.md, release_metadata_v5_1.json and the two ADDENDUM_v5_1 files record that preparation-time state. This Zenodo version publishes those identical v5.1 bytes and supersedes only that historical publication-status wording. The version-5 DOI above continues to identify the earlier numerical baseline; the DOI assigned to this record identifies this version-5.1 archive. The record’s current access and publication state are authoritative. summary: This analysis examines how aggregation and evidence composition shape international comparisons of reported antimalarial treatment failure. Using 244 World Health Organization summaries from 69 countries and territories covering 2010 to 2019, descriptive comparisons assess treatment regimens, parasite species and geographical settings, supplemented by exploratory sample restrictions. The mean reported failure median was 1.87 percent, while 62.30 percent of summaries had zero medians. However, 33.55 percent of zero median summaries contained positive failure maxima, revealing heterogeneity concealed by central values. The ordering of two commonly used regimens reversed across seven country pairs aligned by species, follow up duration and reported study interval bounds. Regional differences persisted within a shared species and treatment category, although means and medians produced different geographical orderings. Restricting observations to summaries representing multiple studies reduced dispersion while preserving a zero median. These findings refine surveillance interpretation by distinguishing favourable central performance from consistency across contributing evidence. International reporting should present distributions, study coverage and comparable analytical groups together to support targeted investigation of elevated failure observations.

summary: This analysis examines whether national submarine cable provision distinguishes retained international connectivity under infrastructure disruption. Using a 2021 topology snapshot covering 173 countries and territories, 294 international cable systems and 1,262 landing records, it combines bipartite network modelling with exhaustive single cable removal and descriptive comparisons. Mean retention was 99.5917% among units with one cable and 99.9286% among those with two, while all units with at least three shared the same score. Landing diversity provided no consistent additional ordering within comparable redundancy categories. Only 21 of 294 removals fragmented connectivity, and five scenarios accounted for 48.17% of cumulative country pair losses. Shared connecting routes explain how multiple national connections can coexist with dependence on distant infrastructure. Geographical groups differed more in infrastructure provision than in retention. The contribution is a linked assessment of national protection and concentrated network consequences, refining interpretations that equate infrastructure quantity with functional independence. The evidence supports evaluating alternative connections against shared dependencies and reporting critical failure scenarios alongside average resilience scores.

summary: ABSTRACT Aim: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of intra-operative frozen section (FS) in the management of abdominal masses and to identify specific technical and interpretive pitfalls that lead to diagnostic discordance. Materials and Methods : This prospective study analyzed 50 cases of abdominal masses at a tertiary care hospital over a two-year period. Intra-operative samples were processed using a cryostat at -20°C to -25°C, stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin, and reported within 30–45 minutes. The FS diagnoses were categorized as benign, malignant, or suspicious and subsequently compared with the gold standard paraffin-embedded sections (PS). Statistical parameters, including sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values, were calculated. Results: Of the 50 cases, 29 (58%) were malignant and 21 (42%) were benign. The gallbladder was the most frequent site of involvement (40%), followed by ovarian and gastrointestinal lesions. FS demonstrated an overall diagnostic accuracy of 98%, with a sensitivity of 96.5% and a specificity of 100% for the detection of malignancy. One case of discordance was noted in a large, multi-loculated ovarian tumor, where a focal borderline component was under-diagnosed as benign on FS due to sampling limitations. The positive predictive value was 100%, and the negative predictive value was 95.4%. Conclusion : Intra-operative frozen section is a highly reliable diagnostic modality for abdominal masses, providing rapid and actionable results that directly influence surgical strategy. While it is nearly infallible for most solid malignancies, cautious interpretation and extensive sampling are required for complex cystic ovarian lesions to minimize the risk of underdiagnosis.   Keywords: Frozen section, intraoperative diagnosis, diagnostic accuracy, abdominal masses, histopathology

summary: This dataset provides the frozen derived bibliographic data, executable analysis code, verification tests, annual results and figures supporting a measurement audit of historical crossover claims in molecular-marker research (1960–2025). It integrates 155,834 eligible work–marker associations, 33 related baseline and exact single-label-omission annual series, and the descriptive finite-panel critical margin frontier F(t). The annual minimum identifies the limiting specification and its year-specific eligible-work population; it is not a trajectory from one unchanged cohort. The package reproduces downstream analyses from frozen eligible records, including baseline persistence, SNP-removal sensitivity, full one-label-omission audits, reported marginal thresholds and Figures 1–3 and S1. It provides offline verification, file-level SHA-256 checksums, data documentation and source-archive provenance digests. The original full OpenAlex retrieval and historical v5 classifier configuration, independently adjudicated method-use labels and the earlier baseline v1.0.0 archive are not included. Accordingly, the results are conditional on archived classification decisions and do not establish validated dates of laboratory-method adoption, sampling confidence intervals or the performance of a reader-facing reporting intervention.

summary: This record contains the supplementary files of the systematic review "Sliding Mode Control of Quadrotor UAVs: A Systematic Review of Convergence Guarantees and Chattering Attenuation" (submitted to Aerospace Science and Technology). ESM_1_search_and_screening.zip - merged and de-duplicated record table (bibliographic data without abstracts), screening rules, every title/abstract screening decision with its reason code, the two validation samples, and the scripts used for de-duplication, screening and the statistics of the systematic map. ESM_2_extraction_sheet.xlsx - extraction sheet of the 2,358 studies of the systematic map, and the full-text evidence coding of the 57 studies selected for full-text analysis (44 included), with the passage on which each coded item is based, a codebook, the independent second coding of a random sample of 20 full texts and the consensus of all disagreements. ESM_3_benchmark_code_and_data.zip - MATLAB code and simulation data of the comparative benchmark of six sliding mode controllers on a 3DR Iris quadrotor model in six scenarios (including position tracking with a common outer loop), and the scripts that generate the figures. ESM_4_supplementary_table_and_note.pdf - Supplementary Tables S1-S3 (analysis of SMC-based controllers; Monte Carlo statistics; position-tracking metrics), Supplementary Figures S1-S3 and Supplementary Note S1 (control laws, gains, allocation and outer loop used in the benchmark). ESM_5_PRISMA_2020_checklist.pdf - completed PRISMA 2020 checklist.
tags: Sliding mode control; Quadrotor UAV; Systematic review; PRISMA; Fixed-time convergence; Arbitrary-time convergence; Chattering; Benchmark

summary: This analysis examines how adaptive computation configurations relate to classification accuracy in language models, informing international debates on computational efficiency. A descriptive reanalysis uses 20 published configuration results from Chinese Book review and English Yelp.P benchmarks reported in 2020, comparing routing arrangements, exit thresholds, and matched distillation settings. Adaptive routing exceeds selected fixed depth alternatives by 0.56 to 2.81 percentage points, with fewer operations in all three computationally usable comparisons. Raising exit thresholds reduces accuracy across both benchmarks, while endpoint computational reductions range from 62.77 to 77.87 percent among usable comparisons. Self-distillation improves accuracy in all four matched pairs, averaging 0.478 percentage points, with larger advantages for Book review. Accuracy losses concentrate differently across threshold intervals, indicating benchmark dependent stopping costs. These descriptive patterns distinguish selective processing, prediction acceptance, and intermediate supervision as complementary configuration decisions. The contribution refines the resource allocation perspective through transparent comparisons of existing evidence. Deployment teams should evaluate threshold intervals separately and compare accuracy alongside verified computational requirements within each intended task.

summary: This analysis examines whether privacy vulnerability rankings remain consistent across text reconstruction procedures, informing international debates on federated learning security. A descriptive secondary analysis uses 72 published benchmark conditions from 2024, covering three attacks, two transformer configurations, three text benchmarks and four batch sizes. Matched comparisons hold the remaining experimental dimensions constant. DAGER exceeds TAG and LAMP in all 24 matched conditions, with average advantages of 61.62 and 49.79 ROUGE 1 score points, respectively. LAMP exceeds TAG in 23 conditions. Increasing batch size from one to eight coincides with lower reconstruction throughout the TAG and LAMP comparisons, whereas DAGER retains ceiling performance on GPT 2 and deteriorates on BERT. Model rankings consequently reverse across attacks. These patterns indicate that aggregation constrains recoverability conditionally rather than providing uniform protection. The contribution is a comparative synthesis showing that observed vulnerability depends on reconstruction capability and model configuration, without establishing causal mechanisms. Organizations should evaluate multiple attacks under matched conditions and distinguish unigram recovery from comprehensive disclosure when interpreting privacy claims.
title: GRADIENT EXPOSURE CONDITIONS AND TEXT RECONSTRUCTION VULNERABILITY IN FEDERATED FOUNDATION MODELS ACROSS PUBLISHED BENCHMARK EXPERIMENTS

summary: Decentralised peacebuilding councils are widely promoted as a means of rebuilding citizen trust in post-conflict states, yet the evidence base for their effectiveness rests largely on observational comparisons that cannot separate the councils' effects from the selection of communities into them. Using a before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and a residual standard deviation of 4.5, the analysis estimates power across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design achieves 80 per cent power to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 56 clusters, a requirement that exceeds the number of municipal units typically available in a single Ivorian region. The regression-discontinuity approach is defensible in principle but fragile in practice, and that its value lies less in producing a definitive estimate than in disciplining claims about what decentralised peacebuilding can plausibly achieve.

summary: Version 5.1.0 reproducibility package for “Feasibility and Portability of Model-Based Duty-Cycle Grades for Marine Fuel Cells” by Eun-Hye Park, Hyo-Chan Kwon and Eun-Joo Park. This complete archive contains executable Python sources, synthetic inputs, frozen computational protocols, numerical tables, selected actual simulated waveforms, first-party figures, provenance and independent numerical checks. It preserves all 827 files of the version-5 numerical baseline at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24037253 and adds 16 disclosure and verification files. No scientific model, input, physical threshold, representative selection or original numerical result is changed. New in v5.1: - Complete five-setting, eight-seed stationary non-Gaussian diagnostic results for 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1 Hz plus exact identity transfer, with signed prediction-error means and seed ranges for both telegraph processes and their phase-randomized controls. At 0.01 Hz, the symmetric and asymmetric telegraph mean errors are +94.2606% and +120.1515%. These separate periodic distribution tests are counterexamples to a general Gaussian absolute-increment accuracy claim, not error bounds for physically screened voyages or estimates of physical aging error. - Explicit calculation conventions: 131,072 samples at 4 Hz, the ideal continuous transfer on the periodic Fourier grid, all circular one-second increments at a 0.25-second stride, and no final voyage-reporting Butterworth filter. The final constrained grades continue to use directly evaluated voyage increments and dwell times. - A fresh isolated execution of the unchanged diagnostic. summary: This analysis examines how aggregation and evidence composition shape international comparisons of reported antimalarial treatment failure. Using 244 World Health Organization summaries from 69 countries and territories covering 2010 to 2019, descriptive comparisons assess treatment regimens, parasite species and geographical settings, supplemented by exploratory sample restrictions. The mean reported failure median was 1.87 percent, while 62.30 percent of summaries had zero medians. However, 33.55 percent of zero median summaries contained positive failure maxima, revealing heterogeneity concealed by central values. The ordering of two commonly used regimens reversed across seven country pairs aligned by species, follow up duration and reported study interval bounds. Regional differences persisted within a shared species and treatment category, although means and medians produced different geographical orderings. Restricting observations to summaries representing multiple studies reduced dispersion while preserving a zero median. These findings refine surveillance interpretation by distinguishing favourable central performance from consistency across contributing evidence. International reporting should present distributions, study coverage and comparable analytical groups together to support targeted investigation of elevated failure observations.
title: ASSESSING ASSOCIATIONS BETWEEN ANTIMALARIAL TREATMENT REGIMENS, PARASITE SPECIES, REGIONAL SETTINGS, AND REPORTED MEDIAN TREATMENT FAILURE

summary: Supporting archive for the article Priced Exact Certification under Untrusted Advice: A Price-Induced Consistency Penalty (Zhizhen Zhao, School of Artificial Intelligence and Information Technology, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine). The article studies policies that buy exact fact-bits at declared per-fact prices, may use untrusted advice to decide what to probe, and must end in a mechanically checkable certificate. It proves that under heterogeneous prices, measured against the cheapest certificate of the realized outcome, requiring perfect consistency with correct advice can force worst-case robustness strictly above the optimal prediction-free ratio. This deposit holds the frozen protocol and the complete proofs, the analysis code, the formal checkers, the execution record and the SHA-256 manifests. One command reproduces the reported empirical result: python -I analysis/d9_recompute.py   It recomputes the weighted cost saving S_D9 = 0.070247 and its one-sided 97.5% lower confidence bound 0.044522 from the published ledger alone, and exits non-zero if either differs from the frozen value by more than 1e-9. The pre-registered claim of a saving of at least 10% was not supported. Contents: protocol/ the frozen protocol, theory freeze and complete theorem proofs; analysis/ the analysis code, the frozen result, the de-identified per-root cost ledger and the recompute script; checkers/ the self-contained formal checkers with their recorded output; execution/ the execution reports, the pinned environment and model, the pre-analysis gate and the amendment freezes; provenance/ the SHA-256 manifests of the frozen packages. MANIFEST.sha256 lists every file in the archive with its hash. What is not here. No raw LOTUS or TCM-MKG source tables are redistributed; both sources are public and pinned, TCM-MKG v3 at Zenodo record 19804367 and LOTUS v4 at Zenodo record 7534083. The cost ledger is de-identified: each formula identifier is replaced by an opaque label G01-G40 and the compound key is dropped, while the stratum, the two policy costs and the inclusion weight are carried over unchanged. Because the estimator never reads the identifier, this changes no computed quantity, which the recompute script demonstrates. The co-primary LLM-advice family was determined not validly evaluable under the frozen model, endpoint and protocol, so it has no result to deposit; the figures of the initial, later invalidated execution are not evidence and are absent in every form. Every empirical statement is source-relative: a recorded row establishes only what a frozen version of a public curated source records. No clinical claim is made or supported by anything in this archive. Licensed CC BY 4.0. This covers the content of this deposit only; upstream rights are recorded in protocol/PRISM_RIGHTS_ATTRIBUTION_v1.1.md .
title: PRISM: frozen protocol, analysis code and verification artifacts

summary: This dataset provides the frozen derived bibliographic data, executable analysis code, verification tests, annual results and figures supporting a measurement audit of historical crossover claims in molecular-marker research (1960–2025). It integrates 155,834 eligible work–marker associations, 33 related baseline and exact single-label-omission annual series, and the descriptive finite-panel critical margin frontier F(t). The annual minimum identifies the limiting specification and its year-specific eligible-work population; it is not a trajectory from one unchanged cohort. The package reproduces downstream analyses from frozen eligible records, including baseline persistence, SNP-removal sensitivity, full one-label-omission audits, reported marginal thresholds and Figures 1–3 and S1. It provides offline verification, file-level SHA-256 checksums, data documentation and source-archive provenance digests. The original full OpenAlex retrieval and historical v5 classifier configuration, independently adjudicated method-use labels and the earlier baseline v1.0.0 archive are not included. Accordingly, the results are conditional on archived classification decisions and do not establish validated dates of laboratory-method adoption, sampling confidence intervals or the performance of a reader-facing reporting intervention.

summary: This analysis examines whether privacy vulnerability rankings remain consistent across text reconstruction procedures, informing international debates on federated learning security. A descriptive secondary analysis uses 72 published benchmark conditions from 2024, covering three attacks, two transformer configurations, three text benchmarks and four batch sizes. Matched comparisons hold the remaining experimental dimensions constant. DAGER exceeds TAG and LAMP in all 24 matched conditions, with average advantages of 61.62 and 49.79 ROUGE 1 score points, respectively. LAMP exceeds TAG in 23 conditions. Increasing batch size from one to eight coincides with lower reconstruction throughout the TAG and LAMP comparisons, whereas DAGER retains ceiling performance on GPT 2 and deteriorates on BERT. Model rankings consequently reverse across attacks. These patterns indicate that aggregation constrains recoverability conditionally rather than providing uniform protection. The contribution is a comparative synthesis showing that observed vulnerability depends on reconstruction capability and model configuration, without establishing causal mechanisms. Organizations should evaluate multiple attacks under matched conditions and distinguish unigram recovery from comprehensive disclosure when interpreting privacy claims.
title: GRADIENT EXPOSURE CONDITIONS AND TEXT RECONSTRUCTION VULNERABILITY IN FEDERATED FOUNDATION MODELS ACROSS PUBLISHED BENCHMARK EXPERIMENTS

summary: Version 1.1.0 — frozen public dataset, 8 November 2026. This release contains 5,154 bibliographic and clinical-trial registry records concerning psilocybin and psilocin, with recorded years 1958–2026. The source snapshot was generated on 8 November 2026 at 02:26:01 UTC. The compilation combines public metadata from PubMed, Europe PMC, Crossref, OpenAlex, ClinicalTrials.gov, bioRxiv, medRxiv and PsyArXiv. It contains 4,377 published records, 463 preprints, 311 clinical-trial records and 3 protocols. Persistent identifiers, source links, publication status and derived annotations are retained. Files and reproducibility The archive includes public SQLite and losslessly compressed SQLite, RDS data frames, CSV, JSON, BibTeX, RIS and LaTeX citation exports, compact projections, annual statistics and a deliberately partial reviewed study-family map. Documentation includes a field dictionary, rights statements, version-specific citation metadata, exact snapshot provenance and SHA-256 checksums. Python validation and a base-R reproduction example are supplied, with technical validation results, an annual-count figure and R session information. SQLite integrity, public-only table scope, record-ID agreement across SQLite/CSV/JSON, annual totals, artifact hashes and exclusion of redistributed abstracts were checked. The RDS file was opened and checked using R. These are technical checks, not a new independent external coverage audit. Records are not independent studies or participants; multiple records can describe the same study. Topic and study-type labels require verification against original sources. The current year is incomplete. Version history This release supersedes v1.0.6 for new use, with a net increase of 336 records. Version 1.0.6 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21333043 ) and its historical validation materials remain unchanged and available for reproducing earlier analyses. No manuscript files are included. The dataset update does not assert that the deployed website corresponds to a particular tagged software release. Rights and scope Source-derived abstracts, registry descriptions, keywords, unrestricted importer payloads, full texts, private user data and account implementation are excluded. CC BY 4.0 applies only to compiler-held rights in the selection and arrangement, normalization, original annotations, validation outputs and documentation. Third-party bibliographic fields remain subject to applicable upstream rights and terms. Included original code is MIT licensed; see the archive's separate rights and licence files. Live access and analysis Project website · Dataset guide · Public software and methods The open webR analysis workspace supports custom browser-side R analyses and PDF, complete LaTeX source, R, CSV and PNG downloads without sign-in. Accounts add private online saving and cross-device access. Its default data follow the living index and may differ from this frozen archive: retain the snapshot actually analysed and cite the exact dataset version used. Historical infrastructure support The infrastructure was initially developed with support from the European Union's Seventh Framework Programme (FP7/2007–2013), through the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Initial Training Network CogNovo, grant agreement No. 604764. Quick start in R After extracting the archive, run x <- readRDS("data/publications.rds") and records <- x$publications . The README provides validation and reproduction commands. Cite this version using DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24051198 ; the all-versions DOI is 10.5281/zenodo.21293525 .

summary: Complete research archive for the study of natural-product label errors in ChEMBL CYP inhibition data: the input extract, the curation files, every intermediate result, and the analysis scripts that produced the figures and tables in the article and its supporting information. The study examines a natural-product flag inherited from COCONUT through ChEMBL, across 14,598 compound-isoform IC50 pairs for 9,347 compounds. Of 500 compounds carrying the flag, 138 (27.6%) were excluded by a criterion combining absent provenance in LOTUS with a synthetic structural signature, together with review of the compounds that criterion retained. The excluded compounds were disproportionately potent inhibitors, and the association survives adjustment for molecular size, testing intensity, aromatic ring count and an independent natural-product-likeness score for the compounds identified individually from structure. Version 1.2.0 adds the material prepared for the first revision. The curation criterion is now validated in both directions against external standards. Against the Natural Products Atlas (version 2024_09), 36,453 compounds curated by hand from the primary isolation literature and independent of both resources the criterion uses, the full rule removes 262: a false-positive rate of 0.72% (95% CI 0.64-0.81%). In a random sample of 50 of the 362 retained compounds, classified independently by two of the authors, 20 are fully synthetic: a false-negative rate of 40% (95% CI 28-54%), with inter-rater agreement of Cohen's kappa 0.83 (0.69-0.96) over four origin classes and 0.92 (0.79-1.00) on the binary question. Because the two rates differ by roughly fifty-fold, the 27.6% is a floor on the mislabeling rate in this dataset rather than an estimate of it. This version also adds a twenty-four-setting sensitivity sweep of the criterion, calibration of the predicted probabilities against the training base rate, the per-isoform decomposition of the curation effect into removal and retraining, the potency association under four compound-level aggregations, and a covariate for how often each compound has been studied. Contents   01_input      the activity extract, with assay and document identifiers   02_curation   the curation files, including the exclusion list   03_results    the results, with the revision outputs in a dated subfolder   04_scripts    the analysis scripts, with the revision scripts in a dated                 subfolder   05_audit      the two-rater origin audit behind Table S17   06_external_tools  the ADMETlab 3.0 and pkCSM reports for the three compounds                 in Table 4 Source data are from ChEMBL 37 (doi:10.6019/CHEMBL.database.37). Two third-party datasets used by the analysis are not redistributed here, each being available from its own archive: the LOTUS frozen dataset used for provenance cross-referencing (doi:10.5281/zenodo.19360665, v11), and the Natural Products Atlas release used for the specificity test added in this version (version 2024_09, 36,453 compounds, MD5 10fd08163f5cda420e104dc21246db4f, from https://www.npatlas.org/download). The revision README records the version and checksum so that a reader can download the Atlas file and confirm they have the one used here. Most revision scripts assert their anchor figures before writing anything: the sweep checks that the published rule excludes 119 compounds, the aggregation and covariate analyses check that the crude odds ratio is 2.47 and the adjusted 1.84, and the supporting-table builders check that every previously published cell reproduces. If an input changes they stop rather than write a table that disagrees with the article. Of 500 compounds carrying the flag, 138 (27.6%) were excluded by a criterion combining absent provenance in LOTUS with a synthetic structural signature, together with review of the compounds that criterion retained. The excluded compounds were disproportionately potent inhibitors, and the association survives adjustment for molecular size, testing intensity, aromatic ring count and an independent natural-product-likeness score for the compounds identified individually from structure. Version 1.2.0 adds the material prepared for the first revision. The curation criterion is now validated in both directions against external standards. Against the Natural Products Atlas (version 2024_09), 36,453 compounds curated by hand from the primary isolation literature and independent of both resources the criterion uses, the full rule removes 262: a false-positive rate of 0.72% (95% CI 0.64-0.81%). In a random sample of 50 of the 362 retained compounds, classified independently by two of the authors, 20 are fully synthetic: a false-negative rate of 40% (95% CI 28-54%), with inter-rater agreement of Cohen's kappa 0.83 (0.69-0.96) over four origin classes and 0.92 (0.79-1.00) on the binary question. Because the two rates differ by roughly fifty-fold, the 27.6% is a floor on the mislabeling rate in this dataset rather than an estimate of it. This version also adds a twenty-four-setting sensitivity sweep of the criterion, calibration of the predicted probabilities against the training base rate, the per-isoform decomposition of the curation effect into removal and retraining, the potency association under four compound-level aggregations, and a covariate for how often each compound has been studied. summary: I study an inverse problem for one-dimensional Brownian-compatible diffusions in which multiple probe responses are observed with independent, unknown multiplicative gains. The central question is whether the shared differential structure of the underlying generator can replace external gain calibration. For a diffusion generator Lq f = q(θ)f ′′(θ) + 1 2 q′(θ)f ′(θ), q > 0, the response to each prescribed probe is available only up to an unknown positive gain. I first estab- lish that a single nonconstant Morse probe uniquely and coercively identifies its gain-weighted dif- fusion coefficient. I then show that two nondegenerate probes determine their relative gain through a scalar compatibility relation implied by the Brownian drift–diffusion constraint. This yields an explicit reconstruction of the diffusion profile up to its unavoidable common scale, represented by a normalized inverse-square-root profile. Under quantitative nondegeneracy assumptions, the recon- structed profile depends locally Lipschitz-continuously on the observations. Numerical experiments illustrate the reconstruction procedure and its behavior under smooth response perturbations. I also describe a conditional connection with planar convex geometry. The results provide a generator-specific mechanism for blind relative-gain calibration and projective identification from probe-response functions without trajectory observations

summary: Reproduction materials for the manuscript “Certifying route decisions under uncertain spatial support of road reports” by Hailong Li and Ya Li. Archive version v38.1 accompanies manuscript version 38. This update sets the author order to Hailong Li, Ya Li and updates the citation and contact metadata. The computational reproduction archive is identical to that in v38. The archive contains the analysis code, derived historical road graph, spatial-support records, scenario inputs, saved results and figure/table sources. It includes the 100-clause report sample, coding protocol, two independent human annotations, pre-adjudication agreement, AI-assisted adjudication records and frozen final labels. The README links manuscript tables and figures to their reproduction commands, and a SHA-256 manifest verifies the packaged files. The experiments examine how mapping a road report to a retained section, a whole road or a point buffer changes route certificates and maximum regret under uncertain dependence. Current held-out results use 28 mapped assertions from 89 retained assertions. Across comparison–task instances, expansion adds 72 certificates and removes none; point buffers remove 110 relative to whole-road references. Historical OpenStreetMap-derived data are © OpenStreetMap contributors and remain subject to the Open Database License (ODbL). Source-text excerpts retain their original rights. The full upstream text corpora are linked through pinned repositories in the provenance manifest and are not included in this deposit. The record license applies to the authors’ original contributions only and does not replace third-party terms. Authors are affiliated with Zhengzhou Railway Vocational and Technical University. Corresponding author: Hailong Li, 11172@zzrvtc.edu.cn. Ya Li: 10917@zzrvtc.edu.cn. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. summary: This analysis examines whether scientific abstract characteristics distinguish supporting from refuting evidence, addressing the interpretation of document presentation in scientific verification. Using the 2020 SciFact benchmark, it analyses 773 annotated claim document pairs covering 693 claims and 437 abstracts through descriptive comparisons, document weighting and partition sensitivity checks. Refuting pairs contain abstracts averaging 32.46 words longer than supporting pairs. The refuting share is 14.1 percentage points higher among structured abstracts, while mean relative evidence position differs by only 0.007. Equal document weighting preserves these pooled directions, but length and structure differences narrow substantially in the development partition. Furthermore, 179 abstracts support some claims and refute others despite unchanged document characteristics. These findings distinguish document presentation from the semantic relationship between evidence and a specific claim. The contribution is a descriptive account of how pooled presentation patterns coexist with partition sensitivity and claim dependent stance. Evidence services and benchmark developers should preserve claim specific provenance and disclose document overlap and weighting choices when reporting aggregate comparisons.

summary: The article addresses the problem of improving the technical preparedness of 13–15-year-old female volleyball players through a differentiated training approach. The relevance of the study is determined by the fact that athletes of the same chronological age may differ considerably in biological maturation, anthropometric characteristics, coordination abilities, physical fitness, rate of motor skill acquisition, and the structure of technical errors. Therefore, the use of identical training loads and technical tasks for all adolescent players may reduce the effectiveness of technical preparation. The study substantiates a methodological system based on the sequence diagnostics → differentiated grouping → adapted technical exercises → individualized feedback → control → correction. Particular attention is paid to the differentiation of exercise complexity, number of repetitions, distance, speed, time pressure, and game-related decision-making requirements. The proposed methodology is aimed at improving technical accuracy, stability, movement coordination, application of technical actions under game conditions, and reducing recurrent technical errors. The article also describes criteria for evaluating technical preparedness and offers a weekly microcycle for differentiated volleyball training.

summary: Analysis code archive for the paper: Sakahira, F., Horiuchi, A., Kubota, S., Sun, G., Wang, Y., Miyata, Y. “Visible and absorbed residues remain distinct in the archaeological record: statistical evidence from untargeted GC–MS fingerprinting of pottery from the Jingtoushan site, China.” This archive contains the complete preprocessing and statistics code used in the paper, all parameters (Supplementary Table S1), and a worked example on simulated data so that the whole pipeline can be run and verified without the measurement data. Contents: archaeolipid_pipeline.py — the full pipeline (RAW→mzML conversion, baseline removal, interfering-ion exclusion, peak detection and integration, anchor-based retention-time alignment, feature-table construction with gap filling, normalization, batch diagnosis, clustering, PERMANOVA, cross-site retention indexing) jts_paper_statistics.py — reproduces every statistical result reported in the paper (batch diagnosis; clustering and Fisher’s exact test; the six single-factor PERMANOVA tests of Table 2; PERMDISP-type dispersion check; within-vessel pair distances) with 99,999 permutations and a fixed random seed example/run_simulated_example.py — end-to-end worked example on simulated data (no measurement data required) params/parameters_S1.csv — machine-readable copy of Supplementary Table S1 scripts_original/, docs/ — the original analysis script and pipeline usage notes, archived as used Data policy: following the paper’s Data availability statement, the raw GC–MS data and the derived feature tables are not included; they are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Requirements: Python ≥ 3.10 with numpy, scipy, matplotlib, pymzml. License: MIT.
title: archaeolipid-jts: untargeted GC–MS fingerprinting pipeline for archaeological pottery lipid residues (Jingtoushan analysis code)

summary: Analysis code archive for the paper: Sakahira, F., Horiuchi, A., Kubota, S., Sun, G., Wang, Y., Miyata, Y. “Visible and absorbed residues remain distinct in the archaeological record: statistical evidence from untargeted GC–MS fingerprinting of pottery from the Jingtoushan site, China.” This archive contains the complete preprocessing and statistics code used in the paper, all parameters (Supplementary Table S1), and a worked example on simulated data so that the whole pipeline can be run and verified without the measurement data. Contents: archaeolipid_pipeline.py — the full pipeline (RAW→mzML conversion, baseline removal, interfering-ion exclusion, peak detection and integration, anchor-based retention-time alignment, feature-table construction with gap filling, normalization, batch diagnosis, clustering, PERMANOVA, cross-site retention indexing) jts_paper_statistics.py — reproduces every statistical result reported in the paper (batch diagnosis; clustering and Fisher’s exact test; the six single-factor PERMANOVA tests of Table 2; PERMDISP-type dispersion check; within-vessel pair distances) with 99,999 permutations and a fixed random seed example/run_simulated_example.py — end-to-end worked example on simulated data (no measurement data required) params/parameters_S1.csv — machine-readable copy of Supplementary Table S1 scripts_original/, docs/ — the original analysis script and pipeline usage notes, archived as used Data policy: following the paper’s Data availability statement, the raw GC–MS data and the derived feature tables are not included; they are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Requirements: Python ≥ 3.10 with numpy, scipy, matplotlib, pymzml. License: MIT.

summary: Figure 2 Circular maps representing the complete mitochondrial genome structural architecture of three Mudaria species generated via Proksee. The maps illustrate the organization and transcription direction of 37 mitochondrial genes, including 13 protein-coding genes, 22 tRNA genes, and two rRNA genes. The directional rings display the forward and reverse gene transcription layout (outermost), GC content variance (middle), and GC-skew asymmetry parameters (innermost).
